News.title: Leicester church fire LIVE: Huge flames take hold of historic building
News.content:
A major fire has taken hold of a church in Leicester

Firefighters are tackling the blaze at the church in the city centre as local residents have been warned to close all doors and windows as thick smoke fills the sky

A UK city centre church is in flames as huge clouds of smoke fill the sky.

St Andrews Church in Leicester is reportedly alight on Wednesday morning.

The building on Jarrom Street is ablaze with fire crews rushing to the scene to tackle the bright red flames and control the thick smoke.

A spokesperson for Leicestershire Fire and Rescue Control said: "There is an incident on Jarrom Street in Leicester City, this is sending smoke over the city. Please keep windows and doors closed!"

This is a live news story, follow below for further updates.

News.title: M1 traffic LIVE: Busy motorway closed near Luton airport after 'oil spill'
News.content:
Police have closed the motorway near Luton following the incident, which involved multiple vehicles and has created an oil spill which requires specialist clean up

Police have closed part of the M1 near Luton after a huge multi-vehicle crash caused an oil spillage.

The southbound side of the motorway has been closed between junctions 11 (Luton) and 11A (Chalton) after the crash, which took place at around 8.45pm. Initially, National Highways closed junctions 11 to 12 on the southbound carriageway, but this has been revised.

National Highways believes an HGV has 'overturned'. It said in its update: "One of the HGVs involved has overturned and come to rest on its side. There is also significant damage to the nearside barrier and boundary fencing, along with a substantial oil spillage across most lanes.

"Traffic that was caught within the closure has now been released past the scene via lane 4.

"Bedfordshire Police and other emergency services remain in attendance. National Highways Traffic Officers are also on scene assisting with traffic management.

"The carriageway will remain closed while emergency services complete their response, followed by vehicle recovery, barrier repairs and carriageway clean-up."

The incident took place only a few miles from Luton Airport, which is open as normal. A diversion has been created for motorists as the motorway is expected to be closed for some time.

News.title: Joe Biden 'secret' audio recordings show heated Obama conversation during presidency
News.content:
Joe Biden 'secret' audio recordings show heated Obama conversation during presidency

Joe Biden served as the vice president of the US under Barack Obama from January 20, 2009, to January 20, 2017 and later served as president from January 20, 2021 to January 20, 2025

View 3 Images Joe Biden and Barack Obama (file image) (Image: Getty Images)

Audio recordings between a former US president Joe Biden and his ghostwriter have been released.

‌



The release on Monday, July 27 comes after a lengthy court battle after the conservative Oversight Project sued the Justice Department. The former US leader had fought to keep the recordings private before abandoning his legal challenge.

‌



The content of the recordings appears broadly consistent with findings that Mr Biden retained classified material after leaving the vice presidency and offer a snippet into his experience working under former US president Barack Obama.

‌



Mr Biden served as the vice president of the US under Mr Obama January 20, 2009, to January 20, 2017. He later went on to serve as the country's 46th president from January 20, 2021 to January 20, 2025.

View 3 Images Joe Biden and Barack Obama in 2013 (file image) (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

In the tapes, Mr Biden discusses notes from his time as vice president, while showing them to biographer Mark Lewis Zwonitzer.

‌



"They didn't even know I had this," Biden says while reportedly referring to handwritten notes he kept from his time in office. Parts of the discussion are redacted because they relate to allegedly classified foreign policy matters.

Mr Biden abruptly stops himself at another point.

"And then — and then the next thing I have here is — this is classified," he said.

‌



The recordings also the details of a tension point between Mr Biden and Mr Obama.

Mr Biden says Mr Obama would "really get p***ed" at him during arguments over how aggressively the administration should respond to the 2008 financial crisis.

"I was a really lonely voice on housing, I was a lonely voice on the middle class. I mean, I thought we should be much more aggressive than putting these guys in jail and the bankers," he says.

‌



"I mean, he used to really get p***ed at me."

View 3 Images Former US presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden (file image) (Image: (Photo by Mark Makela/Getty Images))

The recordings also revisit Mr Biden's decision not to challenge Hillary Clinton for the Democratic nomination in 2016.

Article continues below

He recalled Mr Obama telling him the decision was ultimately his own, but warning it would be "really be an uphill battle."

"The fact is that he didn't think it was doable at that time, that I could, that I could actually go out and get the nomination," Biden said.

"That was my read at the time."

News.title: Japan earthquake live: Dozens still missing as search for survivors continues overnight
News.content:
Multiple people have died while more are missing after a shopping centre collapsed following a huge 7.1 magnitude earthquake on the Japanese island of Kyushu

Dozens of people are still reported missing following the horror collapse of a shopping mall in Japan that caused 'many fatalities' after being struck by a powerful earthquake.

Up to 30 others remain missing at the Aeon Mall in Kumamoto, while employees are also missing at the nearby Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro Plant. Several people travelling in a high speed train were also injured after a chimney stack from the paper company fell on them during the quake, local media reports.

“People are coming in with burns and fractures from being trapped under objects due to the earthquake, and ambulances are constantly bringing in injured people,” a hospital employee told national broadcaster NHK.

“Inside the hospital, there are water leaks and electrical system failures,” they added.

The massive quake measured at the highest possible level seven on Japan's own Shindo "scale of shaking" and has left tens of thousands without power. Kumamoto Airport has been closed indefinitely after the earthquake rocked its runway.

Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that left more than 50 people dead, 1,800 injured and tens of thousands of homes damaged or destroyed.

News.title: France wildfires live: 184 arsonists arrested as 'all regions' at risk of further fires
News.content:
Flames are nearing the French Atlantic Coast with raging wildfires now nine miles from Bordeaux as the city's mayor says he's prepared for 'all eventualities'

All regions of France are potentially at risk of wildfires tomorrow as the country grapples with what President Macron has claimed is the "most difficult situation" his country has dealt with since World War Two.

“We are facing two particularly critical days, with the heatwave and the very dry forest,” Gironde mayor Blandine Sarrazin. told local media. "This is the third fire to start here in the last two and a half days, it's really difficult," she added, telling residents it was not yet safe to return home.

Holidaymakers have been forced to leave campsites, tourist homes, holiday villages and leisure parks around Lacanau, which is around 40 miles from Bordeaux. The order comes as firefighters race against time to bring the fires under control before the country's south-west is blasted by a forecast 40C heatwave tomorrow (Wednesday).

Officials say the largest blaze has "stabilised" but have warned it could still burn out of control again as temperatures rise and humidity falls.

But a number of additional fires continue to burn with no end in sight, as local officials warn that the inferno could continue for months before it is fully contained.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nunez claimed wildfire season is "far from over," and said authorities have arrested 1 84 suspected arsonists since the start of the summer.

Meanwhile in Spain, 63,000 people have been evacuate from their homes near Madrid, with the country's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez calling it "the most painful expression of the climate emergency".

News.title: Woman found dead at remote cottage in Renfrewshire was murdered, police say
News.content:
Woman found dead at remote cottage in Renfrewshire was murdered, police say

Stacy Mair, 35, was found dead at a remote cottage in Renfrewshire by emergency services after reports of concern for a person on Monday morning - police are now treating it as murder

View 3 Images Stacy Mair, who was found deceased on Monday at around 7.50am in the Corsliehill Road area of Houston (Image: Family Handout/PA Wire)

Police are treating the death of a woman found in a remote cottage as murder, while the death of a man at the scene is being treated as "unexplained".

‌



The body of 35-year-old Stacy Mair and a 43-year-old man were discovered by emergency services at Corsliehill Road in Houston, Johnstone on Monday morning, July 27, following reports of a concern for a person.

‌



Police Scotland initially said the deaths were being treated as unexplained, but they have now confirmed they believe Stacy may have been murdered. A post-mortem will be carried out to establish the exact cause of death in due course.

‌



View 3 Images Police officers near to the scene in Houston, Johnstone, Renfrewshire (Image: Ryan McDougall/PA Wire)

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Death of 35-year-old Stacy Mair in Houston being treated as murder. Around 7.50am on Monday, 27 July, 2026, we received a report of concern for a person in the Corsliehill Road area of Houston.

"Emergency services attended, and the bodies of a woman and a man were found nearby. Following a post-mortem examination today, the death of 35-year-old Stacy Mair is being treated as murder.

‌



"The death of the 43-year-old man continues to be treated as unexplained pending the results of a post-mortem examination, which will take place in due course. Detectives from Police Scotland's Major Investigation Team, as well as officers from the local policing division, continue to carry out extensive enquiries to establish the full circumstances.

"At this time, there is nothing to suggest anyone else is involved or any risk to the public."

Detective Chief Inspector Laura Young, of the Major Investigation Team, said: "Our thoughts remain with the families of those affected by this incident. They are understandably devastated, and we are providing them with support through specialist officers at this incredibly difficult time."

‌



View 3 Images The bodies of a man and a woman have been found in what police have described as "unexplained" circumstances (Image: Ryan McDougall/PA Wire)

Chief Inspector Iain Farmer said: "This is a deeply upsetting incident for the families involved, and the impact is felt right across the local community. I am grateful for the support we have received as we complete our essential enquires to ensure the families and local residents get the answers they need.”

"Anyone with concerns or information can contact Police Scotland via 101."

‌



Photos taken by the Record at the scene on Tuesday show multiple police vehicles parked outside a property in Houston and a nearby road. Officers can be seen by the cottage where vans are also stationed in an adjacent field as well as scouring nearby woodland.

The home sits on the main road, with another similar style of property situated just a few hundred yards away.

Corsliehill Road is a narrow rural lane surrounded by farmland and a handful of isolated properties, with little passing traffic. Reports suggest a significant emergency services response was seen in the area with a police helicopter also present on Monday.

Article continues below

The Scottish Ambulance Service has confirmed it received a call at 8.33am and sent four special operations response teams, two ambulances and a critical care team to the scene. A Scottish Ambulance Service spokesperson said: “We received a call at 08.33 to attend an incident on Barochan Road, Houston, Johnstone. Four special operations response teams (SORT), two ambulances and one critical care team were dispatched to the scene.”

News.title: Death row inmate's chilling last two words before double execution in Florida
News.content:
Death row inmate's chilling last two words before double execution in Florida

James Aren Duckett, 68, was confirmed dead early on Tuesday in the wake of a lethal injection cocktail of three drugs at Florida state prison near Starke

View 3 Images James Aren Duckett has now been put to death (Image: Florida Department of Corrections)

A former policeman has been put to death, nearly 40 years after he raped and murdered 11-year-old Teresa McAbee while he was working as an officer in central Florida in 1987. James Aren Duckett, 68, was confirmed dead early on Tuesday in the wake of a lethal injection cocktail of three drugs at Florida state prison near Starke. Duckett is the 11th inmate to be executed by the state in 2026. When asked, he declined to make a final statement and instead chose to respond with “no sir” when asked.

Four minutes later, he was shaken by a prison warden who also shouted Duckett's name, but the rapist and murderer was unresponsive.

View 3 Images Florida State Prison (Image: Douglas R Clifford/Tampa Bay Times/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Hours later, the State of Florida then went on to execute 80-year-old Dominick Occhicone tonight at Florida State Prison, completing the state’s first same-day double execution in over 60 years following the noon execution of Duckett.

Florida has now also put to death its second man in one day for the 1986 double murder of Raymond and Martha Artzner, the parents of his ex-girlfriend, Anita Gerrety.

At around 3am on June 10, 1986, Occhicone knocked on the door of his ex’s parents' Pasco County home. As per court records, he wished to rekindle their relationship, court records show. He left when Anita threatened to call the sheriff.

He returned an hour later and this time, he came with lethal intent. Anita’s father Raymond tried to call the sheriff's office, but the phone line had been cut at the junction box, prosecutors said.

Occhicone then shot Anita’s father Raymond in the face. As per the Herald-Tribune, Occhicone then broke through a locked door and chased his ex through the house, but she was able to get outside with her daughter, she later testified.

She heard gunshots ring out behind her and her mother, Martha Artzner, was later found dead.

Raymond Artzner lived long enough to tell deputies who shot him but died at the hospital, prosecutors said. Occhicone did not deny the evidence later in court, but argued the shootings were not premeditated. He was not believed by a jury of his peers, and has been on death row ever since.

But now, 40 years after the brutal revenge slaying of his ex’s parents, Occhicone’s execution has finally gone ahead after forward after the Florida Supreme Court unanimously rejected all of his final appeals earlier on in the week.

Occhicone therefore became the oldest person executed in modern history in Florida and the second-oldest put to death in the US after the 2018 execution of Walter Moody, who was executed at age 83.

View 3 Images Dominick Anthony Occhicone is dead by lethal injection (Image: Florida Department of Correction)

Occhicone’s death came six hours after the execution of 68-year-old Duckett at noon.

The double executions day is Florida's first since 1964, when Blake Emmett and Dawson Sie were both executed in the electric chair. The last time any state carried out two executions in one day was back in 2017, when Arkansas held back-to-back executions.

Article continues below

Florida’s Republican governor Ron DeSantis has made his state’s death chamber the busiest in the US as the end of his final term approaches. DeSantis has previously said too many families have waited too long to see justice, hence the uptick in lethal injections. Nationwide, the death penalty had been on the decline for more than 20 years. That number has now tracked back upwards behind the increased pace set in Florida. Since 2025, Florida has carried out nearly half the state executions across the US.

News.title: More than 200 wildfires across England and Wales in 12 days as 'risk remains elevated across UK'
News.content:
More than 200 wildfires across England and Wales in 12 days as 'risk remains elevated across UK'

More than 700 wildfires have so far been recorded this year across England and Wales, with the figures not accounting for blazes such as the one in Cairngorms, Scotland

View 3 Images Firefighters in Derbyshire continue to make progress at a major wildfire at Tintwistle Moor (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The risk of wildfires "remains elevated across the UK" as more than 200 incidents have been recorded in the last 12 days.

‌



If fires started in London, the South East or East of England during the heatwave, the blazes could be exceptionally severe due to the hot, dry conditions. An amber heat-health alert has been issued again by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) covering the East Midlands, the East and South East of England and London.

‌



The warning came into force today and will stay in place until Thursday, with the hot temperatures posing a threat to health risks, particularly for those in vulnerable age groups like the elderly. A total of 706 wildfires were reported to fire and rescue services across England and Wales so far this year.

‌



Of those, 208 incidents were recorded in less than a fortnight, between July 16 and 28, the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) said. The figures, however, do not account for wildfires across Scotland and Northern Ireland.

View 3 Images The fire burning through the Cairngorms national park in northern Scotland (Image: RSPB Scotland/AFP via Getty Images)

This means blazes like the one in Cairngorms in Scotland, which firefighters have been battling for two weeks now, were not included in the statistics. The incident, which saw families being ordered to leave their homes, shows "how quickly wildfire activity can increase during prolonged periods of hot and dry weather".

‌



Fire chiefs warned that wildfire risks "remains elevated across the UK", as NFCC explained eight live wildfire incidents are currently being monitored. Firefighters in Derbyshire continue to "make progress at the major wildfire incident at Tintwistle Moor", where 60 crew members were sent today.

Still, figures across England and Wales remain lower than the 788 recorded by this time last year. However, NFCC warned that "continued dry conditions, combined with warmer temperatures and harvesting activity in many rural areas" were creating conditions in which fires can start and spread rapidly.

Images showed widespread brown grass across Blackheath in London, with parched dry grass present in many parks in the capital following the hot weather. It comes as Royal Parks staff were advised not to leave deckchairs under trees over fears branches will fall during hot weather.

‌



View 3 Images A French Civil Security aircraft flying over an area affected by a fire at Camp de Souge Martignas-sur-Jalle, near Bordeaux (Image: SDIS33/MATTHIEU PENZ HANDOUT/EPA/Shutterstock)

Countries across Europe are also burning as large-scale wildfires have hit parts of Spain, France, Greece and Italy. This led to evacuations and significant damage, along with sustained pressure on emergency services, who are now struggling to fight the enormity of the fires.

The NFCC said UK wildfires are typically smaller and different in nature to those seen in southern Europe, adding, however, that the "long-term effects of climate change are increasing the likelihood of larger, more complex and more resource-intensive wildfire incidents occurring".

‌



Phil Garrigan, chairman of the NFCC, said: "More than 200 wildfires in just 12 days shows how quickly the risk can escalate when hot, dry conditions take hold. The scenes we’re seeing across parts of Europe are a stark reminder of what a changing climate means for fire and rescue services.

"We are not seeing fires of that scale in the UK today, but the science tells us we should expect larger, more frequent and more complex wildfires in the future. That’s why we need continued investment in specialist wildfire capabilities, including aerial firefighting support, so we’re prepared for the risks ahead.

"But prevention remains our strongest defence. Most wildfires are avoidable, and we’re asking everyone to take extra care during the hot weather to help keep their communities safe."

Article continues below

Fire chiefs said many wildfires are caused by everyday human activity, adding that "disposing of cigarettes safely, avoiding the use of disposable barbecues in open spaces and taking litter home can significantly reduce the risk of fires starting". This month has been 3C above average across the UK, provisional Met Office data shows.

This means July 2026 could be among the hottest three or four months of July on record.

News.title: Polanski says guillotine re-post was mistake but refuses to apologise
News.content:
Zack Polanski has refused three times to apologise to Nigel Farage for re-posting a photo of a man wearing a t-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel".

Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, said the image showed a "photo of man calling for the beheading of Nigel Farage", which he said could be an "incitement to murder".

The Green Party of England and Wales leader was reported to the Met over the photo, which he quickly deleted, but told the BBC he had not been contacted by police.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, he said he would not apologise for an "inadvertent mistake" that he said Farage had amplified in a "fundamentally dishonest way".

The row kicked off on Monday evening when Polanski shared the photo, which he said was the fifth image in a series of 20 from a party, having accepted a request to collaborate with the Instagram account of a photographer at the event.

Posting a screenshot on X, Reform UK leader Farage said: "If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski."

Asked if he wanted to apologise to Farage, Polanski said: "Well, if I'd done it deliberately I'd be apologising but because this was a mistake I think the important thing is that I point out this was a mistake, that I also make sure that I condemn political violence, and also crucially I make a commitment to be better on social media."

Asked for a second time whether he would apologise, Polanski refused because he said Farage had cropped the image to make it look like he had posted it himself, which he said was "fundamentally dishonest" and only amplified the problem.

Saying he had received a death threat earlier on Tuesday, Polanski added: "The ramping up of the language to say 'this is incitement to murder me' feels like that's also putting me in a dangerous spot."

Given a third chance to apologise, Polanski doubled down and said: "You know as well as I do that as soon as I do that Nigel Farage would run all over social media saying he was correct about incitement to murder and this would all ramp up again.

"I think it's important that I draw a line and don't play his game... It is important that he's kept safe, it is important we condemn political violence, but I also recognise this as the political attack that it is."

"If Nigel Farage wants to apologise for all the times that he's put other people in danger then I will be happy to make an apology," Polanski added.

The Green leader explained he had not read the slogan on the T-shirt when he accepted the collaboration because "what I was seeing was people partying" and he only noticed the man was wearing a rainbow hat as he flicked through.

"It feels quite surreal to be having this conversation," he said, adding: "I think it would be odd for the police to speak to me about that because I think it's quite obvious I've not done anything wrong other than make an inadvertent mistake."

The Metropolitan Police said there was no update on the complaint they had received on Monday.

On Tuesday, Reform asked the monitoring officer from the Greater London Authority, where Polanski is an elected member, to investigate whether he had breached the code of conduct.

Keith Prince, a Reform London Assembly Member, said: "To say that he was unaware of what he was promoting is frankly risible."

A Reform UK source told BBC Newsnight: "It's truly astonishing and quite frankly sickening that Zack Polanski won't apologise for inciting murder.

"He admits it was wrong. He admits it's dangerous, but he still refuses to apologise. Mr Polanski is not fit to lead a national political party."

Asked about the row on Tuesday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said there was a "duty on all politicians to be careful about what they post", especially in light of the death of former MP Ann Widdecombe earlier this month.

News.title: Some parents on benefits to get up to £4,500 for child starting apprenticeship
News.content:
Some parents on benefits will be given up to Â£4,500 a year to encourage their children to start apprenticeships, the government has said.

Under plans to encourage young people into work, families will be offered a bursary to replace Universal Credit payments lost by starting jobs.

The payment is expected to benefit an estimated few thousand households, who currently face losing between Â£17 and Â£330 a week if their children start apprenticeships.

The Conservatives welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's support for apprenticeships, but criticised his plans to fund the bursaries.

The bursary will be paid for from a Â£30m pot, funded through the growth and skills levy, a tax on employers with annual wage bills over Â£3m.

It followed the publication of a Social Security Advisory Committee report, external which warned of the "perverse effects" of the benefits system on young people's employment choices.

It said, for example, single parents with a disabled child could lose up to Â£340 per week in benefits if their child started an apprenticeship, exceeding the expected apprenticeship salary of Â£258 per week.

Because they are classed as paid employment, benefit payments are reduced to households where young people take on apprenticeships.

The committee said the system was hampering government efforts to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).

In a recent report, former Health Secretary Alan Milburn warned that one in six young people could be Neet in the next five years unless urgent action is taken.

Official figures show more than a million people aged 16 to 24 are currently Neet.

The government said its new bursary would remove a barrier to young people taking on apprenticeships, allowing them to "earn and learn".

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: "By providing bursaries to those who need them most and fully funding apprenticeship training, we are making sure cost is not the reason someone misses out."

It is part of a wider package of support for apprenticeships, including funding for apprenticeship training for under-25s and additional support for employers taking on apprentices.

Helen Whately, the Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary, said: "I'm glad Burnham agrees: apprenticeships are a good thing, and we need more of them."

But she said the plan was "uncosted".

"It is spending money already committed elsewhere. So, either it is another unfunded announcement, or Andy Burnham is not being straight with us about his plans."

Burnham has said he is "on a mission" to reduce the number of Neets.

"The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said.

As he continues a flurry of early policy announcements, Burnham on Tuesday set out plans to strike a balance in the education system between prioritising academic and technical skills.

News.title: The evidence that shows today's 20-somethings really do have it worse
News.content:
Young people in their 20s are facing a tougher start to adulthood than any generation in almost half a century, according to analysis of UK data on housing, employment and wealth, carried out for the BBC.

More than 40% of 25-year-olds are now living with their parents, their wages have stagnated and employment has fallen, show the figures which compare key metrics for different generations at age 25 stretching back to the early 1980s.

The findings are underscored by the experiences of young people themselves who, along with parents, have contacted BBC Your Voice about their circumstances, with many saying they were frustrated about being accused by older generations of not trying hard enough.

We asked the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) to gather and analyse government data, external, for the first time, to see if this generation really does have it worse.

The biggest change it found was where those in their 20s are living.

News.title: Uefa and PM criticise Infantino World Cup plan
News.content:
European football's governing body Uefa and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have criticised proposals from Fifa to seek private investment in its competitions, including the World Cup.

Fifa - the sport's global governing body - said it intends to expand "football development funding" to more than $10bn (Â£7.5bn) and invite third-party investment in a new venture.

The story was first reported in the Financial Times and the Times, with the latter claiming the plans could potentially earn Fifa president Gianni Infantino tens of millions of pounds.

In a lengthy statement outlining the proposals, Fifa says it will "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) - to "consolidate" its commercial and event operations.

The plan still needs to be passed by a vote of Fifa's 211 member nations. But if approval is granted, Fifa says Thrive Eternal is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.

Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.

Fifa sources have told BBC Sport there has been no discussion over Infantino, or anyone else, becoming chief executive of FFE.

In its statement, Fifa did say Infantino and the rest of the organisation "has a duty" to control the development of the project. Fifa has not said precisely what that means, or what the specific nature of Infantino's involvement will be.

As part of its pitch Fifa says all member associations will be able to access up to $20m (Â£15m) in "one-off capital" to fund development.

Infantino said every nation should benefit from the riches football creates.

"Parts of the game have turned that popularity into remarkable commercial value - and we celebrate that success and want it to continue, because it lifts the whole game," he said.

"Our job is to make sure the rest of football grows with it: Fifa exists to support sustainable, inclusive development in every corner of the world."

However, Uefa has issued a statement criticising the proposals, which it claimed "crosses a line".

Burnham said going ahead with the idea would mean Fifa had "sold out".

He wrote on X: "Let me say this very directly. Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine.

"The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone's to sell. Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.

"Football belongs to the fans. It always has, and it always will."

The Football Association says it was unaware of Fifa's plans when they were released.

News.title: Amber heat health alerts to come into force as heatwave reaches 35C peak
News.content:
Amber and yellow heat health alerts are set to come into force on Wednesday as parts of the UK endure the fourth widespread heatwave of the year so far.

Temperatures are forecast to peak at midweek with readings as high as 35C (95F) in the hottest places.

Though the heatwave will come to a quick end for many on Thursday, well above-average temperatures in the mid- to high 20s Celsius will persist into the weekend.

The hot weather, paired with a significant lack of rainfall, will exacerbate conditions in many of the driest areas.

News.title: Brits urged to avoid dangerous plug adaptors this summer - what to watch out for
News.content:
Brits going on holiday abroad this summer have been warned to watch out for dangerous travel adaptors, after an investigation suggested thousands may be for sale online.

Consumer safety group Electrical Safety First (ESF) tested 14 products from AliExpress, Amazon Marketplace, eBay and TikTok Shop - and found they all failed to meet UK safety requirements.

It said in some instances the devices could expose users to risk of serious electric shock or electrocution.

AliExpress, Amazon, eBay and TikTok all said they had removed the products ESF flagged from sale, and that they treated product safety as a top priority.

But Giuseppe Capanna, ESF product safety engineer, urged those "heading abroad this summer to think before they buy".

"What looks like a bargain could come at a much higher cost," he warned.

Capanna also said shoppers should buy travel adaptors from trusted retailers "so they can travel with confidence".

ESF tested six regular travel adaptors and eight universal adaptors it suspected could pose safety concerns.

To be sold in the UK, adaptors must not have accessible live parts and only one set of pins should come out at a time.

But the charity found multiple sets could be exposed simultaneously in six out of eight of the universal adaptors it tested.

None of the eight met the required dimensions and mechanical strength, while some pins snapped off under force during tests.

ESF said anyone who tried to remove a broken pin from a socket would be at risk of electric shock.

News.title: Burnham has no scope to increase borrowing, think tank warns
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will have to raise taxes or cut spending to meet his pledges on defence and the cost of living, a major think tank has said.

Burnham has announced a series of new measures since assuming office last week, including cuts to electricity bills and bringing the bus fare cap in most parts of England back down to Â£2.

But the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr) warned the public finances will continue to be squeezed by more persistent inflation as a result of the Iran war.

It questioned whether Burnham had "fully thought through" how his promises would be paid for, but said the prime minister will have to raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere.

Stephen Millard, Niesr's deputy director for macroeconomics, said: "There's clearly no scope for increasing borrowing, so it is about choices."

Labour's manifesto pledge was to not increase taxes for working people - including income tax, VAT and national insurance contributions - which Burnham has said he will uphold.

Millard said Niesr was advocating for cost-of-living measures to be funded through higher taxes â "which could involve tax reform rather than higher marginal rates" â or spending cuts.

He said: "People have talked a lot about the welfare bill â that is an obvious place to look.

"The triple lock on pensions, that is very, very expensive, and will get more expensive as we age."

He also pointed to potentially reforming council tax to move towards a land value tax system, or scrapping some VAT exemptions.

"Once you've done all of that, then I'm afraid I would break the manifesto promise and would be looking at the income tax rate."

Niesr also said on Wednesday it expects inflation to keep rising until February 2027, peaking at 3.8% before falling back to the Bank of England's 2% target.

The think tank said in its latest economic outlook that it does not believe the central bank will cut interest rates until 2028.

Its Director David Aikman said that "treading water is not enough" to prevent the national debt from rising.

"Every major shock this century has ratcheted the debt ratio higher, and none of that increase has been reversed," he said.

The Treasury said the government will stick to its fiscal rules while investing in "the public services people rely on".

"Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of economic stability and national security," a spokesperson said.

News.title: Bystander video shows teen lifeguard's dramatic ocean rescue
News.content:
Video captured by a bystander shows the moment 16-year-old rookie lifeguard Ryder Williams rescued a 10-year-old boy from the ocean at Seabright State Beach in Santa Cruz, California.

The child had been swept about 15 yards (13.7m) offshore when Williams reached him, with several beachgoers also joining the rescue. The operation lasted just over two minutes.

President Donald Trump has since invited Williams to the White House to receive a high civilian honour.

News.title: French Navy carries out 'shooting drill' mid interview
News.content:
A French Navy patrol boat appeared to fire a round of gunshots "without warning" in the English Channel during a BBC interview with the UK shadow home secretary.

Conservative MP Chris Philp was being interviewed about small boat crossings by BBC journalist Michael Keohan as a French warship passed by at 09:15 BST (10:15 CET), about three miles from the French coast.

Keohan said there were 17 shots but "no warnings" from the boat about 300m away, which left Philp believing it was an intimidation tactic to "stop us covering migrant crossings".

The French authorities said it was part of a training exercise, unrelated to the presence of a British ship, which it said was out of range of fire.

Philp dismissed this claim as "not credible", adding: "There were no warnings in place about live firing training exercises.

"It looked and sounded exactly like deliberate intimidation."

News.title: Grieving mum was told baby's ashes were animal remains
News.content:
Ness suffered a miscarriage just before she was due to have her 12-week scan on April 20 2021.

She told how she had treasured the ashes for three years.

"They had sat on my shelf next to my baby scan," said Ness.

In court, prosecutor Chris Paxton KC said "the ashes that Lucy was given could not have been those of her baby".

The barrister did not state that they were of animal origin.

Ness was clear to the BBC, however, that police had told her the ashes were animal remains.

Her disgust at Bush was clear.

She said: "How can somebody with a duty of care do this to my family?"

She and her partner, Callum Ellerby, were told their baby was cremated on 10 May 2021.

"We didn't know the gender," said Ness. "We were not going to know the gender."

The day after the cremation was meant to have taken place, Bush, from Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, rang her and asked her to collect the ashes, which she did.

They were contained in a white china urn with a teddy bear embossed on it, Ness recalled.

When Humberside Police announced they were investigating Legacy in March 2024, Ness rang the helpline set up for anyone concerned.

The force then contacted her to say the ashes she had in her home could not be that of her baby, she said.

Officers explained to Ness that they had checked records at the crematorium and found Bush collected the baby's ashes on 13 May - two days after he had presented Ness and Ellerby with the urn.

She said: "I have felt very up and down. This has definitely impacted on my mental health."

News.title: Naga Munchetty to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years
News.content:
Munchetty, 51, is among the best-paid presenters on the BBC's star salaries list, earning about Â£360,000 a year, according to the latest accounts.

She has interviewed major celebrities and politicians on the programme over the years ranging from Hillary Clinton and Michelle Obama to Sir Keir Starmer, Sir David Attenborough and Sir Rod Stewart.

In 2016, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing.

She has also been at the centre of some controversies during her time on BBC Breakfast.

In 2019, she was initially found to have breached the BBC's guidelines over comments she made about a social media post from Donald Trump about four female politicians of colour.

However, the BBC's director general then reversed that finding after deciding her words were not "sufficient to merit" upholding part of the complaint.

In 2021, Munchetty and co-presenter Charlie Stayt were "spoken to and reminded of their responsibilities" after complaints about their reaction to a government minister's flag. Munchetty apologised for liking "offensive" tweets about the exchange.

In June 2025, the Sun reported details of two alleged incidents which the paper said caused BBC bosses to speak to Munchetty about her conduct.

That came amid reports of behind-the-scenes tensions on the show, and at the same time as the programme's editor Richard Frediani took extended leave following allegations about his behaviour.

Frediani returned to work two weeks later and remains editor of BBC Breakfast.

At the time, the BBC said it did not comment on individual cases but took all complaints about conduct at work extremely seriously. Munchetty and Frediani did not comment on the reports.

The programme won a Bafta TV Award last year for best news coverage for a special about the Post Office scandal.

News.title: Laughter and tears at Dame Penelope Keith funeral
News.content:
Dame Penelope Keith's funeral has been hailed as "wonderful, beautiful and absolutely amazing" by her friends.

The actress, who starred in The Good Life and To The Manor Born, "died peacefully whilst living with cancer at her home" on 29 June at the age of 86.

Crowds lined the streets to say their goodbyes to the "very special lady" as her coffin travelled through her home town of Milford in Surrey before the service at Guildford Cathedral.

Broadcaster, writer and former politician Gyles Brandreth said the funeral was "filled with a mixture of sadness but laughter and gratitude as well because we were celebrating a great actress".

"It was a wonderful way to remember a remarkable person," he told BBC Radio Surrey.

Posting on X later, he said: "There was laughter and tears at Guildford Cathedral this morning - a truly beautiful and deeply moving funeral service for Dame Penelope Keith - what a lady and what a perfect service.

"It caught her completely. She was very special."

News.title: Unsolved Suzy Lamplugh case 'haunts' detectives
News.content:
Police officers investigating the disappearance of estate agent Suzy Lamplugh in west London say they remain "haunted" by the case, four decades after she went missing.

Lamplugh, 25, vanished after leaving her Fulham office to meet a client on the afternoon of 28 July 1986. She never returned and her body has never been found.

As the Metropolitan Police investigation is due to be mothballed next year, cold case detectives say they are troubled by the continuing mystery.

To mark the 40th anniversary of her disappearance, the Lamplugh family has released previously unseen photographs featuring her siblings Lizzie, Tamsin and Richard and her parents Paul and Diana.

In releasing the intimate family images, her siblings described her as "a truly beautiful person inside and out".

News.title: Two-Michelin-star chef brings fine dining to town football club
News.content:
Football fans will have the chance to swap their traditional match day pint and pie for a pop-up dining experience created by a renowned two-Michelin-star chef.

Gareth Ward, the chef behind Ynyshir Restaurant and Rooms near Machynlleth, Powys - which has an almost Â£500 per head tasting menu - has partnered up with Aberystwyth Town Football Club, in Ceredigion.

The collaboration will bring supporters different match day dining experiences, hospitality packages and corporate events throughout the season.

Ward, who has featured as a guest judge on MasterChef: The Professionals, said he was "excited" for the new venture.

The chef-patron said football clubs should be at "the heart of their communities".

The club's team is in the Novira Cymru South division, the second tier of Welsh football.

He added: "I see a real opportunity to bring people together through food and unforgettable matchday experiences and corporate events."

News.title: Schools to offer technical subjects to pupils from age 14 in England, Burnham says
News.content:
Secondary school pupils in England will be able to study subjects like manufacturing and AI in addition to core academic learning under reforms outlined by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The government said the courses, which would be available from Year 10, would be linked to local industries and designed to give children a clearer pathway into work.

Data published this year showed more than one million young people across the UK were not in education, employment or training, the highest level in more than 12 years.

Few details have been published about how the new vocational courses would work in practice and it is not clear how they would operate in areas with low industrial activity.

The BBC understands that the government expects the new pathways into work to be up and running in some areas by 2028.

Later on Tuesday, the government also announced a new bursary of up to Â£4,500 for some families who would lose out on money if their children wanted to do an apprenticeship, because the child benefit they would lose out on would be worth more than the apprenticeship starter salary.

Speaking at a train manufacturing site in Derby, Burnham said: "We've had a system built for too long around the university route and it sends a message to some young people that they're some kind of second-class citizens, and it's just not right.

"They need an education system that works for them as well, that offers a path to all young people, that's balanced between academic and technical."

The prime minister said he was "on a mission" to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training - known as "Neet" - but declined to put a target date on his ambition.

"The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said.

"It's hard to put a firm date on the moment when you can say there are fewer than now."

However, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said while there was a "broad consensus" on improving vocational education, it was "not a big bold announcement".

She told BBC Breakfast: "What's going on there is a drastic shortage of jobs because Labour's policies over the last couple of years have killed job opportunities for young people. This announcement will not solve that."

News.title: Hundreds of thousands of women get morning-after pill via free pharmacy service
News.content:
The morning-after pill, known as emergency contraception, external, is medication designed to prevent unwanted pregnancies. It usually has to be taken within three to five days of having unprotected sex. The sooner it is taken, the more effective it is.

It works by delaying or preventing the release of an egg, but will only prevent pregnancy if ovulation has not already happened.

Alternatively, women can visit a doctor or nurse to have a coil or intrauterine device (IUD) fitted to prevent pregnancy at any time during their menstrual cycle. To be effective, it needs to be fitted within 120 hours or five days of unprotected sex.

The government said making the morning-after pill available free from pharmacies would end the "unfair" barriers and postcode lottery some women faced - with access varying dramatically depending on where they live.

Under the scheme, women can visit their local pharmacy and have a confidential consultation with a pharmacist or trained pharmacy technician, before receiving the medication on the same day.

Prior to this, women had to book an appointment with their GP, sexual health clinic or pharmacy to get the morning-after pill. Women could also access it privately, as they still can now.

In 2024/25, there were around 150,000 NHS prescriptions for the morning-after pill - far fewer than under the new service.

Dr Sue Mann, NHS National Clinical Director for Women's Health, said the pharmacy service was a "major step forward for women's health", with "no appointment, no waiting and no judgement".

"This service is already making a real impact, particularly for women living in more deprived communities, by making contraception easier to access closer to home," she added.

Women can check online, external to find their nearest participating pharmacy. All pharmacists and pharmacy technicians delivering the service have received specialist training to provide emergency contraception and wider contraceptive care.

Fifa spent 1,403 words in a public statement seeking to rationalise their new plan to sell off stakes of the World Cup to private investment, but a few choice phrases are now ringing out elsewhere.

“Shocking.” “Football’s nuclear bomb.” “Worse than the Super League, and bigger than 115.” “The line in the sand.”

None of that is exaggerated because it ties together so many of the extremes that have been pushing, pulling and twisting football, let alone the world, for so long, potentially crystallising so much of what has been coming to dictate its future: what the game should be and what it’s becoming; how it repeatedly shows it has a social value that you can’t buy as so many involved try to financially exploit that; what people say in private and what gets done in public.

You can even roll that right up to the seemingly dry details of governance like how the people who are going to vote on this, the heads of the member associations, are in many cases directly paid by Fifa through positions and committees.

This is when all of that matters most. How are they going to vote?

And, maybe most pertinently given the direction of the sport for so long, where is the resistance going to come from? Uefa have talked a good game, with a statement that directly says this “crosses a line” and rightly asserts the World Cup’s is “not Fifa’s to sell” – but are they finally going to play a hand?

Is this long-running tension going to spill out into a war that football arguably needs? Is anyone going to look at the bigger picture and actually make a stand?

Because, and this really can’t be stressed enough, once you start selling the game off, there’s really no getting it back.

Typical of how football and the world are going, Fifa’s 1,403-word statement of course turned all of this rationale on its head. It’s of a piece with Gianni Infantino’s unhinged Sunday statement about criticism. This announcement was headlined “Fifa intends to expand football development funding to over USD 10 billion subject to approval by Fifa Member Associations”, so duly framed by ideas of redistribution and democracy.

open image in gallery The move comes hot on the heels of a Trumpian-style rant by Infantino defending the 2026 World Cup ( PA )

Once again, a not-for-profit raising money, any money, was automatically elevated as if it’s a good thing without any further thought. The core reality was finally referenced a bit further down, as Fifa spoke of “carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests” in the new Fifa Forward Enterprise programme. That is set to bring the creation of a new company being formed to run the primary competitions, where Fifa would own a majority stake, private investors would have 20 to 30 per cent and then the 211 members a small stake totalling around 20 per cent.

Except, “non-controlling” isn’t how such money tends to really work. In reality, that kind of money brings a lot of influence.

By the same token, for all that Fifa bleated in seemingly endless paragraphs about how such thinking “lifts the whole game” and the need “to make sure the rest of football grows”, those now responsible for voting on this need to actually earn their money and think about the deeper implications.

There are profound concerns here even beyond the core philosophical virtue that the World Cup only belongs to the countries of the world – and, by extension, its football communities – and that’s it. What do they think happens once you allow such interests in? There might be the short-term benefit of being able to point your own national association to newly flush cash reserves of up to $20m – but what next?

open image in gallery Infantino has been called before a US Congressional committee over allegations he sought to curry favour with Trump and his administration ( PA )

Clue: such interests don’t tend to have wider societal concerns; they don’t care for what doesn’t make money. As one source puts it, “the current stakeholders benefit but everyone loses out in the future”. Trickle-down economics don’t work here, as the last few decades of football have made emphatically clear. This is why Celtic or Ajax don’t win the Champions League any more. It’s why every other country suffers a talent drain to Western Europe.

And what would now be directly incentivised – especially through the establishment of a company to run all of this – is the expansion of the Club World Cup and all of the ideas that serve existing wealth, both in the game and society. It shouldn’t be forgotten that Infantino was involved in Super League discussions, with the clubs at one point thinking they had Fifa’s blessing.

The global governing body have now already confirmed that Josh Kushner, brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, has been in talks about becoming the proposed lead investor.

Infantino’s long relationship with the US president suddenly takes on an even sharper perspective, especially among the mooted next steps for this. An excellent exclusive by Martyn Ziegler of The Times has already broached that Infantino would be lined up to run the company as a “commissioner” once his final presidential term expires in 2031. In other words, a lucrative post-presidency life.

open image in gallery Members of the Fifa Council insist they found out about the plan through the media ( Reuters )

When you stand back, this looks a lot like one man using his position – and the sport – for personal betterment. Or, as one senior insider put it, “only in Infantino’s world can things somehow get worse for the game every day”.

It should be what anyone who cares for the sport stands against, but will those with actual say really do that? Will they, as one other insider states, “put their bollocks on the line”?

Some who despise the idea have already marvelled at its realpolitik “genius”, likening it to the fait accompli of the Saudi Arabia 2034 “acclamation” in how everything already looks lined up. Every individual association would get a huge figure – or could sell off some of their share in the new company – so those in power right now are clearly incentivised to vote for it. And this in a world where only a fifth of member associations actually return audited accounts to show how the money is used.

It reminds us how broken the system is, how the reform that was supposed to take place after Infantino succeeded Sepp Blatter never happened. And in that structure, how is this actually going to be stopped when such a financially attractive package is taken to Congress for approval and there are no checks and balances?

open image in gallery Josh Kushner has been in talks about becoming the proposed lead investor, Fifa confirmed ( Reuters )

It all speaks to this central long-running theme of the game being taken further and further away from those who have an actual emotional stake in it; a personal stake – right up to the ownership of clubs. Members of the Fifa Council insisted they only found out through the media, reiterating how the body now works. The FA, chaired by Fifa vice-president Debbie Hewitt, were completely unaware of the proposal and it was not mentioned at Friday’s board meeting.

Many similar figures declared themselves shocked, appalled, disgusted. Except we’ve heard so much of this before. This, more than ever before, is a time to act. Could Uefa countries actually threaten to pull out… or will the individual countries just look at those financial figures?

The world should watch how everyone votes on this. Hiding behind the majority, and pointing to Fifa’s dismally dull politics, will no longer cut it. This is a decision with repercussions way beyond all of that.

This is what all of the politics, all the game’s long problems, were ultimately leading to. This is the line.

Let’s see who stands where.

In an affluent neighborhood in Delhi, electric vehicle charging stations near a popular shopping area were busy with drivers powering up their scooters, trucks and cars.

India's capital city is in dire need of more charging facilities, EV drivers say, to implement an ambitious plan to phase out gas vehicles in one of the world’s most polluted cities.

“Charging facilities are not up to the mark yet,” said Shyam Singh, a marketing executive who owns a two-wheel electric scooter, adding that it is hard for long-distance drivers to switch to EVs because the current battery range is not enough.

Delhi uses a bold approach to mainstream EVs

Delhi adopted a new policy on July 1 that aims to make the vast majority of newly registered vehicles electric by 2027. While existing gas-powered vehicles won't be banned, their numbers are expected to dwindle in the coming years.

Energy experts say the plan is one of the country’s most ambitious electric-vehicle policies and a significant step toward improving the city's air quality and reducing pollution.

The policy provides EV buyers with subsidies and waivers on registration fees and some road taxes, incentives to scrap gas vehicles, and it offers plans to expand the charging infrastructure. It also targets two- and three-wheelers that make up nearly 70% of vehicles in the city: Starting in 2027, any newly registered three-wheeled vehicles and small trucks must be electric, with two-wheelers the following year.

Currently, only about 5% of the 8.7 million vehicles registered in Delhi are electric. But EV registrations have been increasing, with over 100,000 in the past year, most of them two- and three-wheelers. Registrations for new gas-powered cars and bigger trucks will still be allowed for the time being.

The plan, which is expected to cost the local government 150 billion rupees ($1.5 billion), will offer cash amounts of up to 50,000 rupees ($522) for residents who purchase EVs and up to 100,000 rupees ($1,044) for those who scrap their old gasoline-powered vehicles.

“Delhi’s EV policy is one of the most ambitious policies that I have seen in India,” said Jaideep Saraswat, who leads work on clean power and electric mobility at the Vasudha Foundation. The deadlines, he added, send a signal to automakers and consumers that change is “inevitable.”

While states including Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana and Tamil Nadu have offered incentives for electric vehicle owners and manufacturers, cut taxes and pumped money into setting up charging stations, Delhi is the first to phase out gas-powered vehicles.

Going electric can reduce pollution

Severe air pollution in Delhi frequently forces school closures, construction bans and emergency public health measures, especially during the winter months. Vehicles cause about a quarter of air pollution in the National Capital Region surrounding Delhi, and two- and three-wheelers are responsible for nearly half of vehicular pollution in the city.

Ruchita Shah, an energy analyst for the global energy think tank Ember, said the city has long been a clean energy pioneer, including its earlier shift toward compressed natural gas vehicles to cut pollution. She said electric vehicles accounted for about 12.7% of Delhi’s new vehicle sales in the 2026 financial year, compared with 8.3% nationally.

The new policy’s most forward-looking feature, she said, is linking subsidies to tight deadlines after which some internal combustion engine vehicles can no longer be newly registered.

Sunil Dahiya, founder of environmental research organization Envirocatalyst, said cleaner vehicles could significantly reduce public exposure to roadside emissions. Still, he cautioned that the benefits will take time to fully materialize because existing gasoline, diesel, and CNG vehicles will continue to operate for years.

Charging infrastructure is a key hurdle

Some owners of gasoline-powered two-wheelers say this isn't the right time to go electric.

Siddhant Jha, a 22-year-old software engineer and northern Delhi resident, is worried about the longevity of EVs compared with his traditional two-wheeler, and the annual street flooding damaging a vehicle’s electrical components.

“I'd like to wait for a few years for better models and the 150,000 rupees ($1,566) I'll spend (on an EV) will make more sense then.”

Jha is also concerned about EV charging accessibility.

Shah, the energy analyst, said the policy’s success hinges on Delhi building sufficient charging infrastructure and sourcing more supplied power from renewable resources rather than fossil fuel plants. Most vehicle charging now happens at night, when solar power is unavailable, forcing the dependence on thermal power plants to meet demand.

Delhi must also upgrade its electricity grid — especially fast chargers needed by buses, cargo vehicles and cars — to meet the surge in demand and avoid grid failures, said Dahiya, the environmentalist.

Dahiya recommended installing battery storage at charging stations and adopting time-of-day pricing to incentivize charging when renewable power is more abundant.

Delhi's next challenges will be coordinating with surrounding states to decarbonize the electricity grid and public transport electrification, said Saraswat of the Vasudha Foundation.

“As a resident of Delhi, I’m sure each and every one will be extremely thrilled to have this policy. To see that winter where there is no smog, no pollution.”

___

Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India, and can be followed on X at @sibi123. Reach him at sarasu@ap.org.

The U.S. Department of Education said Tuesday it was investigating allegations that a high school teacher in the Denver school district required students of the same sex to kiss in front of a class, and a district in Washington state displayed vials of testosterone in an LGBTQ Pride Month exhibit.

The probes will determine whether the Bethel School District, about an hour south of Seattle, and Denver Public Schools violated a federal law that gives parents the right to opt out of school evaluations on topics including sex behavior or attitudes, the department said.

“Parents must be the decision-makers in matters impacting the most intimate parts of their children’s lives,” Frank Miller, director of the Student Privacy Policy Office at the Education Department, said in a statement.

Denver schools spokesman Scott Pribble said in a statement the district put the teacher on administrative leave and completed an investigation after students raised concerns in March 2025. The statement did not specify what prompted students' concerns.

The Board of Education fired the teacher in May, he said.

“The safety, emotional well-being, and dignity of our students are the absolute highest priorities of DPS,” the statement said. “Our actions to date have been wholly consistent with those priorities.”

Bethel School District said in a statement that the vials in a display at Graham-Kapowsin High School in June were not authorized by school administrators and were immediately removed and turned over to the Pierce County Sheriff's Office. Some vials had a “small amount of unknown liquid,” the district said.

Testosterone is prescribed for gender-affirming care. The district added that it will cooperate fully with the Education Department's investigation.

The two districts are in states headed by Democrats. President Donald Trump is a Republican.

The Trump administration has opened dozens of investigations into schools that make accommodations for transgender and LGBTQ+ students, often taking aim at districts that allow students to use bathrooms or locker rooms that align with their gender identities. It accused Denver schools last year of violating Title IX protections against sex-based discrimination over such a bathroom policy.

Trump officials have also pushed against schools accused of keeping information about students’ gender identities confidential from their parents, which the department says is a violation of federal privacy laws.

The Education Department tied the new investigations to National Parents’ Day on Sunday. The agency said it will be announcing “significant actions” involving the enforcement of parental rights laws through the week.

Pierce County Sheriff's Deputy Carly Cappetto said Bethel school administrators identified the student who brought the vials to campus. No charges were filed, and the juvenile student was referred to a drug and alcohol diversion program, Adam Faber, a spokesman for the Pierce County Prosecuting Attorney's Office, said in an email. He said the vials were not tested for testosterone, which is a controlled substance.

The district said in its statement it is reviewing its protocols for overseeing displays to “ensure all school materials strictly align with our educational standards and community expectations.”

“Our primary focus remains on maintaining a safe, respectful, and focused learning environment for all of our students,” it added.

___

Associated Press writer Collin Binkley in Washington contributed to this report.

The Trump administration Department of Defense has reportedly removed a prominent Obama administration official and Trump critic’s name from an auditorium at the Defense Intelligence Agency in Washington.

The Clapper Leadership Hall, named for former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper, is now the Thomas Knowlton Leadership Hall, named for a Revolutionary War officer considered the father of American military intelligence.

“The Thomas Knowlton Leadership Hall at Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) headquarters honors a true American warrior whose legacy is inseparable from the birth of our nation’s intelligence profession,” Acting Pentagon Press Secretary Joel Valdez told The Hill.

President Trump has long reviled Clapper for his role in investigating Russian meddling in the 2016 election, which intelligence officials concluded showed a preference to boost Trump’s candidacy.

“James Clapper disgraced himself and his career as an intelligence official. His name will no longer be honored at the Defense Intelligence Agency auditorium,” an unnamed senior defense official told The Daily Caller, which first reported the name change.

open image in gallery The Trump administration has reportedly removed the name of James Clapper, the former Director of National Intelligence under President Barack Obama, from a hall at the Defense Intelligence Agency ( AFP/Getty )

“As Director of National Intelligence, he oversaw the politicization of the intelligence community, turning what should have been an apolitical institution into a tool used against his political opponents,” the official added. “That record makes him unfit to be recognized in a building dedicated to the professionals who actually protect this country.”

The Independent has contacted the Pentagon and DIA for comment. Clapper was unable to be immediately reached for comment.

Republicans accuse Clapper of mishandling the Russia investigation during the 2016 election and leaking an unverified dossier about alleged Russian dirt on Trump to the media in early 2017. The president, meanwhile, has accused Clapper of carrying out the “crime of the century” by fueling the damaging “Russia hoax.”

Clapper, writing in a 2025 op-ed in The New York Times, called allegations he politicized the intelligence “patently false,” arguing subsequent reviews of the investigation by the Senate, a Trump-appointed special counsel and the CIA have all confirmed this.

open image in gallery Clapper has denied allegations from Republicans he politicized the investigation into Russia’s election meddling in 2016 ( AFP/Getty )

Clapper has also denied leaking the so-called Steele dossier to the media in January of 2017, as Trump was taking office, telling the Washington Post he did not discuss it with CNN’s Jake Tapper until May, after the claims of the dossier were already public information thanks to news reporting.

The president has targeted Clapper before, revoking his security clearance last year.

This reportedly had the effect of keeping Clapper from attending a graduation ceremony for a CIA K9 officer whose training he sponsored in honor of his late wife, who was an animal lover.

Clapper was also reportedly among the high-profile critics of Trump to be subpoenaed last year in Florida in a federal investigation in which the Trump administration is probing an alleged “grand conspiracy” to sink the Republican’s political campaigns.

Walter Joseph "Jay" Clayton was confirmed by the Senate to be Donald Trump’s next director of national intelligence (DNI), ending a stalemate affecting the reauthorization of key spying legislation.

Clayton’s nomination sailed through the chamber on Tuesday after clearing a procedural vote just a day earlier, teeing him up to be sworn in within days. His takeover of the DNI office (ODNI) will herald the ouster of Bill Pulte, Trump’s pick to lead the agency during its transition period and a figure whose selection triggered a Democratic revolt on Capitol Hill. The final vote was 51-47, with zero defections on either side.

The acting DNI, Pulte, previously led Trump’s efforts to punish his enemies at the Federal Housing Finance Agency. His total lack of background in national security or intelligence led to Democrats opposing his permanent appointment and vowing to keep the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act’s valuable Section 702 powers in the dark while Pulte remains in the role.

Plans for the renewal of that legislation aren’t immediately clear. The Senate has only days left in session before it will go to recess for most of the month of August, as senators return to their home states and in some cases begin the task of jump-starting their re-election campaigns. Before then, the chamber is due to take up several other priorities, including legislation to avert a government shutdown in September.

Clayton’s nomination was expected to pass easily as he was recommended by some GOP senators to be Trump’s pick for acting U.S. attorney in the Southern District of New York last year, a role which saw him prosecuting terror suspects among others. He was not expected to pick up much, if any, Democratic support however, due to his refusal to state outright that Donald Trump was duly defeated in the 2020 presidential election during questioning from Democratic members of the Senate Intelligence Committee during his confirmation hearing.

open image in gallery Jay Clayton's nomination was initially held up by Donald Trump's refusal to give in to Democrats' demands ( Getty )

A topic relatively unrelated to his job, the question of the 2020 election’s actual result has become somewhat of a litmus test Democrats have imposed upon Trump’s nominees and appointed officials as they come before Congress for questioning, in part because lawmakers in the party feel that it is an easy way of exposing whether a given official can stomach departing from the president on a matter around which Trump is known to seek recriminations.

Republican senators are also nearly as eager as Democrats to see Pulte removed from his role, though they have condemned their counterparts for holding FISA’s valuable spying powers on the line. Section 702, which remains up for reauthorization, allows the government to gather electronic records of persons living overseas. Three GOP senators voted against allowing Pulte to serve in his current role as acting DNI, and others, including former GOP Senate leader Mitch McConnell, suggested that he wouldn’t survive a full confirmation vote.

The Democrats’ refusal to back Section 702’s reauthorization over Pulte’s appointment initially resulted in Trump pulling Clayton’s nomination in anger, but pressure from those Republican senators forced the White House to give in.

open image in gallery Bill Pulte, Tulsi Gabbard's replacement, has no background in intelligence or national security ( Reuters )

The ODNI under Pulte has undergone waves of layoffs as the Trump loyalist still in charge has instituted purges of career intelligence officials and others he perceives to be aligned with an anti-Trump “Deep State” working within the government.

Previously, under DNI Tulsi Gabbard, it became an area of controversy and confusion as the president publicly contradicted Gabbard, who was in charge of his intelligence briefings, on the danger supposedly presented by the Iranian nuclear program. Gabbard resigned in May.

A former Democratic congresswoman who underwent a MAGA evolution, Gabbard was largely sidelined from her role and rarely commented on foreign policy matters after her public snub by the president. In January, she stunned many when she personally oversaw an FBI raid of Fulton County’s election offices — the jurisdiction was one where Trump attempted to lean on local officials to change the results of the 2020 election, and where a local district attorney sought his criminal prosecution after the election.

That FBI raid of the Georgia election offices never amounted to any form of serious investigation, and the Trump administration has still declined to go as far as issuing actual charges against anyone the president has accused of illegal activity as it relates to the 2020 election.
