Fujimori's inauguration brings Southern Cone and Andean presidents together in Lima

28th Tuesday, July 2026 - 10:30 UTC Full article

Fujimori will become the first woman to reach Peru's presidency through the ballot box

The presidents of Bolivia, Paraguay, Chile, and Honduras arrived in Lima on Monday to attend the handover ceremony at which Keiko Fujimori will assume Peru's presidency for the 2026-2031 term. The leaders of Argentina, Javier Milei; Uruguay, Yamandú Orsi; Panama, José Raúl Mulino; and Ecuador, Daniel Noboa, are also expected to take part.

Interim President José María Balcázar hosted an official dinner for the delegations on Monday night at the Government Palace in the capital's historic center, and on Tuesday will hand the presidential sash to Fujimori on the anniversary of Peru's independence.

Several delegations arrived with defined bilateral agendas. Bolivia's Rodrigo Paz, on his first visit to the neighboring country, will hold a meeting with Fujimori with the stated aim of “restoring diplomatic dialogue between the two countries,” according to Foreign Minister Fernando Aramayo. La Paz's priorities include setting up a binational cabinet in the short term and advancing the use of the Peruvian port of Ilo, which for landlocked Bolivia holds “commercial, tourism and energy” significance.

Chile's José Antonio Kast had already held a video call with the president-elect on July 10, in which they discussed migration and coordination against transnational organized crime. The two also agreed on the need to revitalize the Pacific Alliance, a bloc in which both countries are full members and which they see as a key mechanism for commercial projection toward Asia-Pacific markets.

Paraguay's Santiago Peña, who arrived with his wife, has bilateral and business meetings scheduled, while Honduras's Nasry Asfura will meet with business leaders and officials to promote cooperation opportunities, according to their respective governments.

Fujimori will become the first woman to reach Peru's presidency through the ballot box, after winning by a narrow margin of 49,641 votes over left-wing candidate Roberto Sánchez in the June 7 runoff. She takes office on her fourth attempt, following three consecutive runoff defeats.

The incoming president assumes office facing two main challenges: citizen security, the population's foremost concern, and political stability in a country where no president has completed a five-year term over the past decade. Her electoral rival turned to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights alleging irregularities, a request the National Elections Board dismissed before proclaiming the results.

World.title: Trump asks the Supreme Court to allow his mail-voting restrictions before the midterms
World.content:
Trump asks the Supreme Court to allow his mail-voting restrictions before the midterms

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:26 UTC Full article

Trump has repeatedly maintained that mail-in voting facilitates electoral fraud

The US government on Monday filed an emergency request with the Supreme Court seeking authorization to implement President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, which lower courts have blocked. The request comes 99 days before November's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.

The filing followed by two days a decision by the First Circuit Court of Appeals, based in Boston, which refused by a two-to-one vote to stay the injunction issued on June 25 by a district judge. That ruling keeps the order blocked in twenty-three Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia, which sued the administration.

The order, signed in March, tasks the director of Citizenship and Immigration Services and the commissioner of the Social Security Administration with drawing up a list of eligible voters, and bars the Postal Service from sending ballots to anyone not on it. The plaintiff states argue that the Constitution reserves the conduct of elections to the states and Congress, not the executive branch, an argument accepted in the earlier rulings.

In its filing before the high court, the administration framed the order as “general policy guidance” and stressed that the Postal Service has not finalized any regulations. The appeals judges had noted, by contrast, that the measure sets rapidly approaching deadlines requiring states to reorganize their procedures immediately, while also ensuring that officials and the public understand the rules governing the September and November votes. A White House spokesperson said the lower courts' decision “is not the final say” and that the administration expects a favorable outcome.

Trump has repeatedly maintained that mail-in voting facilitates electoral fraud. Election officials, courts, and federal agencies concluded that there was no evidence of widespread fraud in the 2020 elections, when that method saw unprecedented use during the pandemic, and noted that the system includes multiple verification and audit mechanisms.

The initiative is part of a broader set of government actions on electoral matters. The administration is pressing Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register on the federal roll and remains stalled in the Senate, and has sued twenty-nine states to obtain copies of their voter registries, which include dates of birth, driver's license numbers, and portions of social security numbers. Courts have blocked access in three states and have yet to rule in the rest.

World.title: Milei announces Starlink deal to bring satellite internet to 6,000 rural schools
World.content:
Milei announces Starlink deal to bring satellite internet to 6,000 rural schools

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:20 UTC Full article

At the time of the announcement, neither the text of the agreement nor any public statement from the company about its terms had been released

Argentine President Javier Milei announced an agreement between the National Communications Agency (Enacom) and Starlink to provide satellite connectivity to 6,000 rural schools that currently have poor internet access or no connection at all. The announcement was made on Sunday during the main event of the 138th International Livestock, Agriculture and Industry Exhibition in Buenos Aires.

According to the president, Elon Musk's company will donate 6,000 complete satellite kits along with 24 months of its highest-capacity service, which includes priority access of up to five terabytes per month per site. “Yes, it's a huge amount. Thank you, Elon,” he said during the speech.

Once that period ends, the equipment will remain at the schools and the regulator will take on the cost of the service for an additional year, covering the subscription, installation, technical support, and monitoring. Enacom sources said those resources will come from the Universal Service Fund, made up of contributions from the telecommunications sector and earmarked for extending access to areas not covered by commercial provision.

At the time of the announcement, neither the text of the agreement nor any public statement from the company about its terms had been released. The president also said the initiative adds to the three million users who, he said, already use the company's services in the country.

Starlink accelerated its expansion in Argentina following the easing of the regulatory framework for satellite services introduced by the current government, and now operates across the entire territory. The Argentine market accounts for about 25% of the company's Latin American operation and ranks among the countries with the highest service penetration, with weekly user growth of around 2%. Most customers are households, a concentration that has led to episodes of saturation in certain areas, such as greater Buenos Aires, Córdoba, and the Vaca Muerta region.

The agreement fits into the relationship Milei has maintained with Musk since the start of his term. The two met in February 2025 in the United States and have kept in frequent contact since. In parallel, Tesla is advancing its commercial entry into the local market, after formally incorporating in the country and appointing its first manager for Argentina and Uruguay.

In the same speech, the president projected an expansion of agricultural output and said the country is in a position to double its grain harvest, though he announced no decisions on export duties, one of the sector's main demands.

World.title: At the Central American and Caribbean Games, powerhouse Mexico builds for the 2028 Olympics
World.content:
Mexico is off to a commanding start at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in the Dominican Republic, reinforcing its status as the region’s powerhouse as the century‑old competition enters its second week.

The Games opened Friday with a music‑ and fireworks-filled ceremony at Félix Sánchez Olympic Stadium in the nation’s capital, Santo Domingo.

Las grandes celebraciones deportivas también son una oportunidad para unir a todo un país. Así vivimos la inauguración de los XXV Juegos Centroamericanos y del Caribe Santo Domingo 2026, una edición histórica que marca el centenario de esta competencia y reúne a los mejores… pic.twitter.com/qbT12Gdozl — Barrick Pueblo Viejo (@BarrickRD) July 28, 2026

They are the oldest regional multiple-sports competition in the world recognized by the International Olympic Committee.

Running through Aug. 8, this year’s edition marks the centennial of the Games, first held in Mexico City in 1926. More than 6,000 athletes from 37 countries and territories are competing in 40 sports.

Mexico is the only nation to have appeared in all 25 editions and is the two-time defending champion, with 13 championships overall.

At the 2018 Games in Barranquilla, Colombia, Mexico won 132 golds among 341 total medals, then raised the bar in 2023 in San Salvador, El Salvador, with 145 golds and 353 medals overall.

Mexico’s best haul all-time was winning 375 medals in the 2010 Games in Mayagüez, Puerto Rico.

So far in 2026, the Mexican team is delivering again, surging up to 106 total medals as the competition moved through day 5 on Tuesday — a haul that includes 38 gold medals with 11 days still to go.

Mexico sits atop the overall table, more than 40 medals ahead of Colombia with 63 and Cuba with 38. The Dominican Republic and Venezuela rank fourth and fifth, respectively.

Mexico’s lead has been built on familiar strengths, such as the taekwondo team registering 14 podium finishes, including gold medals for Daniela Souza and Iker Casas.

In skeet shooting, flag bearer Gabriela Rodríguez — the silver medalist at the 2025 ISSF Shotgun World Championships — delivered as expected, taking the women’s crown, while teammate Luis Gallardo won the men’s event.

Open water swimmer Paulo Strehlke won gold in the 10‑kilometer race, part of a four‑medal haul for Mexico’s open water swimmers over the weekend.

Rowers Melissa Márquez and Aylin Ibarra each won three gold medals, with other gold medals coming in badminton and rhythmic gymnastics.

Other sports being contested include basketball, figure skating, soccer, baseball, cycling and diving, along with netball, basque pelota (similar to racquetball and jai alai), billiards, chess and esports — high‑level video‑game competitions making their debut at these Games.

Mexico sees its performances in Olympic‑core sports in Santo Domingo as a stepping stone toward the Los Angeles Summer Games in 2028.

It has sent over 600 athletes and its A teams in several sports, notably diving, open water swimming, cycling and taekwondo. Last week, a ceremony for the Mexican delegation was led by President Claudia Sheinbaum.

The next major test will be the Pan American Games in Lima, Peru, scheduled for July 23 to Aug. 8, 2027.

With reports from La Jornada, AP, Olympics.com and El Economista

World.title: Mexico eyes tariff retaliation to level playing field for tequila exports
World.content:
Mexico will introduce stricter trade tariff measures for imported alcohols to encourage other countries to reduce tariffs on Mexican tequila, Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard announced during National Tequila Day celebrations on Friday.

National Tequila Day, celebrated annually on July 24, recognizes the world-famous spirit for its economic and cultural value. Tequila production is a source of employment for thousands of families dedicated to agave cultivation and distillation.

Reconocimiento a la industria del Tequila y plan de acción conjunto para aumentar exportaciones a todo el mundo. pic.twitter.com/R06kE34c6N — Marcelo Ebrard C. (@m_ebrard) July 28, 2026

In a presentation, Ebrard emphasized the need to review and dismantle all trade restrictions facing tequila exports to achieve more balanced treatment for Mexican products. “If another country applies 150 tariffs on me, I will say, ‘Hey, I’m going to impose restrictions on your products too,’” explained Ebrard. “It’s going to have to be more balanced.”

The economy minister said that while Mexico is one of the most open countries to international trade, some markets continue to impose tariffs of up to 150% or regulatory restrictions on tequila imports. Meanwhile, Mexico imposes few restrictions on the import of similar products from other countries.

In 2024, tequila exports achieved a value of almost US $4.2 billion, solidifying the product’s position as Mexico’s second most important agro-industrial export, behind beer, according to Agriculture Ministry (Sader) data. Mexican tequila is exported to over 120 countries, with annual exports exceeding 400 million liters.

It was the only spirit to register growth during the past year, with an increase of 1.2%. Global tequila volumes increased at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 7% between 2019 and 2025, and are expected to expand at a CAGR of 2% to 2030, according to the global beverage data company IWSR.

Tequila was granted Denomination of Origin (DO) status in 1974, for its historical connection to specific Mexican regions and traditional production practices, making it the first Mexican product to gain this certification.

The Director General of the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI), Vidal Llerenas Morales, said that the status guarantees that only tequila produced in the states of Jalisco, Nayarit, Guanajuato, Michoacán and Tamaulipas can legally use this designation, which helps preserve the alcohol’s traditional characteristics and quality.

Other Mexican alcohols have since been granted DO certification, including mezcal, bacanora, sotol, charanda and raicilla.

With reports from El Financiero and El Informador

World.title: Opinion: Beyond better buses. A transportation vision for San Miguel de Allende
World.content:
When Mexico News Daily recently asked how San Miguel de Allende can remain the “Best City in the World,” one recommendation stood out: improve the buses. That is an excellent, perhaps obvious, place to start — but it should not be the city’s only transportation priority. San Miguel’s larger challenge is deciding what kind of city it wants to become over the next decade and beyond, as well as what kind of transportation system will support that vision.

Transportation decisions shape far more than how quickly people travel. They affect air quality, noise, safety, neighborhood vitality, economic opportunity, public health and the simple pleasure of walking the streets. The most successful historic cities understand that transportation is not primarily about moving vehicles. It is about helping people reach the places they need or want to go to, while preserving the qualities that make a city worth living in and visiting.

San Miguel has already achieved something extraordinary. Residents and visitors enjoy walking its streets, lingering in its plazas, gathering in cafés and experiencing a vibrant public life. As the city grows, transportation investments should strengthen those qualities — not gradually erode them. That requires a different way of thinking. The question should not simply be, “How do we move more cars or buses?” It should be, “How do we help more people reach more places more easily, while making the city quieter, healthier, safer and more enjoyable?”

The city’s buses remain the backbone of mobility for thousands of residents and handfuls of visitors, connecting neighborhoods with schools, workplaces, markets, hospitals, churches and Centro. But today’s network reflects decades of incremental change rather than deliberate planning. Neighborhoods have expanded, employment centers have shifted and travel patterns have evolved. Tourists have grown in number and diversified in the variety of places they want to visit. Route redesign should begin with understanding how San Miguelenses, expatriates and visitors actually travel today. Rider surveys, passenger counts, GPS data, employer input and travel analysis could identify where people are going, when they travel and where the current system fails them. Bus service should reflect current travel patterns while avoiding unintended consequences — such as increased noise, congestion or safety concerns — that could diminish quality of life on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods.

The city should also consider whether a system focused primarily on Centro still reflects current demand. Direct cross-town routes connecting residential neighborhoods with employment centers, hospitals, schools and shopping areas could shorten trips without necessarily adding more buses. Frequent service on key corridors, coordinated transfers and reliable schedules may serve riders better than infrequent service spread across too many streets.

But better bus routes are not enough; the experience of using transit must also improve. Replacing aging diesel buses with quieter, cleaner electric or low-emission vehicles would reduce noise, improve air quality and make transit more attractive to everyone — not only residents who depend upon it, but also expatriates and visitors who often choose to drive because the system seems unfamiliar, unattractive or unsafe.

Making transit easy to understand is equally important. Clear route branding, well-designed stops, digital maps, QR codes, real-time arrival information and integration with Google Maps can transform uncertainty into confidence. The goal should be simple: riding a bus should feel as intuitive as taking a taxi.

As transit improves, the city has an opportunity to rethink its streets. Historic cities around the world have adopted Complete Streets — streets designed to accommodate pedestrians, transit riders, people with disabilities, deliveries and automobiles rather than prioritizing cars alone. Wider sidewalks, safer crossings, accessible design, better bus stops and carefully managed loading areas can allow transportation and public life to reinforce one another. Cities such as Copenhagen, Curitiba, Pontevedra and San Antonio have shown that giving more space to people can support local businesses, improve safety, reduce pollution and create more vibrant public places.

San Miguel already has examples of its own. Calle San Francisco near the Jardín illustrates how reducing automobile traffic can transform a street from a transportation corridor into a destination. As public transportation improves, the city should identify additional streets where pedestrian activity already exceeds automobile demand. This should lead to identifying opportunities to expand pedestrian-priority corridors while maintaining access for residents, deliveries and emergency services.

Parking should also be part of the discussion. Building more parking rarely solves congestion and often encourages more driving. A better strategy would be to develop mobility hubs at strategic locations outside the most constrained parts of the city. These facilities could combine parking with frequent transit, bicycle parking, taxi services, visitor information and public restrooms. Commuters into and visitors to the city could leave their cars once and continue their journey without adding traffic to the historic center.

Over time, the hubs might also connect with low-speed, electric, autonomous circulators. Pilot programs around the world are testing autonomous shuttles that connect transit stops, pedestrian districts, shopping areas and major destinations. They would not replace buses, but they could eventually provide another option for reducing automobile dependence while preserving San Miguel’s pedestrian character.

None of these ideas requires overnight implementation. The city could begin with demonstration projects: one redesigned bus corridor, a small fleet of cleaner vehicles, improved passenger information, a mobility hub, a temporary pedestrian-priority street or others. Pilot projects allow residents, visitors, businesses, existing transportation providers and public officials to see what works, identify unintended consequences and make adjustments before committing to larger investments.

How can progress — and ultimately success — be measured? Traditionally, this begins with a baseline needs assessment, followed by continuous monitoring as initiatives are implemented. Success can then be evaluated by whether workers can reach jobs more easily, children can travel to school more safely, neighborhoods become quieter and more livable, businesses become more vibrant and more people choose to walk, use public transit or spend time in the city’s public spaces.

San Miguel’s transportation decisions over the next decade will determine whether it becomes more congested — or more livable. Cleaner buses, smarter routes, Complete Streets, expanded pedestrian districts and mobility hubs are not separate projects. They are pieces of a single vision for preserving what makes San Miguel extraordinary. The world’s most admired historic cities are not remembered because they accommodated the most automobiles. They are remembered because they created places where people want to live, work, visit, and resettle.

San Miguel is already one of those cities. Now it has the opportunity to build a transportation system worthy of that distinction.

Johanna Zmud and her husband, Carlos, owned a transportation research consultancy in the U.S. They now live in San Miguel de Allende, where they own and manage a boutique hotel. Johanna continues transportation consulting.

World.title: Mexico gets favorable ruling in Vulcan trade accord violation case — but it’s far from over
World.content:
The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) — an arm of the World Bank — issued a mixed ruling in the arbitration process initiated against Mexico by U.S.-based Vulcan Materials Company.

In what is being framed as a favorable ruling for Mexico, the ICSID dismissed almost all of the company’s claims, except for one measure related to the expropriation of a property operated by a Vulcan subsidiary.

In that regard, the ICSID ruled that Mexico violated the North American Free Trade Agreement, which was still in effect when the complaint was filed in 2018, by shutting down quarrying operations managed by Calica, a Vulcan subsidiary.

Although Vulcan sought US $1.53 billion in damages plus interest and costs, the tribunal awarded the company only negligible monetary damages.

The final decision remains confidential until officially released. Vulcan said it will discuss the ruling during its Q2 earnings call on Wednesday.

Mexico’s Economy Ministry (SE) said the government is “carefully analyzing the ICSID decision to determine what legal actions are available.”

The government had been negotiating with Vulcan to permanently end limestone extraction in what is now a protected natural area in the state of Quintana Roo. Earlier this month, President Claudia Sheinbaum said any agreement would require the company to relocate operations to an environmentally viable site and fund environmental remediation of the affected zone.

In a statement, the SE said that Mexico “reaffirms its commitment to foreign investment that brings innovation, good wages and environmental protection, as well as to respecting the rules and procedures contained in international treaties as a fundamental element to provide the legal certainty that makes economic development possible.”

Vulcan, a producer of ready-mixed concrete and asphalt, filed the complaint with the tribunal in 2018, accusing Mexico of violating NAFTA by repudiating an agreement to unlock a portion of Vulcan’s aggregates reserves and arbitrarily shutting down its quarrying operations in the state of Quintana Roo.

Mexican environmental authorities closed parts of Calica’s limestone operations in Quintana Roo in 2018. The government canceled deepwater port access and shipping privileges even though Vulcan’s concession over the property is valid until 2037.

Operations were completely shuttered in May 2022 (the government claimed underwater limestone extraction was causing environmental damage) and Navy personnel seized the company’s port in March 2023.

In September 2024, the government designated 53,000 hectares between Playa del Carmen and Tulum, encompassing the port and limestone operations, a protected natural area.

With reports from El Economista, Reforma, Aristegui Noticias and Mexico Business News

World.title: CFE: Power outages reduced by nearly 40% since 2024
World.content:
The Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) reported that power outages fell 39% during the first half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2024, attributed to a “historic investment” in the expansion and modernization of the country’s transmission and distribution networks.

Speaking at the Industrial Exhibition of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), Mexico section, head of CFE Emilia Calleja said that system restoration times were also “significantly reduced,” typically resolved within one to three hours.

Calleja noted that improvements in electricity coverage respond to CFE’s updated strategy to enhance and modernize distribution network capacity, as attention had long been focused primarily on generation.

The head of CFE explained that “modern, robust and intelligent grids” allow for the integration of new energy sources, remote operation, anticipation of failures and, above all, a better response to natural disasters.

The latter has a direct precedent in the aftermath of Hurricane Otis, which in October 2023 devastated much of Guerrero’s electrical infrastructure, leaving more than 500,000 customers without power. It took the CFE a record time of seven days to restore service in that region.

“This experience showed us the importance of having a resilient infrastructure, qualified and well-trained personnel, and above all, technology that allows us to respond quickly,” Calleja said.

For this purpose, between 2024 and 2030, CFE is implementing a program exceeding 244 billion pesos, including 15 billion pesos (US $859 million) in 2025-2026 alone, to strengthen distribution with new poles, meters and conductors.

The move is enhanced by the renewable energy plan recently presented by Energy Minister Luz Elena González. In June, González explained that the government aims to add 32,475 megawatts of generation capacity to the national electricity system by 2030, of which approximately 22,376 megawatts — roughly 70% — will come from renewable sources.

Speaking at Sheinbaum’s mañanera, Calleja also highlighted the emblematic project of the Rafael Galván Maldonado Solar Park in Puerto Peñasco, Sonora, which upon completion of its four stages will reach 1,000 megawatts, becoming the largest solar installation in the Americas.

With reports from La Jornada and El Heraldo de México

World.title: Spain’s Repsol is selling half its Gulf oil project to Talos Energy, a US company
World.content:
Spanish oil company Repsol has agreed to sell half of its Block 29 oil and gas development project in the Gulf of Mexico to Talos Energy.

Repsol will bring the U.S. company into its project by selling it a 50% stake in exchange for two payments totaling more than US $50 million.

The transaction is subject to approval by Mexico’s Energy Ministry and the National Antitrust Commission.

Headquartered in Houston, Texas, Talos is acquiring a working interest in Block 29, located in the Salinas-Sureste Basin approximately 88 kilometers offshore of the state of Tabasco. This 3,254 square-kilometer area in the southern Gulf of Mexico has seen more than a dozen deepwater discoveries.

Block 29 contains the Polok and Chinwol oil discoveries, which together are estimated to contain more than 200 million barrels of oil equivalent in gross recoverable resources, along with multiple additional exploration prospects.

The block features a floating production, storage- and offloading-based development concept anchored by existing oil discoveries described by Energy-pedia news as “well-positioned to serve as a hub for future developments and nearby discoveries.”

The two payments offered by Talos are a contingent payment of US $30 million at the time of the final investment decision (FID) and a cash stake of up to US $20 million in the next exploration well. Talos will also be asked for the reimbursement of “certain pre-closing costs.”

Upon closing, Talos will hold a 50% working interest and, together with Repsol, will be the sole participants in the block. The partners expect to reach a FID early next year.

Repsol acquired 100% of the rights to Block 29 in 2025, assuming full operational and strategic responsibility for the asset, after Petronas (Malaysia’s national oil and gas corporation) and Harbour (the largest London-listed independent oil and gas company) relinquished their stakes.

In a statement, Talos Chairman and CEO Paul Goodfellow expressed confidence in working alongside Repsol as progress is made on Block 29.

“This stake adds a high-quality, large-scale development opportunity and significant exploration potential in a proven deepwater basin, further boosting the third pillar of our strategy and strengthening our long-term growth portfolio,” he said.

Talos said the “discoveries and identified prospects target amplitude-supported Miocene reservoirs analogous to fields [the company] has successfully developed and produced in the Gulf of America [sic].” The investment reinforces Talos’ “strategic focus on opportunities where its deepwater subsurface expertise provides a competitive advantage.”

With reports from El Economista, Economía Digital, Energy-pedia news and Offshore Engineer Magazine

World.title: Great escapes: Summertime adventures accessible from Guadalajara
World.content:
Guadalajara is the perfect location for people looking for a quick escape from noise and congestion on a fine summer day. The city is bordered to the north by gorgeous Oblatos Canyon and to the west by Bosque la Primavera, a magnificent pine and oak forest the size of 42,657 World Cup soccer fields.

Guadalajara also happens to sit at the center of an area where all five of Mexico’s main ecosystems converge. This puts tapatios (Guadalajara residents) within a day’s drive of mountains, beaches, deserts, rivers, slot canyons, hot springs and Mexico’s largest lake.

My wife and I described 90 of these sites in our three-volume series “Outdoors in Western Mexico,” no longer in print but available in digital form.

The importance of finding a good guide

These days, I suggest that hikers contact local guides to arrange for excursions out in the blue. The guides know the territory, the people who live there, the weather patterns and the feasibility of transit on a given day. On top of that, you’ll have a chance to contribute to the local economy.

One of those knowledgeable guides is outdoor enthusiast Mike Gallegos. Mike is the founder of Senderismo Guadalajara, which organizes hikes and climbs all over Western Mexico.

500 meters straight down

As I mentioned above, Guadalajara has some great outdoor sites located immediately adjacent to the city. For example, you can take a bus to Parque Puerta de la Barranca at the northern edge of town for a good look at magnificent, 500-meter-deep Cañon de Oblatos, also called Cañon de Huentitán. Very near the park, there’s a steep trail — once part of the famed Camino Real — which takes you to the Santiago River at the bottom. Here you’ll find graceful Puente de Arcediano, the second suspension bridge built in the Americas.

To get back up to the city, Senderismo Guadalajara offers two unforgettable, adrenaline-raising routes. One is via the Árbol de la Bruja (“Witch’s Tree”), while the other takes you up an abandoned cable-car track. Hang on to your hat!

Hot river, cool forest

At its Western edge, greater Guadalajara butts up against the Primavera Forest. Here, Senderismo Guadalajara has an exciting hike following the forest’s famed Río Caliente to the bizarre Cascada Esmeralda, which looks cold and alpine from a distance, but turns out to be hot and steamy up close. At its source, this river literally boils its way out of a spot you may be tempted to call the “Gates of Hell.”

For a totally different experience in this forest, you can hike seven kilometers atop mesas covered with pine and oak trees to reach Nejahuete Tower, better known as Torre Dos. Here you can climb up to a platform manned by forest-fire spotters 24 hours a day. The view from this tower is truly breathtaking.

‘The Tooth’

Another outstanding site on Guadalajara’s perimeter is “El Diente,” located only six kilometers north of the City’s busy Periférico or Ring Road. A veritable forest of giant rocks stands here in total silence except for the grunts of rock climbers who consider the monoliths ideal for perfecting their techniques. These hard rocks were once part of the Earth’s mantle and may be 30 million years old. You’ll enjoy taking Senderismo Guadalajara’s six-kilometer loop hike around the mass of monoliths.

Once you drive out of the city, you’ll find great summertime escapes at every turn.

Stargazing on Ceboruco Volcano

Ceboruco is a massive, still active volcano, 2,280 meters high, in the state of Nayarit, a two-hour drive from Guadalajara. The camino to the top is in good condition — and don’t be surprised if you see road runners along the way.

Senderismo Guadalajara will arrange for you to camp on the flat, grassy floor of an old crater a few meters below a billowing and hissing fumarole, with a spectacular view of the starry sky. The next day, you can hike to another of Ceboruco’s seven craters, from whose rim you can gaze down at a dramatic tongue of lava stretching off into the distance. Those “ants” you see crossing the rubble far, far away are actually buses and semi-trailers!

Comala Falls: Am I in paradise?

A two-hour drive to the southwest of Guadalajara brings you to the foot of an utterly spectacular waterfall. You can practically jump out of your car and straight into the delightful, bubbling pool at the foot of the cascade. “What more could I ask for?” you say, and Mike Gallegos replies: “More than you would ever believe.”

There are, in fact, 11 more waterfalls upstream. Welcome to paradise!

There are other falls and volcanoes near Guadalajara, too. But in case you get a yen for a jungle experience instead, you might drive to Huilotán Ecological Park, 90 minutes north of town, where you can camp next to spring-fed pools beneath mango and fig trees, your eyes peeled for military macaws flying overhead. Oh, did I mention the 100-meter-tall waterfall and the fish-fry dinner?

14 geysers and a psychedelic bell

Next, for something truly different, I recommend the 14 geysers of Los Patitos River, located 30 kilometers north of Huilotán. Of course, there are hot pools, too, so don’t forget your swimsuit.

Finally, how about a little mountain that stands in a category all its own? La Campana (“The Bell”), located 160 kilometers west of Guadalajara, features giant wave-shaped rock formations that look as if they could have been designed by Antoni Gaudí. Don’t forget your camera!

To start exploring Guadalajara’s natural wonders, contact Mike Gallegos at WhatsApp +52 (331) 136-8254.

John Pint has lived near Guadalajara, Jalisco, for more than 30 years and is the author of “A Guide to West Mexico’s Guachimontones and Surrounding Area” and co-author of “Outdoors in Western Mexico.” More of his writing can be found on his website.

World.title: MND Local: Balancing preservation and growth in Puerto Vallarta
World.content:
Puerto Vallarta has always known how to attract people. For decades, visitors have arrived searching for the same things: beautiful beaches, a welcoming community, incredible food and the feeling that life moves just a little differently here. But success brings its own challenges for the people living here year-round.

This week, three stories highlight different aspects of life in Puerto Vallarta: federal concerns about water quality at one of the city’s beaches, the arrival of electric buses aimed at modernizing public transportation, and the ongoing work of protecting the sea turtles that return to the region’s coastline each year.

Playa del Cuale flagged in federal water quality monitoring

One of Puerto Vallarta’s most recognizable beaches, Playa del Cuale, has been classified as unsuitable for recreational use following the latest federal water quality monitoring program.

The Federal Commission for the Protection against Health Risks (Cofepris) included the beach among five in Mexico that exceeded permitted bacteria levels during its most recent testing between June 15 and July 1. Cofepris tests beaches by measuring levels of enterococci bacteria, an indicator used to determine whether seawater meets health standards for activities such as swimming. Beaches that exceed established limits are classified as not suitable for recreational use until conditions improve.

The classification doesn’t mean Puerto Vallarta’s beaches as a whole failed inspection. Cofepris reported that 98.3% of beaches tested nationwide met the required standards for recreational use. However, the result draws attention to Playa del Cuale and raises questions about what contributed to the elevated bacterial levels and what measures will be taken to address the issue. Located near the mouth of the Cuale River, the beach is an area where factors such as rainfall runoff, drainage systems and coastal conditions can all influence water quality.

For residents, the report serves as a reminder of the importance of monitoring and maintaining the environmental systems that support a growing coastal city.

Puerto Vallarta receives first electric buses as public transport changes begin

Puerto Vallarta has taken its first step toward introducing electric public transportation, with the arrival of new electric buses designed to operate along one of the city’s busiest corridors.

The first units arrived as part of a state-backed electromobility project led by the government of Jalisco. Seven articulated electric buses are expected to serve the Francisco Medina Ascencio corridor, connecting important areas of the city, including the hotel zone, Marina Vallarta, Ixtapa and the Centro Universitario de la Costa area.

The buses are designed to carry high passenger volumes and include features such as air conditioning and accessibility improvements.

The introduction of electric buses represents one of the most significant changes to Puerto Vallarta’s public transportation system in years. For residents, however, the success of the project will ultimately be measured by how it performs in daily life.

Public transportation is a major issue for many people who depend on buses to travel to work, school and essential services. As Puerto Vallarta continues to grow, questions about traffic congestion, reliability and accessibility have become increasingly important.

The arrival of electric units marks the beginning of a transition, but residents will be watching how quickly the new system expands and what improvements it brings to everyday commuting.

Boca de Tomates turtle camp reports thousands of hatchlings released

While Puerto Vallarta continues to develop, conservation groups are working to protect one of the species that’s long been part of the region’s natural identity.

The Boca de Tomates turtle camp reported the release of 30,864 sea turtle hatchlings during the latest nesting season, following efforts that protected 521 nests containing more than 36,000 eggs.

The conservation program, located along the northern coastline of Puerto Vallarta, works throughout the nesting season to monitor beaches, protect nests from threats and help ensure hatchlings can safely make their way into the Pacific Ocean. The annual effort depends on the work of conservation staff, volunteers and community members who patrol nesting areas, relocate vulnerable nests when necessary and organize releases once the young turtles are ready to begin their journey.

For residents, the results highlight the role that local conservation organizations play in protecting Puerto Vallarta’s natural environment. While discussions about coastal growth often focus on development pressures, programs like Boca de Tomates demonstrate the ongoing work taking place to preserve local wildlife.

As Puerto Vallarta continues to change, the annual return of sea turtles and the thousands of hatchlings given a better chance of survival through these efforts remains an important part of the region’s environmental story.

Together, these stories offer a snapshot of a city continuing to evolve. Puerto Vallarta’s growth brings new opportunities, but it also highlights the importance of investing in the systems, services and natural resources that support the community that calls it home.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Vivo Brazil Profit Hits US$308M on Mobile, Fiber Growth
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Vivo Brazil earnings for the second quarter of 2026 showed a 17.0% jump in net profit, as Telefônica Brasil (B3: VIVT3), the country’s largest telecom operator, reported net income of R$1.57 billion (~US$308 million). The result, released on July 27, was in line with market expectations and marked the strongest EBITDA growth since the third quarter of 2023.

Key Facts —Net Profit. R$1.57 billion (~US$308 million), up 17.0% year-on-year in Q2 2026. —Operating Revenue. R$15.76 billion (~US$3.09 billion), a 7.6% increase from the prior year. —EBITDA. R$6.58 billion (~US$1.29 billion), rising 10.9% YoY with a 41.8% margin. —Growth Drivers. Mobile postpaid services, FTTH (fiber-to-the-home), and digital services. —Electronics Push. Appliance and electronics revenue jumped 27.8% to R$1.048 billion (~US$205 million), advancing Vivo’s move into consumer-electronics retail. Revenue and Profitability Drivers

Net operating revenue for Brazil‘s top carrier climbed 7.6% year-on-year to R$15.76 billion (~US$3.09 billion). The expansion was primarily fueled by its mobile postpaid segment, fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) broadband service, and a growing portfolio of digital services.

Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) reached R$6.58 billion (~US$1.29 billion). This 10.9% increase from the R$5.93 billion (~US$1.16 billion) recorded a year earlier pushed the EBITDA margin to a robust 41.8%.

For readers unfamiliar with the term, EBITDA is a widely used measure of a company’s core operating profitability. It strips out costs that can vary significantly depending on a firm’s debt structure, tax situation, and accounting choices around large asset purchases. A rising EBITDA margin, such as the one Vivo just posted, often signals that a business is gaining operating leverage — meaning each additional real of revenue is generating proportionally more profit. In Brazil’s high-volume, infrastructure-heavy telecom sector, this metric is closely watched because building and maintaining networks requires enormous upfront capital, and investors want to see those investments translate into efficient, recurring cash generation.

The Push into Consumer Electronics Retail

Beyond connectivity, Vivo is expanding into consumer-electronics retail – and it is already showing up in the numbers. Revenue from appliances and electronics jumped 27.8% year over year to R$1.048 billion (~US$205 million) in the quarter.

By selling devices through its large store network and digital channels, the carrier competes more directly with traditional retailers and captures higher-margin hardware sales alongside recurring service fees – a diversification foreign investors are watching closely.

This strategy mirrors a broader global trend among telecom operators seeking to become more than simple connectivity providers. By controlling the point of sale for smartphones, laptops, and smart-home devices, a carrier can bundle hardware with long-term service contracts, potentially reducing customer churn. In Brazil, where a significant portion of the population still buys electronics through installment plans, a trusted carrier with an existing billing relationship can position itself as a natural financing partner. The open question is whether Vivo can scale this retail push without the inventory risk and thin margins that typically challenge dedicated electronics chains.

Market Position: Vivo vs. TIM and Claro

Vivo operates as the market leader in Brazil’s competitive telecom sector, which is dominated by three major players. Its main rivals are TIM Brasil and Claro, the local subsidiary of Mexican telecom group América Móvil.

The company’s scale in mobile postpaid and fiber broadband provides a defensive moat. While all three carriers compete aggressively on 5G expansion, Vivo’s latest results underscore its ability to grow profitability while maintaining its number-one market share.

For context, Brazil’s telecom market is structured around a national regulatory framework overseen by Anatel, the country’s telecommunications agency. The three-way rivalry among Vivo, TIM, and Claro has shaped pricing and investment cycles for years. Postpaid mobile customers — those who pay a monthly bill rather than topping up prepaid credit — are particularly valuable because they generate more predictable revenue and tend to consume more data. Fiber-to-the-home broadband, meanwhile, has become a key battleground as millions of Brazilian households upgrade from older copper-based connections. Vivo’s ability to lead in both categories simultaneously is a central reason its financial results have drawn consistent attention from analysts covering Latin American equities.

Shareholder Returns and Capital Allocation

Telefônica Brasil has a well-established policy of distributing earnings to shareholders through dividends and interest on equity (JCP). The company continued this practice in the second quarter, though the exact per-share payout amount for the period was not specified in the initial earnings summary.

For expats and foreign investors holding VIVT3 shares on the B3 exchange, these regular distributions form a key part of the stock’s total return profile. The company’s free cash flow generation supports these payouts, even as it invests in network expansion.

Interest on equity, or JCP, is a Brazil-specific mechanism that allows companies to treat a portion of shareholder distributions as a tax-deductible expense, making it a tax-efficient way to return capital. For international investors, understanding the interplay between dividends and JCP is important because the tax treatment can differ depending on one’s country of residence and whether a double-taxation treaty applies. What remains to be seen is how Vivo will balance its capital allocation priorities going forward — specifically, whether the accelerating push into electronics retail will require heavier inventory investment that could temporarily pressure the free cash flow available for shareholder returns.

What It Means for Foreign Investors

For international readers, the results demonstrate the resilience of Brazil’s large consumer market. A net profit of ~US$308 million in a single quarter reflects the scale opportunity in Latin America’s biggest economy, where demand for premium data services continues to rise.

The US dollar figures, converted at a rate of 5.1 reais, offer a clear lens for portfolio evaluation. Vivo’s push into device retail adds a new growth vector, though execution risk remains a factor to monitor in future earnings calls.

Currency volatility is a permanent consideration when evaluating Brazilian equities. The real has historically swung widely against the dollar, meaning that even strong local-currency results can translate into uneven returns for foreign portfolios. Beyond the exchange rate, investors will likely be watching two broader themes. First, whether Brazil’s macroeconomic environment — including the trajectory of interest rates set by the central bank — supports continued consumer spending on telecom and electronics. Second, how the competitive dynamics with TIM and Claro evolve as all three players deepen their fiber and 5G footprints. These factors will help determine whether Vivo’s current margin strength proves durable or faces compression in the quarters ahead.

World.title: TIM Brazil Profit Hits Record US$203M on Fiber, Mobile
World.content:
Brazil · Business

TIM Brazil earnings reached a historic high in the second quarter of 2026, as one of the country’s largest wireless carriers reported a normalized net profit of R$1.036 billion (~US$203 million), a 6.2% increase from a year earlier and its strongest-ever result for a second quarter.

Key Facts —Record Net Profit. TIM Brasil’s normalized net profit reached R$1.036 billion (~US$203 million) in Q2 2026, up 6.2% year over year – its best-ever second quarter. —Net Revenue. Net revenue rose 5.5% to R$6.965 billion (~US$1.366 billion), led by mobile service revenue and fast-growing fiber broadband. —EBITDA & Margin. Normalized EBITDA climbed about 7% to roughly R$3.5 billion (~US$686 million), lifting the margin to 51.5%. —Shareholder Payout. The board approved R$400 million (~US$78 million) in interest on equity (JCP) for the quarter; 2026 remuneration guidance is R$5.3-5.5 billion (~US$1.04-1.08 billion). —Reported. Results were released on July 27, 2026. TIM (B3: TIMS3) is controlled by Italy’s Telecom Italia. The Profit Engine: Mobile and Fiber

TIM Brasil, the Brazilian arm of Italy’s Telecom Italia, saw net revenue climb 5.5% year over year to R$6.965 billion (~US$1.366 billion). Normalized EBITDA rose about 7% to roughly R$3.5 billion (~US$686 million), pushing the operating margin to 51.5% – among the highest in Brazilian telecom.

Management credited two engines. Mobile service revenue kept growing on the back of a higher-value postpaid customer base and disciplined cost control. At the same time, fixed broadband surged as customers adopted TIM’s ‘Ultrafibra’ fiber-to-the-home service, a segment the company is scaling to cut churn by bundling mobile and home internet.

The result extends a run of margin expansion for TIM, which has focused on premium postpaid users rather than chasing low-value prepaid volume. In a mature mobile market, converting revenue growth into record profit signals effective cost management. For context, postpaid customers typically sign contracts and generate higher average revenue per user than prepaid subscribers, who top up credit as needed and can switch carriers more easily. By concentrating on this stickier, higher-spending base, TIM has built a more predictable income stream even as the overall number of mobile users in Brazil levels off.

Why the Record Matters

A record second-quarter profit lands as Brazil’s carriers compete on 5G coverage and fiber reach. TIM operates as one of the country’s ‘Big Three’ alongside Vivo (Telefonica) and Claro (America Movil), and its results broadly matched analyst expectations for the quarter.

The broadband push is central to the story. Fixed-line and fiber revenue has become TIM’s fastest-growing line, diversifying a business long dominated by mobile and giving it a second pillar as smartphone penetration matures. Fiber-to-the-home technology delivers internet via glass cables straight to a residence, offering speeds far beyond traditional copper-wire connections. For TIM, each new fiber customer represents not just a fresh revenue source but also a chance to sell a combined mobile-and-home package, which tends to keep subscribers loyal for longer. This convergence strategy mirrors what large telecom groups have pursued in Europe and elsewhere, though the pace of fiber rollout in Brazil varies sharply by region, with dense urban corridors receiving investment first.

Shareholder Returns

TIM’s board approved R$400 million (~US$78 million) in interest on equity (JCP) for the quarter – a tax-efficient form of dividend common in Brazil. For 2026, the company has guided to total shareholder remuneration of R$5.3 billion to R$5.5 billion (~US$1.04-1.08 billion).

For investors holding TIMS3, those recurring distributions are a core part of the stock’s total-return case, funded by TIM’s strong cash generation even as it keeps investing in fiber and 5G. Interest on equity works differently from a standard cash dividend: Brazilian firms can classify a portion of shareholder payouts as a financial expense, which reduces their corporate tax bill while still putting money in investors’ pockets. The practice is widely used among listed Brazilian companies and is one reason headline dividend yields in the market can look attractive to foreign eyes, though the exact tax treatment depends on an investor’s home country and the applicable double-taxation treaty.

What It Means for Foreign Investors

TIM Brasil is majority-owned by Telecom Italia and listed on Brazil’s B3 exchange as TIMS3. For international investors, the record quarter underscores the appeal of Brazil’s large, data-hungry consumer market and TIM‘s shift toward a convergent mobile-plus-fiber model.

The usual caveat applies: returns for dollar-based investors depend on the Brazilian real. At about 5.1 reais to the US dollar, the quarter’s R$1.036 billion profit converts to roughly US$203 million, but sharp currency swings can amplify or erase gains when translated back into dollars. Beyond the exchange rate, foreign portfolio investors also weigh Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, which influences both the cost of capital and the relative appeal of dividend-paying stocks versus fixed-income instruments. What to watch next is whether TIM can sustain its margin trajectory as fiber build-out costs rise and whether the real stabilizes enough to preserve the purchasing power of those shareholder payouts for overseas holders. Another open question is how the competitive dynamics among the Big Three will evolve if one rival accelerates its own bundled-service discounts, potentially pressuring the industry’s currently healthy profitability.

World.title: LitioMX Lithium Plan Sets 2026-2030 Path for Mexico’s Battery Push
World.content:
Mexico · Business

Key Facts —LitioMX Lithium Plan LitioMX’s 2026-2030 program, published in Mexico’s official gazette, proposes a pre-industrial pilot battery plant. —Battery pilot plant LitioMX plans to install a small-scale industrial plant to produce battery packs and support pilot energy-storage projects. —Core objectives The program lists six objectives, including exploration, developing active battery materials, and strengthening the regulatory framework. —2026 budget LitioMX will remain without investment spending in the 2026 budget proposal, receiving only operating funds, according to Bloomberg Línea. —Sonora focus The lithium strategy is centered on the state of Sonora, though specific deposit development plans were not detailed in the published sources.

LitioMX lithium ambitions are taking clearer shape after Mexico’s state-owned company published its 2026-2030 institutional program on 24 July 2026, outlining plans for exploration, battery material development, and a small-scale battery pack plant.

Lithium production in South America; Mexico is building its own lithium industry (illustrative). Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

A State Monopoly on Lithium

For foreign investors, Mexico’s lithium landscape changed decisively in 2022 when the government nationalized the mineral, declaring it a strategic resource reserved exclusively for the state.

The decree created Litio para México, known as LitioMX, a decentralized public agency with the sole mandate to explore, extract, and commercialize lithium.

No private concessions for lithium mining are permitted. The legal framework bars foreign and domestic private companies from owning lithium reserves or production.

This model mirrors approaches in other resource-nationalist economies, but it leaves international investors watching from the sidelines unless mixed-investment or service-contract frameworks eventually emerge.

Inside the 2026-2030 Program

The newly published institutional program sets six objectives for LitioMX through the end of the decade.

First, the company aims to consolidate exploration, evaluation, and technical management of Mexico’s lithium resources.

Second, it will promote technology to produce active materials for batteries. Third, it plans to establish a small-scale industrial plant to manufacture battery packs.

Additional goals include developing energy-storage projects, advancing circular-economy and performance-improving technologies, and strengthening the regulatory framework for the lithium sector.

The document does not specify a total investment figure, a production capacity, or a concrete extraction flowsheet for any particular deposit.

The Sonora Deposits and Unrealized Potential

Mexico’s most promising lithium resources lie in the state of Sonora, primarily in clay deposits that are geologically complex and commercially untested at scale.

Unlike South America’s brine-based lithium or Australia’s hard-rock spodumene, Sonora’s clay deposits require processing technology that is still being developed globally.

The institutional program confirms a broader Sonora-focused strategy, but the published sources do not verify a finalized extraction plan for a specific deposit such as Bacadehuachi.

Analysts at Speyside Group have noted that Mexico has yet to unlock its lithium opportunity, citing technological hurdles and the absence of a clear path to commercial production.

Budget Constraints and the Pilot Plant

Despite the ambitious program, LitioMX faces immediate financial limitations. Bloomberg Línea reported that the company will remain without investment spending in the 2026 budget proposal.

El Financiero separately noted that LitioMX would only have budget for payroll in 2026, underscoring the gap between strategic rhetoric and fiscal reality.

The small-scale battery pack plant represents a tangible first step, but without capital expenditure funding, the timeline for construction and operation remains uncertain.

No confirmed project partners have been announced for the battery plant or lithium processing plans in the available official documents.

What Foreign Investors Should Watch

The 2026-2030 program signals the government’s intent to move beyond resource nationalism into downstream battery manufacturing, but execution capability is unproven.

Investors should monitor whether Mexico’s broader mixed-investment infrastructure plan, valued at roughly US$325 billion for 2026-2030, eventually creates openings for private participation in lithium-related projects.

Legal firms such as Jones Day have highlighted recent reforms that unlock private investment in strategic infrastructure, though lithium extraction remains firmly under state control.

For now, the opportunity for foreign capital is limited to potential service contracts, technology licensing, or participation in downstream energy-storage projects that do not involve ownership of the resource itself.

The Sonora deposits remain a long-term proposition. Any progress on extraction technology or pilot processing results will be critical signals for the market.

The Road Ahead

LitioMX’s institutional program provides a policy roadmap, but the absence of a dedicated investment budget for 2026 raises questions about near-term milestones.

The battery pack pilot plant, if funded and built, would mark Mexico’s first state-run step into battery manufacturing, a sector dominated by Asian and Western players.

International observers will also track whether the regulatory framework evolves to permit joint ventures or technology partnerships without violating the constitutional ban on private lithium concessions.

For expats and investors following Latin America, Mexico’s lithium story is still in its early chapters, with Sonora’s clay deposits representing both a strategic asset and a technical challenge that has yet to be solved.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is LitioMX and what does it do?

LitioMX (Litio para México) is a decentralized public agency created by the Mexican government in 2022. It holds the exclusive mandate to explore, extract, and commercialize lithium, which was nationalized as a strategic resource.

Can foreign companies invest in Mexico’s lithium sector?

Foreign companies cannot hold lithium mining concessions in Mexico. The constitutional framework reserves lithium exclusively for the state.

Potential opportunities may exist through service contracts, technology licensing, or downstream projects that do not involve resource ownership.

Where are Mexico’s main lithium deposits located?

Mexico’s most significant lithium resources are in the state of Sonora, primarily in clay deposits. These deposits are geologically complex and require processing technology that is not yet commercially proven at scale.

World.title: Bolivia Investment: Paz Secures US$300 Million
World.content:
Bolivia · Business

Key Facts —Bolivia Investment President Rodrigo Paz announced about US$300 million for a highway, Amazon power and police, funded by CAF and the IDB. —Highway project Funds target the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi highway in the Los Yungas area of La Paz department, a key transport link in a rugged agricultural region. —Amazon electricity A portion of the financing supports electrical integration in Bolivia’s Amazon region, building on a prior US$204 million IDB loan for the same purpose. —Police modernization The package includes resources to modernize the Bolivian Police, though specific equipment or training details have not been released. —Broader context The announcement marks the Paz government’s first major investment push backed by multilateral lenders since taking office, amid a severe foreign-exchange shortage.

President Rodrigo Paz announced a roughly US$300 million Bolivia La Paz investment package on July 26, 2026, targeting a key highway, Amazon-region electrical integration, and police modernization. The financing, the new government’s first major push backed by multilateral lenders, comes from the CAF (Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean) and the IDB (Inter-American Development Bank).

A view of La Paz, Bolivia. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

What the US$300 Million Package Funds

The roughly US$300 million package covers three distinct areas. The first is the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi highway, located in the Los Yungas region of La Paz department, a mountainous, agriculturally important zone northeast of the capital city.

A Separate La Paz City Package

During a civic anniversary session for La Paz’s 217th year, President Paz also outlined a local investment package of roughly Bs 1 billion. This city-focused spending targets road infrastructure, including the Escoma-Charazani highway, completion of the Unduavi-Chulumani route, and bridges at four river crossings.

Economic Context for Foreign Readers

The roughly US$300 million multilateral package is the Paz government’s first big investment push since taking office. Bolivia faces a severe foreign-exchange shortage, dwindling gas exports, and inflation pressures that prompted an IMF agreement earlier in 2026.

Political Significance of the Announcement

Paz chose the sesión de honor for La Paz’s 217th civic anniversary to unveil the roughly US$300 million package. The timing underscores the political importance of the department, a traditional stronghold of opposition to the former ruling Movement Toward Socialism party.

What Comes Next for Investors

Foreign investors should watch for the finalized terms of the CAF and IDB financing agreements. The exact disbursement schedules, procurement rules, and project timelines will determine near-term opportunities.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is the Bolivia La Paz investment package worth?

President Rodrigo Paz announced roughly US$300 million in financing from CAF and the IDB for a highway in La Paz department’s Los Yungas region, electrical integration in the Amazon, and police modernization.

What does the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi highway project involve?

The project funds rehabilitation of the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi road in the Los Yungas area of La Paz department. It is one of three components in the roughly US$300 million multilateral financing package.

Is the La Paz city package the same as the US$300 million announcement?

No. The roughly US$300 million package is funded by multilateral lenders for a highway, Amazon electricity, and police modernization. A separate La Paz city package, announced in bolivianos, totals about Bs 1 billion for local roads, health, water, and other municipal projects.

World.title: Dominican Republic Electricity Demand Hits 4,203 MW Record
World.content:
Caribbean · Business

Key Facts —Dominican Republic Electricity Demand National electricity demand hit a record 4,203 MW on July 27, 2026, per the Energy Ministry. —Previous record 4,195.26 MW set on Wednesday, July 24, 2026, just four days earlier. —July records The July 28 peak was the fourth all-time demand record set during the month. —System stability The SENI grid met the record load without blackouts, maintaining stable nationwide supply. —Primary drivers Intense summer heat and increased consumption from economic growth.

Dominican Republic electricity demand surged to an unprecedented 4,203 megawatts (MW) on Monday, July 28, 2026, setting a new all-time high for the Caribbean nation’s power grid as a relentless summer heat wave and accelerating economic activity pushed the system to its latest peak.

Electricity transmission lines (illustrative). Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

A Month of Broken Records

The milestone was recorded at exactly 8:56 p.m. local time within the Sistema Eléctrico Nacional Interconectado (SENI), the national interconnected grid that serves the majority of the country’s 11 million residents. The grid’s coordinating body, known as the Organismo Coordinador (OC-SENI), confirmed the figure.

This new peak shattered the previous record of 4,195.26 MW, which had been set just four days earlier on Wednesday, July 24, 2026, at 9:32 p.m. That benchmark itself had eclipsed a record of 4,185.11 MW established only a day before, on Tuesday, July 23.

The sequence of broken records began earlier in the month, with demand reaching 4,166.52 MW on Thursday, July 16, 2026, at 9:58 p.m. The July 28 peak therefore represents the fourth time the country’s electricity consumption hit an all-time high in under two weeks.

The Heat Factor: Cooling a Tropical Economy

For foreign residents and investors accustomed to the Dominican Republic’s year-round warmth, the summer of 2026 has been exceptional. A prolonged heat wave has blanketed the region, driving residents and businesses to rely heavily on air conditioning, particularly during the evening peak hours when families return home.

Unlike temperate-zone grids that peak in winter for heating, tropical electricity systems like the SENI are summer-peaking. The record-setting times – consistently between 8:56 p.m. and 9:58 p.m. – highlight how residential cooling demand after sunset, combined with still-warm temperatures, creates the maximum strain on generation and transmission infrastructure.

The Ministry of Energy and Mines attributed the surge directly to high temperatures and increased consumption. This pattern mirrors trends seen across other warm-climate grids globally, where more frequent and intense heat waves are shifting baseline demand expectations upward.

Economic Growth Adds to Grid Strain

Beyond the weather, structural economic expansion is a major driver of the Dominican Republic’s rising electricity appetite. The country has been one of Latin America’s top-performing economies, with growth fueled by tourism, free-trade zones, construction, and foreign direct investment.

More economic activity means more commercial office towers, manufacturing lines, hotels, and logistics centers drawing power throughout the day. This rising base load means that when a heat wave spikes residential cooling demand, the starting point is already higher than in previous years.

For expat entrepreneurs and real estate investors, the growing demand signals a market with expanding energy needs. It also underscores the importance of the government’s ongoing efforts to modernize generation capacity and diversify the energy matrix to keep pace with consumption.

Grid Stability Amid the Stress Test

Despite the record strain, the SENI system held firm. Official reports explicitly stated that the grid was able to cover the increase in consumption while maintaining stable service nationwide, with no blackouts reported during the peak event.

This outcome represents a significant achievement for a country that has historically struggled with power reliability. For decades, blackouts and voltage fluctuations were a frustrating reality for households and a cost of doing business for companies operating on the island.

The stable performance under maximum stress suggests that recent investments in generation plants and transmission infrastructure are delivering results. For foreign investors, grid reliability is a critical factor when evaluating the Dominican Republic as a destination for operations that require uninterrupted power, such as data centers or advanced manufacturing.

What This Means for Foreigners and Investors

For the expat community and international businesses, the record demand carries both reassurance and a cautionary note. The grid’s ability to meet 4,203 MW without incident is a positive signal of improved resilience in the country’s electricity sector.

However, a series of broken records in rapid succession indicates that the margin between peak demand and available generation may be narrowing. While the exact installed capacity of the SENI was not specified in the July 28 report, sustained demand growth will require continued capacity expansion to maintain the stability demonstrated during this event.

Investors in tourism, real estate, and industry should monitor future announcements from the Ministry of Energy and Mines regarding generation projects. The Dominican Republic has been actively incorporating natural gas and renewable energy sources, a diversification strategy that becomes more urgent as consumption records fall with increasing frequency.

The Broader Regional Context

The Dominican Republic’s demand spike is not occurring in isolation. Across the hemisphere, grids from the United States to Brazil have been setting summer records as heat waves become more intense and persistent.

The largest US grid, PJM Interconnection, also reported record demand in early July 2026.

For Latin America, where air conditioning penetration is still growing, the upward trajectory of electricity demand is expected to be steeper than in more mature markets. The Dominican Republic, with its high tourism exposure and expanding middle class, sits at the intersection of these trends.

As the country continues to position itself as a hub for nearshoring and digital nomads, a reliable and scalable electricity system will be fundamental. The events of July 2026 offer a real-world test that, for now, the grid has passed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was the new record for Dominican Republic electricity demand?

The national electricity demand reached a new all-time high of 4,203 MW on Monday, July 28, 2026, at 8:56 p.m., according to the Ministry of Energy and Mines and the grid operator OC-SENI.

Why is electricity demand spiking in the Dominican Republic?

The surge is driven primarily by an intense summer heat wave that has increased air conditioning use, combined with rising base consumption from sustained economic growth in tourism, construction, and free-trade zones.

Did the record electricity demand cause blackouts?

No. Official reports confirmed that the SENI grid was able to meet the 4,203 MW peak load while maintaining stable service nationwide, with no blackouts reported during the event.

World.title: Portonave Plans US$392M Navegantes Port Expansion
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Portonave Navegantes Portonave will invest R$2 billion (~US$392 million) to expand the Navegantes container terminal in Santa Catarina. —Capacity target Annual container handling capacity to rise from 1.5 million TEU to 2 million TEU after completion. —Depth target Access channel and berthing depth to move from under 14 meters to 17 meters, dependent on a separate federal concession. —Timeline Works began in January 2024, with the first stage completed in September 2025 and the second stage running through the second half of 2026. —Ownership The terminal is controlled by Terminal Investment Limited (TiL), the ports arm of Swiss-based shipping giant Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC).

Portonave Navegantes, the Santa Catarina container terminal controlled by MSC’s Terminal Investment Limited (TiL), is pushing forward with a roughly R$2 billion (~US$392 million) modernization plan. The private terminal aims to lift its annual capacity from 1.5 million to 2 million TEU and prepare for a deeper access channel, intensifying a capacity race among southern Brazil’s ports.

A Brazilian container port (illustrative). Photo: Wikimedia Commons.
