How did he get to Syria?

After not getting where he wanted with MSF, he travelled to Türkiye and then into Syria.

Again, the journalists questioned the path he took — saying that route would lead him directly into IS territory, and that he would have known that was the case.

"I didn't actually know how to come into Syria, I didn't have a plan, because I was concerned about being involved with any group, I really didn't have an idea of what group to come from," Kamleh said in the interview.

"By chance, [Islamic State] controlled that region that I came to, and there were only two cities to come through that I heard about from other people.

"So the only way to come to Syria at that point, when I came, was to end up in the [Islamic State] territory — for me, it didn't make an issue if it was [Islamic State] or the other groups at the time."

Loading...

What did he do while in Syria?

Kamleh told the German team he was working as a doctor in the area.

"I was running emergency and the ward and the nursery. "[The] majority is normal reasons children would come to hospital — sickness or what it might be, premature birth, whatever it might [be]. "And the other side is, yes, children coming in injured with amputations or burns. Every injury you can imagine, I've seen it."

He said IS provided him and his family with a house to live in.

"I go to the hospital every day. "If they need me to come after hours, they call me, there's a phone. "It's a normal life, it's just a war zone."

The status of Islamic State-linked Australians stuck in Syria has become a major issue for the federal government. (ABC News: Baderkhan Ahmad)

He argued being a specialist paediatrician kept him separate from the IS fighters.

"If I was a doctor for big people or a surgeon, it would be a problem because — then I'm dealing with soldiers or officials, that's an issue, I will always argue that," Kamleh claimed.

"I came to do my job, and I did my job, and I was known to be a doctor for children, but I was not a soldier."

But he conceded he may have been killed if he refused IS orders. That was an issue which was referenced, in part, to his appearance in the group's propaganda videos.

Kamleh was arrested in Baghuz, the scene of a major battle by coalition forces against IS in 2019.

Did he support Islamic State ideology?

In one part of the interview, the journalist asked Kamleh about the enforcement of hard-line Islamic law by IS.

And it is clear he tried to distance himself from it, but was wary of condemning it.

"If people were caught committing adultery, they would be stoned to death, or people who were caught stealing, which is in line with the religious side," he said.

"If people were caught stealing, they would have their hands cut off — so I was aware that was occurring. I'll be honest, I didn't see it.

"I saw a few people come in before getting their hands cut off because the surgeons prepare them to get their hand amputated."

'ISIS bride' court challenge Legal experts say the Commonwealth would have risked losing a High Court challenge to counterterrorism laws if it stopped the Australian woman from returning home.

He was pressed on whether he believed that was appropriate.

"Right or wrong is not for me to argue; that's on the religious side, and if God says someone who steals that amount of something should have his hand cut off, who are you or me to argue that?" he said.

"I'm Muslim, so I can not argue against my own religion — as if I'm arguing against God, it's blasphemy, I can't do that."

Kamleh insisted it was just following the Quran.

"Go into any shop and buy the Quran, there's no other version to it, that's what it says," he said.

"If you want to open the book on human rights, we could argue both sides — what the West were bombing in Raqqa was definitely not alongside human rights.

" Getting a hand cut off is a small problem compared to … how many hundreds of children I would see injured from bombings who were innocent civilians from Western planes. "

Does he have any contact with his family?

Kamleh said he wanted to see his wife and children again, but he didn't know where they were.

He also said he had no contact with his family back in Australia.

"They didn't know I was coming," Kamleh said.

"I remember discussing with my mum … I wanted to test the water; I asked her if I could come to Türkiye, to the border, to help the Syrians, civilians.

"She said impossible. It's even close to a war zone. She said you'll not go, and she threatened me; she said if you go, I'll tell the authorities, and I will have your passport cancelled.

"Family are not willing always to know you're coming to a dangerous situation even though your intention is good."

What is Kamleh being investigated for?

A June statement by the Iraqi Supreme Court revealed there was an ongoing investigation into the man, including allegations his "activities were not limited to providing medical services."

"He adopted the extremist group's propaganda, advocating for terrorist activity not to be confined to conflict zones — a message reflecting the extremist ideology promoted by the terrorist groups during that period," it said.

Last week, the federal government said it would not provide assistance to "any Australian who made the horrific choice to join a dangerous terrorist organisation".



"We've been very clear that for some individuals in this cohort, returning to Australia would mean facing the full force of the law," a spokesperson said in a statement.

World.title: China's singing sailors could be latest weapon in fight for South China Sea
World.content:
A sailor stares mournfully across the ocean, remembering a lover left onshore.

A sleek coast guard ship glides through an endless ocean, passing dolphins and coral reefs.

And a gentle guitar swells to an emotional high, as a singer warbles in a melancholy, smooth falsetto.

This isn't an ordinary love song; it's a declaration of devotion to China.

"Patrolling the South China Sea, guarding every sunrise and moonset over the sea," the singer proclaims.

"Guarding the distant flickering lights of myriad homes, and guarding in my heart little you and the little me."

The song, I Miss You On the South China Sea, was first released by Chinese state media earlier this year, complete with a slick music video showcasing coast guard vessels and personnel.

The music video is filled with idyllic shots of patrol boats like this. (Supplied: China Military Bugle)

An English translation version debuted this month, almost exactly 10 years after an international tribunal ruled Beijing's sweeping claims to the hotly contested waterway were not valid.

It might be slightly unconventional, but experts say it's part of a broader propaganda push to reinforce China's claims to the South China Sea — and to humanise the sailors on board the vast flotilla of Chinese Coast Guard vessels that try to enforce it.

Or, in the words of the singer, "Guarding you and me in my heart, and our beloved motherland."

What was the South China Sea arbitration?

The South China Sea has been a point of contention between China and the Philippines, among others. (AP: Aaron Favila)

Several nations have made various claims to islands and waters within the Western Pacific Ocean for generations, but tensions between China and the Philippines reached boiling point during the 2012 Scarborough Shoal stand-off.

The Philippines took the dispute to the United Nations Convention of Law and the Sea to test China's historic claims to the waters within the so-called "nine-dash line".

The tribunal found China's claims had no legal basis and China had violated the Philippines' sovereign rights, however, China has refused to accept or recognise this ruling.

On the 10th anniversary of the ruling, 14 nations including Australia, the US and the Philippines released a joint statement reaffirming their "unwavering commitment to maintaining a free and open Indo-Pacific that is peaceful, stable, and rules-based, anchored in international law".

"We reaffirm that the Award rendered ten years ago by the Arbitral Tribunal is a significant milestone and is final, legally binding, and definitive between China and the Philippines," the statement said.

The ABC has contacted China's Defence Ministry and Coast Guard for comment, but has not yet received a response.

Complex history missing in action

Personnel from the Philippines Navy and China Coast Guard clashed in the South China Sea earlier this month. (Reuters: CNC Photo)

This fraught and contested history is omitted from I Miss You On the South China Sea, which sticks with picturesque shots of ships at sunset and the romantic musings of the anonymous Chinese sailor at its heart.

Sections of the music video were purportedly filmed on one of Asia's most contested maritime features, the Scarborough Shoal, where Beijing is planning to establish a nature reserve.

The idyllic imagery is a long way from the usual news stories about the Chinese Coast Guard in the South China Sea, which typically hits the international headlines during its episodic confrontations with the Philippines coast guard, like the skirmish last week when personnel allegedly struck each other with oars, sticks and wooden batons.

In contrast, not a soul or vessel from another country features in the music clip, which shows a Chinese Coast Guard vessel in splendid isolation, tracing long arcs through empty waters, disturbed by nothing more threatening than a seagull.

"Azure sky, crystal sea, chasing gulls, blazing sun, patrolling the South China Sea," sings the protagonist.

"Guarding endless loneliness, endless vastness, and guarding this sea, this peace and harmony."

China's claims in the South China Sea cut through the majority of its neighbours' claims. (ABC News: Jarrod Fankhauser)

There are also a few slightly awkward notes, at least in the English language version.

At one moment the mysterious Chinese sailor sings that his bond with his lover proves the principle of "quantum entanglement", a term used largely by physicists who have suggested that particles of the same origin, and which once were connected, will always stay connected.

Who is the song for?

A sailor calls a loved one back home during the music video. (Supplied: China Military Bugle)

Graeme Smith, an associate professor at the Australian National University, said the song reflected the regime's "obsession with soft power" and "desire to shape the international narrative".

"It's something that China's been trying to do for a very, very long time and I think they're getting a bit better at it," he said.

But Dr Smith said the "emotional themes" and narrative suggested the song was targeted at a domestic audience and only translated after it had become a hit at home.

"That plays great in China, but probably not so much in the rest of the world," he said.

"And that's why it feels weird — because we were never the intended audience."

While the video may not top the charts outside of China, the country's reputation is on the rise in parts of the Asia Pacific.

China expert Graeme Smith says the video is part of a soft-power push. (Supplied: Pobke Photography/ANU)

A recent Pew Research Center study found most citizens in Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Sri Lanka and Pakistan had a favourable perception of China.

Recent polling from the Lowy Institute also found Australians now trusted China almost as much as the US, largely thanks to a dramatic fall in trust in America following the election of President Donald Trump.

But Dr Smith said China could lose its goodwill if it pursued its agenda too aggressively.

"They need South-East Asian countries to be on board with them," he said.

"Particularly these days with the world order shifting so drastically, they don't want to push so hard that they alienate ASEAN countries and push them towards America."

Not all content is made equal

China, like many nations, has a long history of music, films and literature that help reinforce national pride and priorities.

In times of conflict, lovers separated by duty is a well-worn storyline in both the East and West.

But China has also used music to highlight its technological and economic achievements, such as in 2019 when state news agency Xinhua released a rap ahead of its annual parliament meeting, the two sessions.

But this month, state-run newspaper China Daily was heavily criticised by the Filipino government for releasing an AI-generated video that depicted its countrymen as monkeys.

Manila demanded the "racist" and "offensive, distressing and unacceptable" video be removed.

World.title: Gold Coast nurse with rare disorder awaiting third kidney transplant
World.content:
Gold Coast nurse Daniel Hoepner spends his days responding to medical emergencies and helping save lives.

But, unbeknown to many of the patients he cares for, he is also waiting for life-saving treatment of his own.

The 30-year-old is living with kidney failure and is waiting for his third kidney transplant after being diagnosed with a rare disease shortly after birth.

Despite spending six hours every second day on haemodialysis to filter his blood, Mr Hoepner continues to work full-time as a clinical nurse consultant in the Clinical Response Unit across Gold Coast University Hospital and Robina Hospital.

Daniel Hoepner was diagnosed with congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type. (Supplied: Daniel Hoepner)

"I definitely don't make it known to patients. I think they've got enough going on to not be worrying about their nurse being unwell," he said.

"But I actually found when I wasn't working, I was a lot more tired.

" [Work is] something to take my mind off it, something to do, keep my brain active, and obviously my body active too. "

Mr Hoepner has spent his entire life in and out of hospital after being born with congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type (CNF), a severe genetic disorder that causes the kidneys to leak large amounts of protein into the urine.

The condition leads to severe swelling, kidney failure and, ultimately, requires dialysis and kidney transplantation for survival.

"When I was born, my mum saw something was wrong. I was just like a little football, really swollen," he said.

"She took me to a couple of doctors and they kind of just said I was just a fat baby, which is normally a good thing but, in this case, it wasn't, unfortunately."

Daniel Hoepner continues to work as a nurse. (Supplied: Gold Coast Health)

Because he was too small for a transplant, Mr Hoepner began dialysis as a baby and remained on treatment until he was six years old, when he received his first kidney transplant from his stepfather.

The transplant gave him more than 16 years of improved health before it began to fail, just as he was starting his nursing career.

"I'd just finished university and had just started a job," he said.

"Then I just started becoming a lot more unwell."

His mother wanted to donate one of her kidneys but was not a suitable match.

Instead, she donated to a stranger through the Australia and New Zealand paired kidney exchange program, which in turn allowed Mr Hoepner to receive a compatible kidney from another donor.

But now, that second transplant is failing and Mr Hoepner has once again joined the donor list.

This time, it's his partner who has stepped forward, offering to donate her kidney in the hope it will lead to Mr Hoepner receiving another life-saving transplant.

Daniel Hoepner with his family. (Supplied: Daniel Hoepner)

While balancing full-time nursing with regular dialysis treatments is challenging, Mr Hoepner has learned to adapt.

"I've always wanted to work in a profession where I could make a real difference in people's lives during some of their most difficult moments," he said.

"Even now, after becoming a dialysis patient myself, that motivation hasn't changed.

"I've learned to be organised, listen to my body and make the most of the time I have.

" Nursing is a huge part of who I am, and continuing to work gives me a sense of purpose and normality beyond being a patient. "

The latest figures from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare show just over 1,000 kidney transplants were performed across Australia in 2024.

Natasha Rogers, the head of transplantation at Westmead Hospital, said while transplant numbers continued to rise, receiving three or more kidney transplants remained uncommon.

"We have the Australia and New Zealand Dialysis and Transplant Registry that reports on all the kidney-transplant activity across the nation and probably only about 1 to 2 per cent of recipients will have had three or more kidney transplants," Professor Rogers said.

"So, it's pretty unusual."

Natasha Rogers says receiving three or more kidney transplants is uncommon. (Supplied)

Regardless, she said Mr Hoepner's ability to continue working while undergoing dialysis was "impressive".

"Having kidney disease and having to do dialysis is a full-time job by itself. It's very labour-intensive," she said.

" Dialysis does not make you feel great and you go from one treatment to the next to stay alive, essentially, and to pair that with full-time work is amazing. "

Although Mr Hoepner doesn't know when a suitable kidney will become available, he hopes sharing his experience will encourage others facing similar challenges not to put their lives on hold.

"Keep making memories, keep setting goals, and keep hoping," he said.

"A transplant can give you a new chapter, but your life is still worth living today."

World.title: Hospital defends treatment of man later shot by police
World.content:
Cairns Hospital's chief executive has defended the treatment provided to a man who was shot by police hours after he was released from hospital.

Police took the 28-year-old to hospital on Friday night under an emergency examination authority after he was allegedly found jumping naked on cars near a major Cairns shopping centre.

He was released from hospital within hours and on Saturday evening was shot by police while allegedly armed with two knives.

Officers also accidentally shot a 50-year-old bystander while responding to the incident.

The Queensland Police Union (QPU) has demanded any investigation into the shooting extend to the man's earlier presentation and discharge from hospital.

QPU general president Shane Prior said it took six officers to restrain the man at the shopping centre.

Police took the man to hospital under an emergency order the night before he was shot. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

The Cairns and Hinterland Hospital and Health Service (CHHHS) previously told the ABC the man's treatment began within half an hour of his arrival at the emergency department.

At parliamentary budget estimates in Brisbane yesterday, CHHHS chief executive Leena Singh defended the hospital's actions under questioning from Labor MP Mark Bailey.

"I can confirm the particular individual received the appropriate medical treatment on his presentation," Ms Singh told the hearing.

In a further statement to the ABC, Ms Singh said a preliminary review found CHHHS clinicians "acted appropriately and in accordance with Queensland Health policies, relevant legislation and their professional clinical judgement".

"Our health service works closely with Queensland Police Service and other partner agencies every day to provide the best possible care for our community.

"We remain committed to that strong collaboration."

The man has been charged with eight offences, including wilful damage, attempted robbery and going armed to cause fear.

He is due to appear in court tomorrow, having had his case adjourned twice this week while recovering in hospital from the shooting.

Leena Singh addressed the incident at budget estimates. (ABC Far North: Christopher Testa/File)

A spokeswoman for Health Minister Tim Nicholls said Queensland Health worked with investigating officers "including examining interactions between the alleged perpetrator and the health system".

The Police Ethical Standards Command is investigating the shootings.

Cairns MP Michael Healy said the man's hospital presentation and discharge needed thorough investigation.

"I would then expect to see some kind of communication to the broader public as to what measures [CHHHS] have taken to ensure it doesn't happen again," he said.

" Very reasonably the community would expect some answers to this and I think they are well and truly within their rights to ask that. "

Specific criteria to detain patients

CHHHS answered general questions about the process followed when a patient was detained and brought to hospital under an emergency examination authority.

It said patients underwent a comprehensive clinical assessment by qualified clinicians.

However, hospitals did not have legal authority to detain a person against their wishes unless specific criteria were met under the Mental Health Act.

The Cairns Hospital assessed and treated the man the night before he was shot by police while allegedly armed. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

"Patients experiencing drug or alcohol-related mental health symptoms are assessed and treated using the same clinical principles as any other mental health presentation, with care tailored to their individual needs," Ms Singh said in a written statement.

"Any patient needing ongoing care will be provided a bed.

"Approximately 40 per cent of all presentations to the emergency department result in the patient being admitted to hospital.

"Where appropriate, patients are referred for follow-up care on discharge.

"Information is shared with other agencies only where clinically appropriate and authorised under relevant legislation."

World.title: Taylor denies giving money to group at centre of NSW corruption probe
World.content:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has denied he ever gave money to a Liberal faction at the centre of a NSW corruption probe into branch stacking.

The right-wing group known as the NSW Reformers included former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw, who had a loose association with Mr Taylor through Catholic Schools NSW boss Dallas McInerney.

During a hearing on Tuesday before the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), Mr Whitelaw was shown a screenshot of a message sent from lobbyist Robert Assaf to a group chat including key figures being investigated by the inquiry.

The screenshot was of a message exchange between Mr McInerney and Mr Assaf.

It read: "I have breakfast club with ministers this Thursday morning. Who can I get an update from? Re SCD progress in last six to 12 months. "I want to shake down Angus for 10k."

Mr Whitelaw said while he could not recall seeing the message, he assumed it was referring to federal Liberal MP and now opposition leader Mr Taylor.

Under repeated questioning on Wednesday, Mr Taylor denied five times he had made any payment.

"No payment was made," he said.

Asked if he disputed the text messages seen by the inquiry, he said he was "not a party to proceedings" and would not be giving a "running commentary".

"I'll let the commission do its job," he said.

Mr Taylor said he has not been approached by the commission and would not entertain "hypotheticals" about giving evidence.

Taylor will not say if he was asked to contribute

Pressed on whether he was ever asked to give money to the NSW Reformers group, Mr Taylor repeated his denial that a payment was made and would not confirm if he was aware of the group or its activities.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the corruption watchdog that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday. These are some of the key players embroiled in the donations investigation.

The inquiry was shown another group chat message sent by Mr Whitelaw claiming Mr McInerney had secured a $15,000 payment and ongoing monthly donations of $3,000 for the group's work from Mr Taylor.

Mr Whitelaw said he did not remember sending the message or the donation being made.

"Potentially, Dallas [McInerney] had told me something that was incorrect," Mr Whitelaw said.

"I'd be very surprised if Mr Taylor made any financial contribution."

World.title: Son of a gun Hewitt takes top-100 scalp in ATP first
World.content:
Cruz Hewitt's victory in his ATP Tour main-draw debut is set to rocket the son of a gun up the world rankings.

Fresh off a run to the Wimbledon boys final, Hewitt beat former world number 37 Marcus Giron — currently ranked 85 — 6-3, 6-4 in Washington DC on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST).

The Australian, who didn't face a break point, became the fourth man born in 2008 or later to win a tour-level match and the youngest Washington match-winner since Japan's Kei Nishikori in 2007.

The teen qualified thanks to walkovers after leading both Dusan Lajovic and top-seed Zach Svajda and has surged 255 places to number 357 in the ATP's live rankings.

He'll play the winner of countryman and mentor Alex de Minaur and former world number three Stefanos Tsitsipas in the next round.

Cruz Hewitt's (right) win at the DC Open means he could face countryman Alex de Minaur next up in the round of 16. (Getty Images: Paul Morigi)

He had warmed up with father Lleyton, the former world number one, two-time major winner and 2004 Washington champion, who told him to lap up the moment.

"[He told me] mainly to enjoy it, because it was my first tour-level match … and to take every point one-by-one, to enjoy the atmosphere and to enjoy the crowd and that is what I did," he said.

Cruz said he was handling the pressure of carrying the Hewitt name "as best as I can".

"There is obviously a little bit of pressure, but I try to take the positives out of it as well, and I am happy with how I am dealing with it so far," he added.

"I am really happy with how I competed today. I came out and started pretty well, and I am thrilled to get through to the next round."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

De Minaur is defending his title in the American capital and fresh off a two-day Portofino honeymoon after marrying fellow pro Katie Boulter in Tuscany last month.

"It was an amazing time, everything we could have ever imagined," said De Minaur, who is coming off the disappointment of an upset fourth-round Wimbledon loss.

"It was like our own little movie. We were able to celebrate with family and friends and have a very small honeymoon.

"Then we're on a flight here to Washington and getting our heads screwed back on and back to being tennis players."

AAP

World.title: Local transmission of H5 bird flu 'very, very likely', SA government says
World.content:
South Australian authorities say it is "very, very likely" the H5 strain of bird flu is spreading locally, in what would represent the first known cases of local transmission of the virus.

The state has identified 11 more suspected cases of H5 bird flu, seven of which are in the state's South East and four on Kangaroo Island.

While officials are still waiting for final testing results, "due today or tomorrow", SA's Primary Industries Minister Clare Scriven said it was "extremely likely" to represent "localised distribution" of the virus.

Of the suspected cases found in the South East, one case was at Southend, one was at Cape Jaffa, two were at Port MacDonnell, and three were at Beachport.

Of the suspected cases on Kangaroo Island, one was found at Seal Bay and three were found at D'Estrees Bay on the island’s south coast.

"What we've seen around the world is we can't stop H5 bird flu and there has of course, in every other continent around the world, been local transmission," Ms Scriven said.

"So it was pretty much inevitable that it would occur.

"We'll wait for the scientific definitions to say whether we are considered to be at that point now but certainly if we're not it's likely that it will be quite soon."

Ms Scriven said the results were expected later on Wednesday or on Thursday.

Beach tours temporarily cancelled

Ms Scriven said authorities were "temporarily pausing" on-beach tours at Seal Bay to help protect the local seal population.

"So that people can be kept separate from the seals, knowing that the seal population is so very vulnerable," Ms Scriven said.

"Less human interaction means that there’s higher levels of resilience to all diseases or all threats and risks to the Seal Bay population."

She said guided tours along Seal Bay Conservation Park's boardwalk would continue.

"Additional Department of Environment and Water rangers have been deployed to Kangaroo Island to assist with ensuring that those guided tours can continue," Ms Scriven said.

"We know the Seal Bay experience is incredibly valuable to so many people and that will be able to continue, just not on the actual beach itself."

Commercial poultry remains in the clear

South Australia's first confirmed case was in a giant petrel found on the Fleurieu Peninsula on June 14.



On Sunday, the CSIRO confirmed two native birds which were found dead on separate beaches in SA tested positive for the H5 strain.

One greater crested tern was found near Robe and the second was found near the Semaphore Surf Life Saving Club, the first time a case has been detected on a metropolitan beach in SA.

On Wednesday, Ms Scriven said there had been no detections of H5 bird flu in commercial poultry across SA or the rest of the country.

World.title: Tradies swap swags for dongas on wheels to retain workers out bush
World.content:
Dolly Thompson is a woman of few words, but what she does say makes you listen.

She is an outback road worker who often spends weeks and even months living and working in some of the most remote corners of Queensland.

"I'm used to that kind of life, it doesn't worry me," Ms Thompson said.

"You're better off being out in the camp than what you are in town."

The roadside workers can be deployed anywhere in a large remote shire about the size of Tasmania. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

She may have a point. With a population of about 360, the Barcoo Shire Council's mobile road train accommodation is a far cry from the rough-and-ready camps of the past.

There is hope the mounted accommodation will attract more skilled workers to the bush and beat the competitive conditions of industries such as mining.

From swags to dongas on wheels

The triple-trailer road train is currently set up on the Quilpie to Windorah Road, while the Barcoo Shire has another mobile camp home at Windorah and another further west towards Birdsville.

The person in charge of this road camp is Jason Beilby, construction supervisor with the Barcoo Shire Council.

Jason Beilby has been working in outback Queensland for decades. (ABC Western Qld: Jay Carstens)

He has been working on Queensland's roads for about 20 years so he has seen and lived in very different accommodation.

"Ten years ago we were very rough camps," Mr Beilby said.

" We were living in the bush … and we found that to employ people we just had to upgrade, and that's fair enough. "

Today's road train accommodation is fitted with bedrooms and ensuites, kitchens, dining areas, laundries, and access to streaming services through personal and shared TVs.

A kitchen within a mobile road train camp has all the sauces you need. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

"They've got every little mod con that you can find," Mr Beilby said.

He said the workers enjoyed the more modern dongas which had helped attract more people to the job and retained them longer.

"We've got to employ people so we've got to give them good, comfortable accommodation," he said.

"Twelve hours out in the sun [and] you do want to come home to comfort, and that's a good sales point for employees to get them to come here and work."

A mobile roadside camp set-up using triple-trailer road trains between Windorah and Quilpie. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

Mr Beilby said another welcome feature was that the accommodation could be packed up quickly and moved to the next location.

"We back the trucks underneath, they're all on cables. They just lift all the verandahs up, and we move. It's very simple," he said.

"[In] some places we're 300 to 400 kilometres from the nearest town so they're pretty self-sufficient.

"I think all shires should upgrade, but it depends on their structure. [Our shire] is the size of Tasmania."

Roadside workers can stay on-site without having to drive hundreds of kilometres to accommodation. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

Community-driven ideas the engine-room

Keeping a secure workforce in remote towns can be particularly challenging compared to cities, or even rural communities, due to the distances involved.

Foundation for Rural and Regional Renewal's (FRRR) head of grants Jill Karena said that meant remote communities were often solving complex problems.

"Remote communities are not short of imagination and innovation," Ms Karena said.

"The distances are greater, the costs are higher, skilled workers can be much harder to access and keep, and the services often travel in-and-out."

Ms Karena said the best ideas often came from those who lived locally, but added that outside support through funding could help "back that ingenuity".

A spokesperson for the Barcoo Shire Council said the mobile workers' accommodation had improved its staff retention, having built triple-trailer road train accommodation camps since 2022.

All roadside workers in the main camp have remained with the council for more than five years, while some, like Ms Thompson, have stuck around for more than a decade.

There's plenty of skilled worker jobs in the west, but sometimes the mines get first dibs. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

"When I first come out I came out with my husband and learnt how to drive machinery and that," Ms Thompson said.

She stayed, in part because of the community and work culture.

"They're fun to be with. They all help out," she said.

World.title: ‘Doing their best to survive’: Inside Bordeaux’s wildfire refugee centre
World.content:
WorldEuropeBushfires ‘Doing their best to survive’: Inside Bordeaux’s wildfire refugee centre David Crowe July 29, 2026 — 11:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bordeaux: The cheers erupted across the cavernous hall when a voice came over the loudspeaker to tell hundreds of evacuees some good news. “The residents of Le Haillan, Eysines and Mérignac can return home,” said the organiser at the front of the hall. Residents evacuated from the wildfires in an emergency shelter set up at the Parc des Expositions de Bordeaux on Tuesday. Bloomberg Suddenly, there was a moment of hope for some of those who had fled the Bordeaux wildfires and spent much of the past week sleeping on camp beds in exhibition halls that usually host trade fairs. Here in Hall 2, one of three vast spaces with rows of beds and trestle tables, the applause signalled the relief for families that knew their homes were considered safe – at least for now.



Firefighters battle a blaze outside Lanton, in south-western France, on Tuesday. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva For other families, however, the anxious wait continues because emergency authorities fear that new areas are in danger as the wind shifts, even as some villages emerge unscathed. The air was cool inside the Parc des Expositions de Bordeaux at dinner time on Tuesday (about 2am on Wednesday, AEST) as volunteers sorted pillows and sleeping bags, while others served food to people who lined up calmly with their plates. Outside, however, the temperature climbed to 35 degrees and the wind picked up as the day wore on, bringing the smell of wildfire into the hall for anyone standing near the door.



After five nights here, some families seemed to have settled into the emergency conditions. A mother and father sat at a trestle table with three children, two grandparents and a small brown dog. Two young girls danced to pass the time. A young boy raced by on a tricycle. The city authority, the Bordeaux Metropole, raced to find shelter to deal with the biggest evacuation of its kind in France since the Second World War. About 60,000 residents were told to leave their homes in Le Haillan and parts of Mérignac and Eysines to the west of Bordeaux. Loading But there could be no privacy in this open space, with every camp bed on public view. The toilets were in a series of demountables outside the hall. Visiting media were told not to walk through the beds and chairs to chat to people about how they escaped the firestorm. “They’re fed up with being asked,” said one organiser.



Three volunteers at the emergency accommodation centre for evacuees in Bordeaux. From left to right: Alexia Bacquet, Chloé Bacquet and Lysa Guinle. David Crowe Alexia Bacquet, 38, an English teacher, volunteered to help after the evacuees flooded into this temporary town. She has been making coffee for three days. “It’s really crazy – we needed many, many people to help us,” she told this masthead. “My job is to help them to have just a little moment with a smile, and to ask them: ‘Did you eat something today, did you drink some water, how are you?’ It’s really important.”



Her sister, Chloé, 28, is a psychologist who has been volunteering with a group that has helped evacuees deal with the stress of leaving their villages and fearing the loss of their homes. “It’s been horrible for them to leave their homes because they don’t have any time to pack up their boxes or to take clothes,” she said. Volunteers sort donated clothing and food for those evacuated from the wildfires in the Gironde region. Bloomberg “They are doing their best to survive the situation. “I thought it was really important to be here to help people and just be there for them – and to bring flowers, because we have flowers here to just bring them joy.”



People collect food at a temporary shelter in Bordeaux. AP Photo/Eva van Dam Another psychologist, Lysa Guinle, 26, said organisers were asking some of the volunteers to stay overnight because the need for support was so great. “All the people are telling me that they are tired and exhausted, and a bit disoriented,” she said. “They are very happy and glad to have the people here to stay with them, to just talk. It’s very helpful.” Firefighters in south-western France have been racing against the clock to bring blazes under control before heatwave conditions worsen this week. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva



Authorities have evacuated 220,000 people across the Gironde region in south-western France, but that number may fall as people return to some communities. Related Article Bushfires How extreme weather in Europe and North America is signalling a new era of fire danger for Australia The shift in the wind on Tuesday, however, increased the danger to the north of the fire and led authorities to evacuate 4000 people from the beach resort of Lacanau Lake, as well as nearby Lacanau. Two firefighters died last week in the effort to douse a blaze near Bordeaux’s airport, just near the evacuated neighbourhood of Mérignac. Four were injured on Monday. More than 2000 firefighters are now battling the Gironde fire, which has destroyed about 240 homes. Some people have refused to evacuate areas close to Bordeaux, amid a debate about whether the historic city is in danger from a fire that is only 15 kilometres away.



While conditions in the city were hot and dry on Tuesday, the blue sky was visible and daily life continued. This was an improvement on Sunday, when a westerly wind brought thick brown smoke through the city. Inside the exhibition halls, a different kind of daily life has taken hold. Some families may have to remain for many more days. The forecast for Wednesday, when temperatures could reach 39 degrees, has officials worried about more fires breaking out. Alexia Bacquet said she would volunteer again on Wednesday. She also seemed ready to keep serving coffee if it would help in the days beyond. “We will see what they need.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: The $3m seawall dilemma splitting home owners as the ocean closes in
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life The $3m seawall dilemma splitting home owners as the ocean closes in David Barwell July 29, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The battle over a controversial seawall on the Central Coast has become the latest flashpoint in a growing conflict along the NSW coastline as communities grapple with the escalating cost of protecting beachfront homes from severe erosion, intensifying storms and rising sea levels. The NSW Land and Environment Court has approved a permanent 90-metre seawall designed to protect three beachfront apartment blocks at The Entrance North, overturning the Central Coast Council’s refusal of the project and delivering a decision likely to reverberate well beyond the disputed stretch of coastline. This photo shows the proximity of apartment blocks to the sea at The Entrance North, where a proposed seawall has been approved. Standing up to 1.5 metres high, the reinforced concrete structure will protect dozens of strata units on Hutton Road that have become increasingly exposed after decades of erosion and major storms, including in 2020 and 2025, which destroyed protective dunes, eroded backyards, and contributed to the beach losing 35 metres of width since 2020. The decision comes as councils across NSW face mounting pressure to respond to increasingly destructive storms and coastal erosion while balancing demands from beachfront home owners against concerns over environmental impacts and public beach access.



The Hunter and Central Coast Regional Planning Panel last month rejected a proposed $17 million seawall at nearby Wamberal Beach after receiving 637 public submissions, citing unresolved environmental concerns. Land and Environment Court Commissioner Joanne Gray found The Entrance North seawall was an appropriate response to the site’s “persistent” coastal hazards and would protect both private property and public safety. An artist’s impression of the seawall which has been approved for construction at The Entrance North. Central Coast Council The decision follows emergency intervention by the NSW government in the wake of the 2025 storms, when emergency coastal protection works were authorised to place 15,000 cubic metres of sand and 6000 tonnes of rock along the shoreline while authorities considered a permanent solution. However, the proposed seawall exposed deep divisions within the community, attracting more than 100 submissions from residents, surfers and environmental groups.



Central Coast Council opposed the development, arguing it would create a “hard, regular, man-made and visually dominating structure” that would detract from the natural landscape. Opponents warned the wall would impede beach access, damage shorebird habitat, accelerate erosion on adjoining beaches and create an unsightly barrier, with one submission describing it as “worse than the Berlin Wall”. The court determined that the seawall would provide protection from “persistent” coastal hazards. The project also split apartment owners, with some claiming they had never endorsed the proposal and warned construction costs could exceed estimates, leaving residents facing levies of up to $294,000 to fund the works. Supporters argued worsening climate change impacts had left residents with little alternative.



Peter Horton, director of Horton Coastal Engineering, which represented the owners in the court appeal, said the seawall would provide 60 years of protection and end uncertainty. “It’s been enormously stressful to be exposed to this risk over many years – a constant fear that the next storm will be the one that washes away their homes, an asset that is completely uninsurable,” he said. Related Article Good Weekend ‘We grabbed the cat and got out’: The waterside dwellers facing rising sea levels Horton said NSW’s planning laws made it “almost impossible” for howeowners to secure approval for permanent seawalls and argued future coastal protection works should follow a funding model used to protect beachfront homes at Collaroy and Narrabeen, where landowners pay 80 per cent of construction costs and state and local governments cover the remainder. In her judgment, Gray acknowledged the broader planning dilemma as coastal hazards become more frequent and severe.



“The desire to live on the beach, combined with a historic lack of planning controls, has resulted in the degradation of natural coastal protection and left residential development exposed to severe coastal hazards,” she wrote. World.title: Victorian Labor leadership LIVE: Premier Ben Carroll mulls cabinet appointments following Jacinta Allan’s resignation
World.content:
Labor’s promised changes to boost integrity will be meaningless unless the government properly funds the anti-corruption watchdog, the Greens said.

Ben Carroll said his priority as premier will be to set up a royal commission into corruption in the construction industry, appoint a special prosecutor to work with the commission, and give IBAC follow-the-money powers sooner.

But Greens leader Ellen Sandell said that expanded powers for IBAC need to go hand-in-hand with adequate funding for the watchdog.

Greens leader Ellen Sandell. Simon Schluter

The Independent Broad-Based Anti-Corruption Commission previously said it was underfunded by the Labor government.

“The new premier is really trying to rewrite Labor’s history of corruption-plagued scandals across Victoria, but he has not even committed to giving our anti-corruption watchdog IBAC the full suite of powers that it needs to go after corruption in Victoria ... and he hasn’t promised to give them the funding that IBAC has asked for,” Sandell said.

“We actually need an anti-corruption watchdog that can look into corruption wherever it occurs.”

World.title: Andrew McConnell, the man behind Gimlet, buys St Kilda’s iconic Stokehouse
World.content:
Eating outRestaurant news Andrew McConnell, the man behind Gimlet, buys St Kilda’s iconic Stokehouse As a young chef, Andrew McConnell used to work for the family that owns Stokehouse. Now he’s buying their restaurant. Dani Valent Updated July 29, 2026 ,first published 10:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stokehouse, the 36-year-old jewel of St Kilda and perhaps the suburb’s best known restaurant, has been sold to Trader House, the restaurant group owned by one of Melbourne’s most well-known chefs, Andrew McConnell and his wife Jo McGann. Outgoing owners and operators Frank, Sharon and Hugh van Haandel will hand the property over in October. “We’ve built a venue that is truly cross-generational,” says Frank van Haandel. “Everyone has a story at Stokehouse.” The upstairs dining room boasts bay views. Those who could tell some of those stories include famous customers over the decades such as Barack and Michelle Obama (and their security detail), Noel Gallagher of Oasis, Robert De Niro and Paris Hilton. MotoGP ace Valentino Rossi turned up in a tracksuit, defying the first floor dress code.



The kitchen has been a forging ground for some of Melbourne’s most prominent chefs, including Asian-influenced Michael Lambie (now at Juni), mod-Oz originator Andrew Blake and seafood gun Maurice Esposito. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Andrew McConnell and Jo McGann of Trader House, who have added Stokehouse to their portfolio. Josh Robenstone Current executive chef Jason Staudt is originally from Canada; he moved from Sydney’s Aria in 2019, seeing the restaurant through the pandemic with a focus on sustainability, employing locals and steering the downstairs area from a hard-drinking party zone to more of a wine-focused local lounge room. McConnell and McGann are not planning wholesale shuffles to menus or personnel until a 2027 refresh. They’re in the midst of opening Cote Basque, their first Melbourne restaurant since 2020’s smash hit Gimlet, both in the CBD. “Our intention is not to change what makes Stokehouse special,” says McConnell. “We have enormous respect for its history and for the team that has helped shape it. We’re inheriting strong foundations, and we’re committed to investing in its future while preserving the qualities and the people that have made it so well loved.”



The property includes the hatted fine dining restaurant upstairs, casual dining downstairs at Stokehouse Pasta and Bar, and an outdoor kiosk that’s been through several iterations. ‘When he sets up a restaurant, he is very convincing with it.’ Frank Van Haandel speaking of Andrew McConnell in 2018. Liam Ganley owns large venues The Fifth Province and Freddie Wimpole’s in St Kilda. “I think it’s amazing,” he says of the new deal. “They [Trader House] are the best operators in the state. It’s a good news story for St Kilda.” It’s a strong move for Trader House, which is in expansion mode in a tough economy, perhaps showing that the future of restaurants is in consolidation and group buying power. As well as its seven Melbourne venues, it also has a footprint in Queensland, having opened Supernormal Brisbane and Bar Miette in 2024. The sun sets on Stokehouse’s current chapter in October. Arianna Leggiero



Andrew McConnell has a long attachment to St Kilda. He was head chef at Circa The Prince in the mid-2000s, also owned by Frank van Haandel, then in partnership with Frank’s brother John. McConnell’s last restaurant in the seaside suburb closed in 2018 after multiple attempts to make a site on Fitzroy Street work, first as Golden Fields, then Luxembourg and finally Supernormal Canteen. Trader House has owned Meatsmith butcher store on Barkly Street, St Kilda, since 2017. Ganley will be watching how Trader House manages the cooler months. “Driving trade in winter is the real struggle in St Kilda, especially on the beach,” he says. “It will be interesting to see how they tackle that.” The foreshore site of today’s restaurant has been a hospitality venue since 1908, initially as tearooms. Stokehouse opened on New Year’s Day 1990 and was a favourite for celebrations and seafood-studded special occasions until it was destroyed by fire in 2014. Frank Van Haandel outside Stokehouse in St Kilda. Griffin Simm Frank van Haandel rebuilt the property as Australia’s greenest restaurant. Food waste is composted on site, and the temperature is controlled by geothermal piping that extends 80 metres beneath the building. “It’s a building that will stand for 100 years, a legacy I am proud of,” says van Haandel.



As well as being a previous employer, van Haandel is a long-time admirer of McConnell’s knack with hospitality. “When he sets up a restaurant, he is very convincing with it,” he told the Australian Financial Review in 2018. “The food suits the identity of the business, the decor, staff and the delivery. He bridges fine dining and more casual and approachable really well. I don’t think anyone in Melbourne does it better.” Barb Dight has co-owned Acland Street’s Cicciolina almost as long as Stokehouse has been running. “I’m happy to have another quality operator in St Kilda and, as a local, somewhere else to eat,” she says. “After 33 years, I can see the pendulum always swings and St Kilda is on the up with lots of fun and diverse places. Trader House will add to the mix in a big way.” Related Article Special series Banned words, dossiers on diners: Inside the invisible details at Melbourne’s famed Gimlet Related Article Special series The quiet Millennial who inherited Stokehouse and is preparing for its next chapter

World.title: Huge delays as Sydney motorway closed due to emergency safety works
World.content:
Sydney commuters have been hit by hours-long delays after the discovery of a faulty fan inside the M5 tunnel overnight triggered emergency works on Wednesday morning, closing the motorway in the city direction during the peak. Motorway operator Transurban has warned that the 25-year-old eastbound tunnel is likely to remain closed until about 3pm, but it hopes to be able to reopen the tunnel in time for the afternoon peak. Traffic came to a standstill on the M5. Nine News Premier Chris Minns said the closure had thrown many people’s commute into chaos, and the roads minister would seek answers from Transurban about its maintenance schedule and the chances of a repeat incident. “I know that’s cold comfort for people that were stuck in traffic this morning. I’m genuinely sorry about that,” Minns said. “It’s not good enough.”



The toll road operator had closed the tunnel to conduct routine maintenance in the early hours of Wednesday when workers discovered safety problems with a fan inside the tunnel. A decision was made on safety grounds about 4.16am to replace the fan and keep the eastbound lanes shut after 5am, despite the looming morning peak. The ongoing closure caused eastbound traffic to queue back as far as 13 kilometres to Milperra during the morning. Two cranes and other equipment were called in for workers to replace the fan, which is one of 147 in the eastbound tunnel. Transurban’s general manager for WestConnex, Denise Kelly, said workers discovered that the fan was faulty during the routine inspection overnight.



“We evaluated it to see whether or not it could be fixed in situ while it stayed up in the roof cavity. That was decided not to be the best course of action, and the best course of action was actually to remove it,” she said. She texted Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison about 4.42am to inform her of the decision to replace the fan and keep the tunnel closed, and the pair later spoke. Kelly confirmed that Transurban was aware at the time of its decision that the tunnel would have to remain closed during the morning peak. “That was the immediate advice to the minister and to the traffic management centre ... that it would be closed for the morning peak,” she said. “We made that call very early, adjusted all of the signs and messaging, and put messaging out on links.”



Related Article Roads Motorists stuck in Sydney’s M4 tunnel for hours after bulges found in roof She apologised to motorists for the major delays caused by the closure, but said that safety had to be prioritised. Transurban is still assessing what caused the faulty fan. Earlier, Transport for NSW coordinator-general Howard Collins urged commuters to avoid the motorway “at all costs” due to the emergency works forcing the closure of the city-bound lanes of the M5 between King Georges Road in Beverly Hills and Marsh Street in Mascot. The agency has advised motorists to use alternative routes to travel into the city, and to plan extra time for the commute. Alternative routes include the M8 motorway and a diversion route sign-posted by the M5. In December, motorists were stuck in one of the city’s M4 motorway tunnels for hours after major disruption was caused by two bulges found in the roof of the westbound tunnel beneath Ashfield in the inner west.
