World.title: ‘Things aren’t as stretchy and flexible’: Shane Gould on the reality of sex in your 60s
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend ‘Things aren’t as stretchy and flexible’: Shane Gould on the reality of sex in your 60s Benjamin Law July 29, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each week, Benjamin Law asks public figures to discuss the subjects we’re told to keep private by getting them to roll a die. The numbers they land on are the topics they’re given. This week, he talks to Shane Gould. The Olympic gold medallist, 69, is the only person to hold every world freestyle record from 100m to 1500m simultaneously. She was Australian of the Year in 1972 and was awarded an AM in 2018. Shane Gould: “My Christianity is a very practical thing: it’s about being an activist, environmental and social.” SEX You trained hard and grew up in the spotlight as a champion teen swimmer. How did all of that affect your capacity for crushes and romance? Well, actually, there were huge opportunities to be in relationships and develop socially. The great thing was that we were always semi-naked in our swimsuits, so there would be “accidental” touches, brushes against a package. I only had sisters, so … [Laughs] What kind of guy were you attracted to growing up? When I was young, there was a boy at school who was tanned with blond hair. Strong, athletic, not super-big, nicely proportioned. He was beautiful, my physical ideal.



What kind of guy are you attracted to now? It’s the mind that attracts me now: thoughts and thoughtfulness. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Dolly Doctor’ talked us through puberty. Now she’s talking us through menopause Is that what you find in your husband? [Gould married swimming coach Milton Nelms in 2007.] Definitely. We had a talk just now, actually, over coffee about the sentience of animals; he’s a vegetarian. We have differences of opinion, but we can talk and go deep. What do you envy about younger generations when it comes to sex? They’ve got more information about consent, better access to contraception, and it’s not considered dirty to talk about pleasure and feelings. What do you not envy about younger generations when it comes to sex? Just hooking up for a short time: the honeymoon phase is over after three months. There’s no maturing into a long-term relationship, which may not be explosive but is deeper.



You’re 69 years old right now. Do you feel sexy at this age? I don’t like looking in the mirror, but I have started wearing colour. A taxi driver in Melbourne once said to me, “I hate winter in Melbourne because all the women wear black and grey!” So I thought, “OK, well, there’s a good tip.” So colour helps me to feel sexy. Also, I think I’ve got nice hands … [shows hands]. You do have shockingly youthful-looking hands. I’ve been looking after my skin a lot more. I also feel sexy when I feel my muscles working. I’ve been doing yoga for about six months now: that’s making me feel a lot more relaxed, calm and in touch with my body in a different way. Sex in your 60s. What should I expect? The reality is, things aren’t as stretchy and flexible. You’ll need more lubrication … But desire can still be as urgent and, if you’re with your long-term mate, you’ve worked out how to be attractive to each other and what turns each other on. It just takes more time and thoughtfulness. DEATH How has death impacted you? Losing animals is good preparation. When I was 17, a horse I loved had to be put down. That grief is very real.



What human losses have you felt the most? My mother dying in 2013 at 84. But she had sorted out her life, so even in her old age and her dying years, she was teaching us girls how to die and be prepared for death. She chose the music for her funeral and even organised all her photo albums. You’re 70 in November: is death on your mind more? Definitely. I’m reviewing my will at the moment, as well as enduring power of attorney. Is this a confronting process for you? It is. All these questions have come up. So I need to go for a swim or a walk on the beach and think about things: really meditate and process. What do you think happens after we die? I don’t really worry too much about what happens in the afterlife. I’m more interested in what happens here and now. RELIGION



Tell me about your faith. When I had an evangelical sort of rebirth – at about 17 or 18 – I was involved with people who prioritised social and environmental justice. So that has sustained me: an approach to Christianity where you practise not just a personal faith, to feel good spiritually, but to actually do good works. My Christianity is a very practical thing: it’s about being an activist, environmental and social. Gould in 1971. Edward Beresford Golding/Fairfax Media Would you describe yourself as religious? Well, there’s religion and there’s faith. I want to make that distinction. I have a faith; I’m not religious. Tell me about the distinction for you. Religion is a structured, bureaucratic hierarchy. People in the church have done terrible things – war and invasions – in the name of God, and I deplore that. But there are people inspired by faith. There’s this idea of the “leap of faith” from Søren Kierkegaard, the 19th-century Danish philosopher: that faith transcends reason, logic and rational evidence. You actively commit to the unprovable. And in what do you have faith? That I’m loved. And that whatever comes my way, I’ll be given the capacity to deal with it. I might be distraught and frustrated, but it will be OK.



Of the seven deadly sins – pride, greed, wrath, envy, lust, gluttony and sloth – to which one are you most susceptible? Pride. But you’ve got a lot to be proud of! [Smiles] I do. Shane Gould is a contestant on The Traitors, airing from August 4 at 7.30pm on 10 and 10 Streaming. diceytopics@goodweekend.com.au Get the best of Good Weekend delivered to your inbox every Saturday morning.

World.title: ‘Why have I been trying to be someone I’m not?’: How Gretel Killeen found her way back
World.content:
‘What happened to playfulness in our lives?’ asks The Traitors host Gretel Killeen. ‘How did we become so focused on the most miserable elements of our existence?’

For years, the comedian and reality TV host tried to tone herself down. Now she’s embracing the chaos.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

While filming reality game show The Traitors, Gretel Killeen began to question some of the choices she’d made over the years. “I thought, ‘Why have I been trying to be someone I’m not all this time?’” says the original host of Australian Big Brother. “I toned down how I dress because I didn’t want to be looked at. I toned down the things I say because I didn’t want to draw attention to myself. When you’re in the public eye, you can forget who you actually are. It made me realise that I don’t play enough in life.” Now 63, the veteran broadcaster, comedian and author is making up for lost time – and she’s having a blast. When I first interviewed Killeen in 2009, she styled herself in jeans and a brown jacket for the photo shoot. This time, she opts for a fabulous turquoise suit, a vivid orange blazer, snakeskin-patterned boots, a beret, several elaborate rings and a black toy cat, which she strokes in the manner of a Bond villain. She also brings a piece of her own artwork to use as a backdrop, having taken up painting several years ago. Under the glare of the public spotlight, Killeen began toning herself down. At 63, she’s done trying be someone she’s not. Sam Mooy “I used to think fancy dress parties were embarrassing,” she says. “Talk about being a slow learner, but it’s only now that I realise why people like them: they’re being given permission to play and have fun.” In The Traitors, Killeen encourages contestants to be as naughty as they wish. She certainly leads by example; in the first episode, she makes her grand entrance by stepping out of a coffin in a blood-soaked wedding gown.



Based on a Dutch format, the hit series has spawned 40 international adaptations, including an earlier Australian iteration presented by Rodger Corser. Filmed in a splendid New Zealand manor, this new season features 22 former reality show contestants and judges from programs including Australian Idol, Australian Survivor, The Bachelor, The Block, MasterChef Australia, the Real Housewives franchise and Drag Race Down Under. The premise is simple: Killeen secretly anoints a few members of the group as “traitors”, instructing them to covertly murder as many “faithfuls” as possible. Meanwhile, the faithfuls try to unmask the traitors during roundtable banishment ceremonies, where accusations fly thick and fast. If they rid themselves of every traitor by the final episode, they share in a prize pool worth up to $250,000. If they fail, the remaining traitors claim the lot. Killeen, dressed as a widowed bride, as host of The Traitors Australia. “It’s about human behaviour, which I’ve always been fascinated by,” Killeen says. “To succeed, you have to be liked and not stand out so you’re not perceived as a threat. It’s a bit like how women have had to be in the world. I’ve been in many meetings where women are the smartest people in the room, but they pitch their ideas as though they’re an afterthought.” Editor's pick Streaming ‘There’s been dumb luck’: Patrick Brammall on Colin, Hollywood haters and what’s next When Killeen arrives for our interview at Channel Ten’s Pyrmont headquarters in inner Sydney, she greets me warmly before frowning at the seating arrangement. “I like to see people’s faces when I’m talking to them,” she explains as we drag the sofas closer together. “It’s much nicer this way.” Killeen is terrific company: intelligent, funny and entertainingly discursive. While she deems this last trait a weakness, I find it refreshing. “Just wait until you have to edit the transcript,” she counters. “Then you’ll be going, ‘Oh my god, this needs a flow chart.’”



When I spoke to her 17 years ago, she was promoting her “gleefully exaggerated memoir”, The Night My Bum Dropped. The book satirised the “you can have it all” ethos that, as Killeen put it, made many women feel they ought to “run a global empire, raise a family, help a crippled dog give birth and do the ironing while having multiple orgasms”. “That was the real me,” she admits now. “And it was the real me having a kind of breakdown. I remember thinking, ‘People are reading this and not realising [how accurate it is]’. But that’s life, isn’t it?” A protest by evicted housemate Merlin Luck, in the fourth season of Big Brother, became one of the most talked-about TV moments of 2004. Although Killeen has been on our screens since the late 1980s, Big Brother made her a household name in 2001. As Australia’s first major reality TV host, she is also regarded as one of the genre’s finest. This is no surprise: she earned the marks to study law but quit to pursue live comedy and has since worked in radio, TV and musical theatre; acted and directed; performed for the troops; and authored more than 30 books. Related Article Reality TV ‘No filters, no fame-hungry pigs’: Inside the original Big Brother As one critic observed, she lent a “muted wit, maturity and a wry smile to Big Brother, without ever being condescending”. Yet others were incensed by the very existence of the program. “Big Brother elevated average Australians to a position of importance, which may have been threatening to those who liked the hierarchy of the status quo,” Killeen says. “And because we had such enormous numbers of people watching, some decided that was a sign the show wasn’t very smart. I think they’re ill-informed judgments.”



Since stepping down from the series in 2007, Killeen has competed in other reality series including The Masked Singer, Celebrity Come Dine With Me, Go Back to Where You Came From and The Amazing Race: Celebrity Edition. But The Traitors is her first major reality hosting role since Big Brother. One thing that attracted her to the project was the chance to be intimately involved in its production. She decided to play the host as a character of her own creation: a vampish widow with a string of ex-husbands who perished in mysterious circumstances. She even created a scrapbook detailing her character’s backstory. Loading “When Ten and the production company said to me, ‘Yeah, we can do it this way’, it was so exciting to me,” she says. “It’s very uncommon in television now because everything is so scripted and we were going the complete other way.” The Traitors, Killeen says, illustrates many interesting aspects of human psychology. This includes our innate desire to form tribes and our susceptibility to confirmation bias, which makes us prioritise information that reinforces existing beliefs while dismissing contradictory evidence. In The Traitors, contestants are required to test the strength of their arguments against those of their fellow players. In the real world, however, many of us self-sort into ideological silos, where our opinions are constantly reinforced by social media algorithms. This makes it deceptively easy to assume our views are more widely shared than they actually are. “But The Traitors also shows that we all have this desire to play,” Killeen says, noting that the physical challenges offered participants a welcome reprieve from their scheming and second-guessing. “It’s a release for people to be running around and getting out of their own heads, because they’re connecting with the real world.



“We live in a society where loneliness is at epidemic proportions and as a grandma, I think, ‘What happened to playfulness in our lives? Where did it go? It’s so fun and joyful and healthy, so how did we become so focused on the most miserable elements of our existence?’” Killeen with one of The Traitors’ contestants, comedian Rhys Nicholson, who is a judge on Drag Race Down Under. When I ask her to answer her own questions, she doesn’t hesitate. “Money and accessories are measurable,” she says, “but the joy or kindness you give other people are not, so we dismiss them from the equation.” Killeen, who has an adult son and daughter with her ex-husband, tries to keep her private life out of the spotlight. “Your life is not an entity that has a picket fence around it,” she says. “Even though I might want to comment on my life, there are other people whose lives will be impacted by those comments.” KiIleen was part of a chat show hosted by Mike Walsh (centre front) that aired on the ABC in 1987. ABC But she needs little prompting to talk about her passions, including painting. (She accepts commissions to create original artworks through her website.) “I grew up in an environment where academia was more important than artistic pursuits,” she says, while praising her father for prioritising his four daughters’ education at a time when many dads did not. “To know that I can hold my own in an academic arena gives me a strength … although I was ignoring the fact that the largest percentage of my character is artistic. With writing, I have to keep peeling the onion and getting back to what my voice is. With painting, I’m just a conduit and I try not to let my brain interfere with the work.”

World.title: Aidan Murphy was 0.21s away from history. He’s confident he can beat anyone
World.content:
SportAthleticsCommonwealth Games Aidan Murphy was 0.21s away from history. He’s confident he can beat anyone Michael Gleeson July 29, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Aidan Murphy had just done something no Australian had ever done – except the bloke who did it 0.21 seconds before him. Murphy, the overlooked man of Australia’s new sprint generation, broke 20 seconds for the 200 metres at the nationals earlier this year. He would have been the first – not even Gout Gout had run a legal time under 20s. Ready to race: Australian sprinter Aidan Murphy. AAP But in that same race, the Queensland teenager breasted the line a fraction of a second ahead of Murphy. So Murphy’s extraordinary effort of 19.88s became slightly less extraordinary, and lost in the dizzying Gout hoopla. “It’s hard to comprehend when you do it [run sub-20] but you have still got someone out in front of you. What I had done hit a lot later, I think,” Murphy said.



“It was one of those times where it was like ‘shit, I just did that’. You know what I mean? And then now, how do you replicate that? So I think that’s kind of what basically my whole team has been focusing on, and you know why we’re here.” The assumption afterwards was that Gout’s appearance in the race helped drag Murphy to his sub-20 time. “I think it’s pretty easy to think that as well, but we went back through the data and it was actually the other way around,” Murphy said. “I was the one pushing Gout. So I guess it was one of those things where we were both just there at the right time. More than, you know, one of us getting over the line first. “He definitely had that top speed advantage over me in that last 50. I don’t think there was ever a moment where I was like, ‘Yep, I’ve got this in the bag’, because nature of sprinting is you never know who’s going to win ’til the finish line.”



Related Article Commonwealth Games First shoes, now speed suits: Australia joins arms race to get an edge in athletics Murphy explained his confidence going into that race, with his times in training and in competitions running into big headwinds. “We had been quietly sitting on a very big time drop for a lot of months,” he said. “We were ready to drop something big.” Murphy has been a 400m runner, so was not in the conversation along with another Australian sprint star, Lachie Kennedy, and Gout for the 200m. But he ran it at nationals and broke 20s, and he will run it in Glasgow where there is no 400m race on the card.



The field is strong in Glasgow, although the Cayman Islands didn’t send an athletics team, so the US college champion Jaiden Reid won’t be in the field. Reid is the world-leading runner this year for the 200m, having clocked 19.66s. Still, there will be two other sub-20 runners with personal bests better than Murphy’s, one of them South Africa’s Sinesipho Dembile, who has run a 19.74s. “You have to put times out of your head and just run the race. That was my exact mentality going into nationals. On paper, I shouldn’t have been anywhere near Gout, and yet I was. How did that happen? Because you need to flip a switch in your brain to get you to run the times you need to be able to run to be competitive, and that is exactly what I will do at Glasgow. It’s just another faster guy at this point. It’s just another Gout. “I think we can do something special here.” Murphy’s mum is the former sprinter Tania Van Heer, a two-time Commonwealth Games gold medallist and sounding board for her son as he navigates his breakout run and first Commonwealth Games.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games as it happened: Kennedy smashes record to win silver in 100m; Southam gold leads medal rush at the pool “It has been good having her around training and competitions more regularly now more than ever. “It has been pretty stabilising for me where I’ve had a breakout, and you sort of almost get lost in where your ceiling is. “There’s always going to be a bit of competitive rivalry between us about who has more international medals, which I think is great. I’ve obviously got a bit of work to do before I catch up to Mum.” Get around our Commonwealth Games coverage

World.title: Fiji conjoined twins prepare for life-saving surgery in Saudi Arabia
World.content:
A pair of rare conjoined twins in Fiji - who were born ten months ago as part of a set of triplets - are about to have separation surgery in Saudi Arabia.

Twins Di Cecea and Jesipeli Kikau were born eight weeks premature with their sister, Hossana, at the Colonial War Memorial (CWM) Hospital in the capital, Suva.

"The doctors said this is the first case of conjoined twins in Fiji in 20 years," their mother Akenata said in a video shared by Fiji's Health Ministry.

"When they were born the doctors said they might only survive for a few days. We are grateful to the nurses, doctors and medical staff here at the hospital for their service," she said.

With the girls having survived against the odds so far, the next stage of their fight for life takes them to the other side of the world.

The Saudi Arabia government has fully funded their entire trip, covering airfares and accommodation for the triplets and their parents. Facebook / Ministry of Health & Medical Services - Fiji

Bound for Riyadh

The twins' parents, Akeneta and Watisoni Vulimaiigiladi of Rewa, have been searching for a country to perform the surgery since the girls were discharged from hospital eight months ago.

Australia and Saudi Arabia were among the contenders, and finally the Saudi Arabian government offered to fund the multi-million-dollar surgery, as well as the family's airfares and accommodation, under a humanitarian programme.

The twins and their parents are due to leave Fiji for Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, where the girls will undergo complex surgery at the King Salman Hospital in the capital, Riyadh.

Conjoined twins Di Cecea and Jesipeli Kikau fly out to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia on Wednesday to the King Salman Hospital, where a multi-million dollar, life-changing separation surgery awaits them, Fijii's Health Ministry said. Facebook / Ministry of Health & Medical Services - Fiji

Fiji's government is covering the cost of a medical escort to accompany the family on their journey, adding that the gesture from Saudi Arabia was proof of the "incredible bilateral relations between the two countries".

"We are thankful that the Ministry of Health can assist us, when we went back home (eight months ago) we were worried about the twins because I am affected when I watch them and see the other kids," Akenata said

"I get emotional but I know that there is a living God who will ensure that they live."

This is the second case of conjoined twins in the Pacific region in the past year, after brothers Sawong and Tom Kevin were born in a remote village in Morobe Province in Papua New Guinea last October.

World.title: Hawke's Bay growers abandon bid to save McCain factory after equipment pulled
World.content:
A group of vegetable growers in Hawke's Bay are ditching their plans to save the McCain factory.

In May, McCain announced it was closing its frozen vegetable factory in Hastings, a decision that's impacting more than 100 growers of peas, beans, corn and carrots.

A group of growers and local mayors asked McCain to pause the closure of its factory so they could carry out a feasibility study and try to find a solution for a possible takeover.

The growers' interest in the McCain facility was on the basis that the processing equipment would be part of the sale and remain in place, allowing frozen vegetable production to continue.

But now they've had to abandon the idea after McCain reportedly told them the equipment is no longer available.

Grower spokesperson Hew Dalrymple said the growers had explored the opportunity thoroughly and in good faith, but had ultimately been left with no option other than to withdraw their offer.

McCain Foods vegetable processing plant in Hastings. (File photo) Supplied / Google Maps

"This is an incredibly disappointing outcome for us all, but on learning the processing equipment is no longer available, that fundamentally changed the situation.

"While this particular chapter has come to an end, it doesn't diminish our commitment to finding a future for vegetable growing and frozen vegetable production in Hawke's Bay. Our growers remain committed to exploring what opportunities may still exist," he said.

Hastings District Mayor Wendy Schollum said it was a disappointing outcome.

"We have worked alongside growers throughout this process, and I want to acknowledge the enormous effort they have invested over recent months to explore every possible option.

"This is a disappointing outcome for the workers, growers, contractors and businesses connected to the plant, but it is about far more than one facility. Hawke's Bay is one of New Zealand's key food-producing regions, and vegetable growing and processing are vital to local jobs, our regional economy and the country's food security," she said,

Schollum said discussions with the government are ongoing, and Central Hawke's Bay mayor Will Foley said government support will be critical in determining whether there is a sustainable future for vegetable growing and processing in Hawke's Bay.

Hastings District Mayor Wendy Schollum (L) and Central Hawke's Bay Mayor Will Foley. (File photo) RNZ / Supplied

"This industry has been part of our region for generations. We owe it to our growers, workers and communities to continue exploring every opportunity to retain and grow that capability into the future," said Foley.

The councils said they would continue working alongside growers, industry and government to determine whether there remains a viable future for vegetable growing and frozen vegetable processing in Hawke's Bay.

World.title: Glasgow Commonwealth Games: Nauru claims second bronze, adding to Pacific medal tally
World.content:
Nauru has a second medal at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, adding to the Pacific Islands medal haul at the event.

Femily-Crystie Notte, 17, claimed a bronze medal on Tuesday night in the women's 63kg category in weightlifting.

Notte lifted 100kg in the snatch and 116 in the clean-and-jerk.

The gold went to Canada's Maude Charron with a Games record total of 232kg, while England's Sarah Davies Smale took silver.

The top four lifters all surpassed the previous Commonwealth Games record.

"Since joining the Commonwealth Games in 1990, Naoero has proudly upheld a tradition of winning medals on the Commonwealth stage," the Naoero Weightlifting Federation wrote in a Facebook post.

Notte ensured that this proud legacy continues, it added.

All the Pacific Island medals have so far come in weightlifting: a silver to Samoa, a bronze to PNG and two bronze medals to Nauru.

Athletics

No Pacific runner has been able to get past round one in the men's 400m or 800m.

Papua New Guinea's William Camilus Peka ran a personal best time of 49.88s in Heat one of the men's 400m, finishing seventh in the field of eight.

Fiji's Howard Tapuaiga Siila ran a season's best time of 55.96 seconds in heat two, while he was still 9.41 seconds behind the slowest qualifier.

The PNG pair of Adolf Kauba, who ran 50.06s in Heat 5 to finish seventh, and Daniel Baul, in Heat 6 in a time of 49.34s to finish fifth, were also in action.

Boxing

Pacific boxers have fallen at the quarterfinal stage in a number of events overnight.

PNG's Flora Loga was beaten in her 65kg quarterfinal by Scotland's Caitlin Rainey when the referee stopped the fight in the second round. She was behind on all five judges scorecards at that time.

Niue's Karen Te Ruki Pasene, lost on unanimous points decision to Northern Ireland's Kaci Rock, also in the women's 65kg division, suffering three knockdowns in the process.

In the men's 90kg, Niue's Duken Holo Tutakitoa-Williams, who was favoured to win a medal, lost his quarterfinal to Welshman Connor Williams.

There might be medal prospects in Fiji's Jasmine Daunakamakama, who is apprearing in the women's 57kg quarterfinal against Sri Lanka's Keshani Hansika on Wednesday night, and Samoan duo Michael Seko in the men's 90kg and Marion Ah Tong in the men's 70kg.

If the three make it past the quarterfinals and into the semifinals, they will be automatic qualifiers for bronze medals.

Tonga's 3x3 women basketball team (from left) Mele Finau, Ana-Rachael Enari, Selai Niu and Leslia Finau at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Photo: TASANOC. Facebook / TASANOC

Basketball

Tonga women's team lost 21-12 to Uganda in the repecharge to qualify for the semifinals.

Leading Tonga's campaign, where they won three and lost two of their pool matches, were the United States of America's Finau sisters, Lesila and Mele.

The Tongans beat hosts Scotland 12-10, Papua New Guinea 12-10 and Singapore 14-10.

They lost 21-8 to New Zealand and 21-4 to England before their semifinal play-off clash against Uganda.

Tonga's 3x3 women basketball team had the Finau sisters plus Ana-Rachael Enari and Selai Niu.

"It's more than just a match," Mele Finau told the Commonwealth Games media in Glasgow.

She said the opportunity to represent Tonga at the Commonwealth Games alongside her sister carried special meaning following the death of their father.

"We haven't played together since high school, so I'm about to get emotional," she said.

"It's so amazing, especially since our dad passed. This is the main reason why we are doing this, representing him and representing the country."

Bowls

In the men's pairs event, the Niue pair of Tifaga Tupuiliu and Keith Papani lost to Wales 2-0 in their game.

Cook Islands Epii Poila and Jason Lindsay took the India team to the wire in their clash, winning the first set 5-2 but then dropping the second 6-5. The game went into tie-break, with India winning 1-0 to take the game home.

In the women's singles competition, Catherine Papani lost to Guernsey's Ali Merren 2-0.

But Cook Islands Emily Jim proved too tactical for Malta's Connie-Leigh Rixon, winning both sets 5-4, 9-6.

England's Sam Tolchard, who had lost to Fiji's Rajnesh Prasad in his opening game in the men's singles, took home the gold medal with a 2-0 win over Malaysia's Izzat Shameer Dzulkeple, while the English women pair of Amy Pharaoh and Sian Honnor won gold in the women's double, also defeating Malaysia in the process.

Swimming

Cook Islands swimmer Jacob Story finished eighth in the men's 200m breaststroke final.

The 18-year-old Story clocked a time of two minutes and 14.48 seconds, finishing last of the finalists but swimming half a second faster than his qualification time.

The gold went to Filip Nowacki, claiming Jersey's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medal.

Also in the pool, Fiji's Anahira McCutcheon qualified for the semifinal of the women's 50m freestyle but not the final.

She clocked 25.45s in heat eight.

Nafanua Hamilton of Samoa finished fourth in her heat of the women's 200m individual medley, in a time of 2 minutes 25.37s.

PNG's Josh Tarere was fourth in the men's 50m butterfly heats with a time of 27.05s, while Fiji's Reuben Taylor finished fourth in his heat in 26.18s, and PNG's Thomas Chen eighth with a time of 26.68s in the same heat.

Tonga's Finau Ohuafi was fith in his pool in 25.60s, Johann Stickland of Samoa second in his heat in 24.91s, while Fiji's Hansel McCaig recorded a time of 25s flat to finish fifth in his heat.

Fijian David Young missed out of qualifying for the final rounds by .03 seconds, stopping the clock at 24.28s, just outside England's Matthew Hamilton, who qualified in 24.25s.

The PNG trio of Jhnayali Tokome-Garap, Roxanne Kirarock and Joanna Chen finished second to fourth in their heat of the women's 50m freestyle, while Tonga's Vaoahi Afu finished second in her heat.

But all four did not make it into the semifinals.

Meanwhile, the Malolo Swimming Club have congratulated their two swimmers representing Tonga, Vaoahi Afu and Finau Ohuafi, on their performances.

The club said Afu recorded a personal best time of 29.43s in the women's 50m freestyle, while finishing second in her heat.

Ohuafi, finished off fifth in his men's 50m Butterfly race.

"Finau delivered another strong performance in a quality international field, capping off a successful Commonwealth Games campaign that included an outstanding personal best in the men's 50m freestyle earlier in the competition," the club said in a statement.

"Congratulations to both athletes for proudly representing Tonga Aquatics, and Team Tonga on the Commonwealth Games stage.

"Your commitment, discipline, and determination continue to inspire the next generation of swimmers."

Both, like other Tongan swimmers, train in the open sea back home in Nuku'alofa as the country does not have a proper swimming pool where the swimmers can train and compete in.

Weightlifting

Nauru's Marcinary Cook finished ninth in the men's 88kg, with a total lift of 290kg. He lifted 130kg in the snatch and 160kg in the clean and jerk.

New Zealand's Olivia Shalom Selemaia, who has Pasifika heritage, did not qualify when she competed in the women's 69kg.

Samoa's Emmnauel Shalom Palota Ulimasao is set to compete in the men's 94kg on Friday morning.

Australia's Fiji-born lifter Eileen Floanna Maria Cikamatana is also scheduled to compete on Friday in the women's 86kg, in a field that also includes Samoa's Sefulu Seuao, Vanuatu's Ajah Pritchard Lolo and New Zealand Fijian Litia Sipola Nacagilevu.

The competition continues until 2 August.

Australia leads the medal tally with a total haul of 80 medals at the moment, which is made up of 35 gold, 18 silver and 27 bronze.

Canada has replaced England at number two with 13 gold, 10 silver and 12 bronze, while England sits third with 10 gold, 18 silver and 15 bronze.

New Zealand are eighth, with three gold, seven silver and three bronze to their name.

World.title: AFT Pharmaceuticals eyes 'multi-billion-dollar markets' for products still in development
World.content:
AFT Pharmaceuticals says its portfolio of projects opens the business up to multi-billion-dollar market opportunities.

The maker of Maxigesic said it had eight patented projects, 24 off-patent injectables and a range of other projects in the early stages of commercialisation.

Managing director Dr Hartley Atkinson said the company had a record of successfully developing and commercialising innovative medicines that delivered returns to shareholders.

He said the company had grown 17 percent year on year and expected to see that to continue as the projects under development hit the market, though it will take some time.

"It's just classic pharma. It takes time to do the clinical studies and that side of things, which is well underway.

"Really, these products can access potentially multi-billion-dollar markets, and that's really what we're aiming at. We're not trying to slow down; we're trying to ramp things up."

He said the research and development costs were funded from its retained earnings.

"We've always funded our R&D out of retained earnings that we make from selling other existing products, and the plan is that we will carry on and fund them in the same manner."

Atkinson said the company was also investing more into its market hubs.

"The one we're developing at the moment is the United States, which is the most complex one. But certainly the UK and Canada and South Africa, Singapore, Hong Kong, New Zealand, Australia are all well underway and well in progress."

Those hubs would look after smaller markets with standard licensing agreements.

World.title: David Tamihere faces two-month wait to find out if he will be retried
World.content:
David Tamihere will have to wait another two months to find out whether he will be retried over the 1989 murder of two Swedish backpackers in Coromandel.

Tamihere appeared at the High Court in Auckland on Wednesday on the charges he was first convicted of in 1990 but which were quashed by the Supreme Court in March.

The Supreme Court said it was up to Crown prosecutors to decide whether to hold a trial again.

Crown prosecutor Alysha McClintock told the High Court on Wednesday the Crown needed more time to decide whether it would try Tamihere again for the murder of Urban Höglin and Heidi Paakkonen.

The file had been with her office four less than four months, McClintock said. "There is an important process to go be gone through here to assess all the evidence."

Tamihere's lawyer James Carruthers said with a trial potentially a year away, the defence team was in the dark about the case.

"We're 13 months out from a trial date, dealing with events 37 years in the past," he said.

"We currently don't have any certainty about the case against Mr Tamihere, the evidence being relied on, the witnesses and exhibits being relied on."

They were dealing with events that happened 37 years ago and did not know what evidence or witnesses the prosecution was relying on.

Justice Mathew Downs agreed to the extension requested by the prosecution but gave it a deadline.

It must make a decision by the end of September, and Tamihere will appear again in October.

Crown solicitor Alysha McClintock at the High Court in Auckland on Wednesday. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

Justice Downs addressed Tamihere.

"Understandably you wish to know today whether that decision will take place," he said.

But giving the Crown more time was in the interests of justice, he said, as the granted the extra time, with the September deadline.

Arriving at court, Tamihere, who is now in his 70s, said he was feeling good but did not know what to expect.

He has been out of jail since 2010 when he was released on parole.

When the convictions were quashed, he was freed but is still facing the two murder charges.

Leaving court, Tamihere said he was not frustrated by having to wait longer - that it was "par for the course."

"I've gotten used to it - it's been 30-odd years or so," he said.

He was leading a normal life and "living quietly," he said.

The background

Höglin, 23, and Paakkonen, 21, were last seen in Thames in 1989.

Their disappearance and the subsequent trial was one of the country's highest profile crimes.

Many aspects remain a mystery.

Höglin's body was found in 1991, after Tamihere had been convicted, but Paakkonen's body has never been found.

At the time the couple went missing, Tamihere had been living in the bush in the Coromandel for about three years.

Much of the Crown's original case was circumstantial.

It included evidence that Tamihere had been seen driving around the Coromandel region in the couple's ute.

Tamihere admitted dumping or selling their possession but maintained he had never met them.

The Crown's case also relied on testimony from former inmate Robert Conchie Harris who said Tamihere told him he killed the Swedes. However Harris was convicted of perjury over evidence in 2017.

The appeals

Tamihere first appealed his convictions in 1992, after Höglin's body was found wearing a watch that a prosecution witness had initially said he had seen at Tamihere's house.

The body was also 70km away from where the Crown first suspected he had been killed.

That appeal was unsuccessful but the 2017 perjury conviction of Harris prompted a new round of appeals from Tamihere.

In 2024, the Court of Appeal declined to quash the convictions, saying despite the problems with some crown evidence, there was still enough to safely say Tamihere was guilty.

The Supreme Court released its decision in March that finally quashed the convictions.

David Tamihere at the High Court session on Wednesday. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

It said Harris's evidence meant the trial was fundamentally unfair, and that there had been a "radical recasting" of the crown case since the original trial.

That effectively meant the case had never truly been tested by a jury.

The court said it was possible a jury would still find Tamihere guilty, but that could only be decided in a retrial.

Timeline

April 1989 - Heidi Birgitta Paakkonen and Sven Urban Höglin are last seen in Thames.

December 1990 - Tamihere is convicted of murdering the couple and sentenced to life imprisonment.

1991 - Höglin's body is found near Whangamatā.

1992 - The Court of Appeal rejects Tamihere's appeal.

1994 - Tamihere is denied leave to appeal to the Privy Council.

1995 - Witness C - later revealed as Roberto Conchie Harris - swears an affidavit retracting his evidence.

1996 - Harris retracts his retraction.

2010 - Tamihere is released on parole.

2016 - A private prosecution alleges Harris lied at Tamihere's trial.

2017 - Harris is sentenced after being found guilty of perjury and not guilty of perverting the course of justice.

2017 - Harris appeals the perjury convictions and sentence and fights to keep his identity hidden.

2018 - Harris drops his appeal against the perjury convictions.

2018 - The High Court revokes suppression order for Witness B, another prison informant.

2020 - Justice Minister Andrew Little announces Tamihere's case is going back to the Court of Appeal after a Royal Prerogative of Mercy is granted.

November 2023 - The Court of Appeal hears Tamihere's case.

July 2024 - The Court of Appeal declines to quash Tamihere's convictions.

December 2024 - The Supreme Court grants leave for the case to be heard there.

August 2025 - The case heads to the Supreme Court sitting in Auckland.

World.title: Kiwi family fly to Queensland to join shot police officer
World.content:
An Australian police officer is recovering in hospital after being shot on the job.

Constable Jordan May was shot in the leg during a call-out in Yengarie on Queensland's Fraser Coast on Friday afternoon.

The ABC reported May was injured while police attempted to engage in with a man following reports of a disturbance.

An emergency declaration was made under the Public Safety Preservation Act following the shooting, the ABC reported.

In a post on the Queensland Police Union's Facebook page, May said he wanted to show his gratitude.

"I want to thank everyone involved in looking after me, from my colleagues in Maryborough to the amazing hospital staff here at the RBH.

"I'm on the mend and have the support of friends and family who have not left my side. I'm looking forward to getting back on my feet and I can't wait to get out of hospital."

7 News reported that May's family members had flown from New Zealand to be at his bedside.

The union's president Shane Prior and North Coast Regional rep Jake Lacy said they had been to the hospital and spent time with May and his brothers.

"The community will rightly focus on the officer who was shot but they should not overlook for a moment the incredible bravery of the police who risked everything to bring him out of that situation alive," the union said in its post.

"The QPU will be there to help Jordan through his recovery and hopefully back to duty."

7 News reported 45-year-old Adam O'Shea, the man accused of shooting May, was found dead at the property from a suspected self-inflicted gunshot wound.

World.title: Human Rights Commission warns Treaty clause overhaul increases legal uncertainty
World.content:
The Human Rights Commission (HRC) is urging the government to scrap its planned amendment of Te Tiriti o Waitangi clauses, warning it could create more confusion and deepen division.

In a submission published on Tuesday, the Commission said the government's proposals were "constitutionally regressive" and risked weakening Treaty protections.

In May, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the coalition would change or remove references to the Treaty of Waitangi in 19 pieces of legislation "in the interests of increasing certainty and supporting compliance".

But HRC Indigenous Governance Partner Dayle Takitimu said it would have the opposite effect.

Human Rights Commission Indigenous Governance Partner Dayle Takitimu. Te Kāhui Tika Tangata Human Rights Commission

"The government said it wants clarity, but many Māori, legal experts, the Waitangi Tribunal, the Human Rights Commission, and international bodies say the review risks doing the opposite: weakening protections, reducing accountability, and increasing conflict.

"Achieving clarity - if that is the aim of the exercise - doesn't require watering down obligations to the bare minimum.

"Certainty and clarity are better achieved by following agreed human rights standards which support honouring treaties and respecting Indigenous peoples' human rights."

The Commission concluded that the government's plan downgraded Te Tiriti obligations and was "likely to increase, not reduce, uncertainty and litigation risk."

The changes risked intensifying racial tension and harming Crown-Māori relations, it said.

It also criticised the review, which recommended the changes, saying Māori had not been properly consulted throughout.

The review was secured by New Zealand First during coalition negotiations with National after the last election.

The Commission called on the government to abandon its changes and instead work with Māori on any replacement.

"Te Tiriti is not a side issue or a drafting inconvenience; it is part of the constitutional and human rights foundation of Aotearoa," Takitimu said.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

In a statement, Goldsmith said the coalition did not agree or accept that its actions amount to "lowering the threshold of Treaty obligations".

In May, the government announced it would remove references to the Treaty principles in seven pieces of legislation.

Another 10 would be watered down, and two made "more specific".

At the time, Goldsmith said iwi would be consulted, and all New Zealanders could have their say through the select committee process.

"Over the last 30 or 40 years, Parliament has made all sorts of references to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. Sometimes it's 'honour', or 'have regard to', or 'give effect to', or 'take into account'," Goldsmith said.

World.title: NZ track cyclist Nick Kergozou in hospital, ruled out of Commonwealth Games
World.content:
New Zealand track cyclist Nick Kergozou has been hospitalised in Glasgow and will miss out on competing at his third Commonwealth Games.

The endurance rider from Invercargill sustained a back injury during training.

The 30-year-old is in hospital in a stable condition and is being supported by his family. He is expected to make a full recovery.

Fellow track cyclist, Keegan Hornblow, will replace him in the Men's Pursuit event.

Hornblow is at his first Games.

New Zealand team chef de mission, Nigel Avery, expressed the team's sympathy for Kergozou.

"We know this is a hugely disappointing outcome for Nick after all his hard work in getting to the Games.

"The New Zealand team is right behind him as he now focuses on recovery and we look forward to seeing him back in competition when he's ready."

World.title: FIFA boss Infantino unveils $20b plan to sell World Cup to Kushner consortium
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino's plan to create a $US20 billion ($AUD28.68 billion) company running the World Cup with private investors, including the Kushner family, has been attacked by the European football body, UEFA.

"It is not FIFA's to sell," UEFA said in a statement. "None of us are the owners of football."

Infantino's plans to form a commercial subsidiary, called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup, were first reported by The Times of London.

Players and fans made the World Cup a success, but the politics shouldn't be forgotten The biggest ever World Cup brought diverse communities together and galvanised its non-traditional footballing co-hosts, but the concerns raised from the start have not disappeared in the positive afterglow.

FIFA said in a statement FFE would raise up to $4.2 billion later this year to help fund development programs "based on an initial equity valuation of $20 billion by carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests."

FIFA is working with JP Morgan while intended investors include Thrive Eternal launched by Joshua Kushner, whose brother Jared Kushner is a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.

The men's World Cup that finished this month only deepened the political and personal ties between Trump and Infantino, and fuelled concerns about those ties, including from UEFA.

"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially," UEFA said, responding to the reports of selling stakes in FIFA competitions.

FIFA is a Swiss-based not-for-profit association of its 211 national member federations worldwide.

The brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner (pictured), is among the potential World Cup investors. (Reuters: Kent Nishimura)

Those members must approve any plan and would get the chance "to access up to $20 million in one-off capital," FIFA said.

"This is about the democratisation of football worldwide," Infantino said in a FIFA statement, which added that "a consultation process has begun".

UEFA, however, said it took reports of the project "extremely seriously. So should every national Football Association".

"This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross," said UEFA, which comprises 55 of the FIFA members.

FIFA's $20M offer to member federations

FIFA boss Gianni Infantino (pictured) has promised to "unleash the commercial potential" of the World Cup. (Getty Images)

The outline of Tuesday's surprise announcement was, FIFA said, detailed by Infantino to members who met in Manhattan on July 18 ahead of the World Cup final. There, Infantino promised to "unleash the commercial potential and opportunity that FIFA has".

FIFA's statement about its proposed project led on how much money each of its 211 members could get through 2038 in the "FIFA Fast-Forward Program."

Instead of the promised $8 million each in development funds through the 2027-30 World Cup commercial cycle, it would be $20 million, then $22 million and $24 million in the following cycles.

FIFA banked record World Cup income of about $12 billion from the 2026 tournament, which had unprecedentedly high prices for tickets and hospitality across the US, Canada and Mexico.

World Cup winners Spain will be one of six nations hosting matches at the 2030 World Cup.

It already was unclear how that money could be matched from Spain, Portugal and Morocco co-hosting the 2030 men's edition.

Member federations could choose if they wanted to take part in the new financial opportunities, FIFA said.

"FIFA would retain sole control of FFE and exclusive authority over football governance, competitions, match calendar, and all regulatory and sporting decisions," the soccer body said.

FIFA's integrity standards were called into question during the World Cup, including by team coaches, Norway's soccer federation and a top European public body, the Council of Europe.

FIFA's previous attempt to privatise assets

Infantino has built stronger ties with Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (pictured) throughout his tenure as FIFA boss. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

The project announced is the second time in Infantino's increasingly controversial 11-year presidency he has tried to push through a multi-billion-dollar deal with private backers.

In 2018, Infantino proposed a secretive $25 billion offer over 12 years with SoftBank of Japan to create new global competitions, including an expanded men's Club World Cup, seemingly backed by Saudi Arabian money.

That ultimately failed after meeting fierce resistance from UEFA, which saw threats to its prize assets: the Champions League and the European Championship.

Infantino still built closer ties to Saudi soccer and the kingdom's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman. Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 World Cup and largely funded the revamped men's Club World Cup hosted in the US last year.

What does this mean for Infantino's future?

The financial success of the just-ended World Cup has made it likely that Infantino will be re-elected next year unopposed for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

At his re-election by acclaim in 2023 in Rwanda, Infantino suggested any CEO delivering similar financial results would be kept in the job forever.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Speculation has swirled for years that Infantino might want a different global role in soccer beyond his FIFA presidency, which is due to end when he is 61.

The Times reported on Tuesday that a CEO-like commissioner role of the new FFE operation could be created for Infantino.

"This has never been discussed," FIFA said in a statement on Wednesday (AEST). "However, the FIFA president and the FIFA administration will and must have leading roles in this entity — if approved."

There was no timetable suggested for debate and decisions by FIFA, its ruling Council chaired by Infantino, and the 211 members.

FIFA is scheduled to hold an online congress on November 23 to confirm hosts of the Women's World Cup editions in 2031 and 2035.

AP

World.title: Quick hits: Record beaten five times in 10 minutes, pool haka thrills
World.content:
New Zealand swimmers pay tribute to a victorious teammate by performing the haka, a Pakistani lawn bowler fits in some work shifts and a weightlifting record falls a staggering five times.

Here are the quick hits from day five of the Commonwealth Games.

1. 'Super proud' New Zealanders

Lewis Clareburt and his New Zealand teammates perform the haka after his victory. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

New Zealand swimmer Lewis Clareburt received a double honour after winning the men's 400-metre individual medley final.

Aside from being awarded the gold medal, Clareburt was the recipient of a haka proudly performed by his New Zealand teammates.

The Tollcross International Swimming Centre crowd also appreciated the gesture.

"People really respect it [the haka] around the world and it makes me super proud to be a Kiwi," Clareburt told reporters.

The crowd erupted when the New Zealanders performed the haka. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Clareburt won the men's 200m butterfly earlier in the swimming program.

2. Lawn bowler works double shift

Mohammed Ayub Qureshi competing in the lawn bowls. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

No-one can accuse lawn bowler Mohammed Ayub Qureshi of not being a multitasker.

Qureshi competed for Pakistan in the men's singles event while also working at his restaurant in Glasgow.

Last Friday afternoon local time, he faced off against Scotland's Jason Banks before heading to the restaurant to work the evening rush.

Showing what the Commonwealth Games are all about, Qureshi invited Banks to drop by for a meal after the Scot sealed victory.

Loading Instagram content

"I was too scared before I played him in case he spiced up my food too much," Banks said.

It is the second time Qureshi has represented Pakistan at the Commonwealth Games in the city that has been his home for more than 50 years.

3. Record falls again and again

Hafizuddin Bin Roslin Muhammad ended a run of record-breaking lifts. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

What could possibly be better than seeing the Commonwealth record broken at a Commonwealth Games?

Well, seeing the same one be beaten five times in the space of 10 minutes or so would probably do it.

That is exactly what happened in the men's 88-kilogram weightlifting competition, with Cameron McTaggart, Braydon Kennedy and Hafizuddin Bin Roslin Muhammad all achieving new standards in rapid succession.

New Zealander McTaggart started things off with a 154kg lift.

That was swiftly bettered by Canada's Kennedy, who lifted 155kg with his first attempt.

McTaggart tried to better that, but missed at 157kg with his final snatch.

Then Malaysian lifter Muhammad entered the chat.

Neither he nor Kennedy could get 160kg up on their first attempts at the weight, but Muhammad did so on his second.

Then Kennedy threw up 161kg, so Muhammad added another kilo for the newest and final record of 162kg.

4. Aussies snare two golds in an hour

Breanna Scott won gold on the beam. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

Breanna Scott already had a gold medal from this Commonwealth Games when she stepped out onto the balance beam on Tuesday.

After she flipped off it at the end of her routine, she had a second.

"It's pretty overwhelming to be honest, none of it has sunk in yet," she told Channel Seven after the final.

"The team gold was such a special medal for all of us, and that was really the main goal coming into this.

"All of us in finals now getting these extra little medals is just topping it off."

She, and the rest of the Australian team, barely had time to let it, to be fair.

Jesse Moore delivered a superb routine to secure gold. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

An hour or so later, Australia had a second gold of the session.

Jesse Moore broke his duck to claim a sensational gold on the parallel bars.

His was Australia's ninth gymnastics medal of these Games.

5. Athlete on track twice in 34 minutes

Howard Tapuaiga Siila competing in the men's 800m heats. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Howard Tapuaiga Siila knew he had a full schedule on his hands when he arrived at the Scotstoun Stadium on day five.

The Tuvalu athlete was entered in both the men's 400m and 800m heats, which is a daunting task at the best of times.

But for Siila, there was only 34 minutes between the start of each race.

He took off in his 800m heat at 11:33am local time, finishing eighth in 2:32.38.

Siila was back on the track for the 400m at 12:07pm, finishing eighth via a time of 55.96.

Both were season-best times.

Competing in both events was planned, but there was one hitch.

"When I decided to enter the races we weren't sure of the scheduling," Siila told reporters in the mixed zone.

World.title: 'Biggest cheat in cricket history': Clicking scandal causes outrage
World.content:
An amateur cricket match in England has become a viral sensation after allegations of cheating were shared on social media.

A video, which claims to show a fielder clicking his fingers to imitate the sound of a bat connecting with the ball before a player is called out, has been viewed millions of times on X.

The poster of the video described it as "about the worst case of cheating I've ever seen in cricket".

Loading Instagram content

"First slip clicks his fingers to imitate an edge, bat nowhere near it and given out," the post read.

The video of a match involving North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League team Saltburn has been greeted with outrage online and generated headlines around the world.

TV presenter Piers Morgan weighed in, describing the player involved as the "biggest cheat in cricket history" and wondered how many batters' days "has he ruined?"

The league said in a statement on X that it had received a formal complaint regarding a game on Saturday, but did not reveal which teams were involved. However, it is understood the investigation is focused on the clicking.

"A full investigation has been initiated and until such time as the formal processes are complete no further comment will be made," it said.

There was no immediate response when The Associated Press contacted the league and Saltburn for comment.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: 'The Aussies are on fire' on a night where that should've been impossible
World.content:
In the land of lochs, the announcer at Scotstoun Stadium couldn't figure out the first half of his name, but Lachlan Kennedy's performance on a sodden night in Glasgow ensured Australia will never forget it.

The weather on Tuesday night couldn't have been much more Scottish.

It was teeming basically all night, to the point the women's high jump final was halted for 45 minutes and the women's hammer throw probably should have been.

There were only two brief windows when the rain turned from a downpour to a drizzle, and it just so happened to be the moments "Lacklan" Kennedy was welcomed to the newly laid blue track.

The support crew was working overtime to make things vaguely manageable. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

It sounds like the sort of apocryphal tale told about Don Bradman in an era before the footage existed to prove your grandad was lying to you.

But it really happened.

To be clear, it wasn't dry, but no wetter than the night in March when he beat rising superstar Gout Gout in the 200m at the Maurie Plant Meet.

That established him once again as not just a fast runner, but a man capable of performing under the most intense pressure. A man plying his trade against a boy still figuring his out.

And Kennedy did it again on the biggest stage, winning Australia's first men's 100 metres medal at the Commonwealth Games with silver behind Cameroon's Emmanuel Eseme on the second night of an athletics program that has been backed to deliver so much for Australia.

After not running a heat, Lachie Kennedy came straight out and made a statement. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"It's all about rising to the occasion. I'm a big believer in you've got to bring your best when it matters most," Kennedy said.

"That's what we've been training for all season. We've all been planning for this competition here and my coach has clearly outdone himself."

It seems extreme to say he obliterated the national record of Patrick Johnson by taking it from 9.93 down to 9.85, but 0.08 of a second means something different to folks like Kennedy than it does us mere mortals.

In the 58 years since Jim Hines broke the 10-second barrier in the 100 metres, only 232 more have people dipped into single digits.

Aussie sprinters storm to 100m medals Lachlan Kennedy and Torrie Lewis set new national records in claiming 100m medals, while a host of Australians take gold across athletics and swimming.

The margins are so fine in the jewel in the athletics crown that there have been 1,550 legal runs in 0.42 of a second between 10 flat and Usain Bolt's world record of 9.58.

Most are from the United States, Jamaica and spread across Africa, and just two from Australia, with Kennedy the only one since 2003.

Kennedy stands alone in some respects, but is proud to be part of a pack pushing each other towards greatness.

Gout's rise trained a spotlight on the team, whose performances with that attention have proved it warranted.

"Aussie track is clearly in the best spot it's ever been, our team is so strong … We're in a real golden age," Kennedy said.

That was clearly evident as Kennedy — after running alongside compatriot Eddie Nketia, who finished sixth in the final after laying down a PB of 10.03 in the semis — was still talking to the media in the mixed zone when Torrie Lewis won bronze in the women's final.

Loading...

"The Aussies are on fire," Kennedy said as he cheered Lewis on to the team's third of six medals on the night.

Lewis also set a new national record, but rather than breaking a record that had stood for 23 years, hers had barely stood for 23 hours.

Lewis's 10.99 in the women's final came after her 11 flat in the semi, which lowered her own record of 11.04 from a week prior.

All in an event she wasn't even sure she wanted to compete in.

Torrie Lewis followed Lachie Kennedy into the history books. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Lewis is a beneficiary of the controversial automatic qualifiers into the semis of her pet 200m event, where she'll be hoping for more silver (or better) ware before the relays kick off in the ultimate representation of what this team can do.

"I have a day off tomorrow, luckily with the bye, then Thursday see how I pull up for the semifinal and hopefully I can do something special there as well," she said.

Lewis and Kennedy were the headlines due to Australia's historic lack of truly exceptional flat sprint talent since the days of Raelene Boyle.

We've jumped at a few false dawns and sometimes athletes have been unable to live up to those expectations, while field sensations like Steve Hooker, Nina Kennedy, Eleanor Patterson, Matt Denny, Nicola Olyslagers and a cavalcade of women's javelin chuckers have been consistently brilliant.

The anachronisms of the Commonwealth The Commonwealth Games continues to roll on despite calls to decolonise our lives, with Scotland of all places a strange venue to stage two celebrations of the British Empire over the past 12 years.

They were again on Tuesday night: Patterson and Olyslagers went 1-2 to continue their impossibly consistent excellence in the high jump, and 22-year-old Lara Roberts broke through for her first major international medal.

Patterson said it was "phenomenal" to see the runners joining the jumpers and throwers in contention for medals.

"I was out there and you get to have a lay of the land and you understand what's going on," she said.

"I definitely took in my stride that there was a lot of Aussies there and seeing how well everyone was doing.

"Athletics in Australia, it's going off. I want the whole of Australia to know that we're taking it to the world, we're representing Australia very well and we're not bad, we're pretty bloody good."

Back on the track Ky Robinson kicked off the stunning hour and a half with victory in the 10,000m.

Australian athletics has had a number of these special nights of late, so much so that it risks becoming expected.

Australians have become so used to success in the pool that we have become somewhat blasé about the brilliance of our aquatic elite, but for now, on relatively dry land in Scotstoun there really is no other word for it.

That was special.

World.title: 'My time': Young gun Southam dethrones Chalmers in 100m final
World.content:
Kyle Chalmers has been dethroned as the Commonwealth Games 100m freestyle king in Glasgow, the "Big Tuna" having been reeled in by young friend and rival Flynn Southam in a landmark changing-of-the-guard moment.

With a potential record-breaking 10th Commonwealth gold in his sights, Chalmers had his proud record of never having been beaten by an Australian in major international competition dismantled by 21-year-old Southam in the Tollcross pool.

Southam's glory, fuelled by indignation at how he'd been somewhat dismissed as just a relay workhorse, set the tone for yet another medal-laden session of Dolphins' domination on the penultimate night of the program.

Jenna Forrester sealed her own golden treble in a remarkable breakthrough meet, adding a thrilling 200m individual medley triumph to the surprise 200m backstroke and 400m IM titles she'd already annexed.

And the night kicked off with 22-year-old Queenslander Kirralee Hayes taking the para gold medal in the 50m freestyle S13 final, and another Australian, Jenna Jones, taking bronze.

But Southam's win took pride of place, the young Fremantle-born, NSW-raised prospect finally fulfilling his potential as the most likely successor to "King Kyle", clocking a searing 47.13 seconds to bronze medallist Chalmers' 47.74. The pair were split by Welshman Matt Richards (47.64).

"Me and Kyle have utmost respect for one another. But it's my time to shine, and I know that," boomed Southam.

"I've been due for this, and this is my breakout meet. Four years ago, I came here as a little boy — but now I'm a man, and I belong here."

Flynn Southam says the Commonwealth Games are his breakout meet after winning gold in the men's 100m freestyle. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

For Chalmers, though, cheered on by his wife, Norwegian international swimmer Ingeborg Loyning and baby daughter Astrid, there was a mixture of frustration that he couldn't land the 10th gold and 12th medal that would have taken him past the great Ian Thorpe as Australia's most successful men's swimmer ever at the Games.

Port Lincoln's 28-year-old maestro is likely to still have a chance, though, in the 50m butterfly final on the final day of competition in what could be his final appearance at the Games.

Admitting that he knew the passing-of-the-baton moment was inevitably coming at some point soon, Chalmers had hoped to delay it but was happy to tip his hat to the young gun after being the first to congratulate him.

"I'm completely fine with it," Chalmers said.

"I'd rather be in the race for that to happen than be retired and seeing them swim faster than maybe what… well, he hasn't quite got me just yet, but it's very close to what my best ever was.

"When we were able to sit in the medal presentation, I really said, 'You know, this is your moment. I'm so proud of you, enjoy your moment, enjoy singing the anthem.'

"I truly am so proud of him."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Southam had signalled his intentions at the start of the week when he clocked a sizzling lead-off relay leg of 47.09, which was just a hundredth of a second slower than Chalmers' all-time best and quicker than the South Australian star's 2026 best by half a second.

"It's pretty incredible. I had a lot of people doubting me and saying my success only comes from relays, and that's really pissed me off and motivated me to be the best in the world," said Southam.

"Doubt always comes up, I was doubting myself as I was walking out, but it's about being able to turn that voice down and believing in yourself.

"I have Australia on my cap, I don't have just my name, so it's bigger than me."

Another medal came Australia's way with William Petric taking silver in the 400m individual medley behind New Zealand's double champion Lewis Clareburt.

AAP

World.title: 'Absolutely wild': Australian gymnasts top off Games with two more golds
World.content:
Breanna Scott and Jesse Moore have added to Australia's gold medal bonanza at the Commonwealth Games, taking out individual apparatus titles to finish their campaign in Glasgow.

Just minutes after Scott nailed a flashy balance beam routine to take out the title on her speciality apparatus, Moore hit every mark on the parallel bars to win another gold for Australia at Glasgow International Arena.

Scott scored 13.933 points for her routine, beating Singapore's Amanda Yap (13.233) and Lia-Monica Fontaine (13.00) of Canada.

Australian teammate and defending 2022 Birmingham champion Kate McDonald was last in eighth (12.166) after recovering from near-falls.

"[Balance beam] is definitely my favourite when it's going well," Scott said.

"It's kind of crazy, to be honest. It definitely hasn't sunk in yet.

"The last three days have just been absolutely wild.

"The team gold was such a special medal for all of us, and that was really the main goal coming into this.

"All of us in finals now getting these extra little medals is just topping it off."

Scott wrapped up in Glasgow by winning her third medal and second gold medal.

She had contributed to Australia's dominant team all-around victory, before claiming silver in the women's individual all-around.

Backing up Scott, Moore found redemption on the parallel bars after missing the podium for the rings and pommel horse events.

Jesse Moore won his third gymnastics medal in Glasgow, winning gold in the men's parallel bars. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Australia's leading men's gymnast heading to Glasgow, Moore scored 14.000 points to pip Cypriot veteran Marios Georgiou (13.800 points) and Canada's Felix Dolci (13.300).

Scott and Moore's titles meant Australia medalled on every day of the five-day gymnastics competition in Glasgow.

Australia won nine medals, including four gold, behind Canada with 16 medals, seven of which were gold.

Moore said the gold medal was a weight off his shoulders.

"There's definitely been a bit of pressure building into these Commies with medal chances," Moore said.

"I knew I had one last crack to really have a go.

"This routine, I've done for years, so I could really trust myself and really go for it.

"I'm pretty stoked to get the gold."

The 23-year-old will leave the Games with three medals, having won a team bronze and an individual all-around bronze.

McDonald missed out on adding to her individual uneven bars gold and finished sixth in the floor routine final, ahead of 2022 Birmingham breakout star Georgia Godwin in seventh.

James Hardy settled for a fifth-placed finish on vault after claiming floor and rings bronze the day before, while 19-year-old Ritam Malik finished sixth on the parallel bars.

Australia's gymnastics medals

Gold (4): balance beam, uneven bars, team all-around (all women), parallel bars (men)

Silver (1): all-around (women)

Bronze (4): floor, rings, all-around, team all-around (all men)

AAP

World.title: 'Very bad look': Brisbane defender given three-game ban
World.content:
Brisbane defender Ty Gallop has been suspended for three games for a serious misconduct act he admits is a "very bad look".

Gallop pleaded guilty at the AFL Tribunal on Tuesday night for what he described as retaliation on Mitch Georgiades after the Port Adelaide forward grabbed his broken thumb.

The 20-year-old had tackled Georgiades to the ground during Sunday's clash in Brisbane and, after the ball left the area, shoved the Port attacker face-first into the turf.

Gallop played the match with strapping on a broken right thumb.

"Mitch has grabbed my thumb as I have gone to stand up," Gallop said, adding Georgiades' action was intentional.

But Gallop expressed remorse for retaliating, saying he had phoned Georgiades to apologise.

"Looking back now and watching the footage, I understand that the retaliation to what happened wasn't fair," he said.

"I have gone out of my way to push him down, which I am sorry for and I do regret. I'd like to have that time over again.

"It's a very bad look and there's no room for it in footy."

Gallop said his retaliation was an "immediate reaction".

"I have grabbed the back of his jersey and pushed him back into the ground," he said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I think I play a hard brand of footy but I play a very fair brand of footy as well … it was purely out of retaliation."

Under questioning from the AFL's counsel Nick Pane, Gallop agreed his act was totally unreasonable and unacceptable.

Pane asked the tribunal for a three-game suspension.

"Georgiades' head made forceful contact with the ground," Pane said. "The action had significant potential to cause serious injury."

The Port spearhead wasn't hurt in the incident.

Gallop's counsel Adrian Anderson said the 23-gamer had "lashed out" but argued for a two-match ban.

"There is a context here," Anderson said.

"It's different where someone has a broken thumb and it's grabbed and they react in the heat of the moment."

After hearing just over one hour of evidence, tribunal chairman Jeff Gleeson KC and members Darren Gaspar and Scott Stevens returned a verdict some 50 minutes later.

AFL Saturday live North Melbourne survives a nervy finish to break a decade-long drought against Essendon as star ruckman Tristan Xerri rubs blood on Andrew McGrath's face in a heated exchange.

Gleeson said the tribunal gave no weight in its deliberations to Gallop's thumb being grabbed before his misconduct.

"The vision of the serious misconduct is startling in the degree to which it is unsportsmanlike," he said.

Gallop is the sixth AFL player suspended on a serious misconduct charge and the second this season, following North Melbourne ruckman Tristan Xerri's three-game ban for wiping blood onto the face of Essendon captain Andrew McGrath in a match in March.

Gallop will now miss Brisbane's games against Carlton, Hawthorn and Gold Coast, and will not be available until the round 24 games against Collingwood at the MCG.

AAP/ABC

World.title: National records tumble as Australia's athletics team stuns in Glasgow
World.content:
Eleanor Patterson won her second Commonwealth Games gold medal in the women's high jump on day five in Glasgow, leading home an Australian 1-2 on another stunning day for Australia.

Patterson was one of nine Australian gold medal performances, taking the team to 35 gold medals for the Games so far.

Twelve years after first triumphing in Glasgow as a teenager, Patterson equalled the Games record of 1.96m in a rain-interrupted final.

She managed the height with her third and last attempt before unsuccessfully attempting a new Games mark of 2m.

Patterson edged out Australian teammate and world champion, Nicola Olyslagers (1.93m).

Olyslagers failed with her three attempts at 1.96m and settled for silver.

On a big night at the main stadium, Lachie Kennedy and Torrie Lewis both missed out on gold, but broke 100m national records while capturing medals.

Kennedy ended Australia's agonising wait for a men's Commonwealth Games 100m medal by taking silver.

Lachlan Kennedy took time off the Australian national 100m record with a silver medal on night five in Glasgow. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Australia's fastest man ran a personal best 9.85 seconds, beating Patrick Johnson's mark of 9.93 set in May 2003. It took a Games record to beat Kennedy, with Cameroon's Emmanuel Eseme stopping the clock at 9.83.

Nigeria's Kayinsola Ajayi (9.90) was third, with Australian Eddie Nketia (10.06) back in sixth.

Lewis broke her own 100m national record in the semi-finals then broke it again in the final, finishing third in 10.99.

New Zealander Zoe Hobbs (10.93) won gold ahead of England's Amy Hunt (10.98).

Kennedy's silver was Australia's first medal in the men's 100m since 1962, when Michael Cleary took bronze.

Kennedy broke 10 seconds and lowered his personal best twice on the night, including a 9.94 in his semi, despite wet and windy conditions.

"It's all about rising to the occasion," Kennedy said after a wet and windy night.

"I'm a big believer in you've got to bring your best when it matters most. That's what we've been training for all season.

"To be able to come out here in those conditions, against a field like that, and to be able to run a time like that just goes to show how much faith I have in my team and all the people supporting me back home."

There was also joy for Ky Robinson, who completed an unprecedented 10,000m double for Australia when he finished strongly to hold off several rivals and claim gold.

Robinson won in 27:48.93 ahead of India's Gulveer Singh and Isle of Man's David Mullarkey.

Ky Robinson completed an Australian double in the 10,000m events, winning the men's race on night five. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

His triumph followed Rose Davies becoming the first Australian woman to win the event at the Commonwealth Games.

In the pool, Lani Pallister set a new Commonwealth Games record in winning her third gold of the meet.

Pallister won the 800m freestyle in a time of 8:11:12, beating New Zealand's Erika Fairweather.

Australia's Molly Walker took the bronze.

Pallister has now won the freestyle middle and distance triple — the 400, 800 and 1,500m freestyle.

In all, Australia won a total of five gold medals in the night session at Tollcross Swimming Centre.

In artistic gymnastics, Australia finished with two more gold, as Breanna Scott won the women's balance beam and Jesse Moore took out the men's parallel bars title.

Catch up on all the action from day five of the Games in our blog below.

AAP/ABC
